<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:groups}
For a once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy $\varphi$, set $A_\mp=\operatorname{coker}(\varphi\mp1)$, so that $|A_\mp|=|\operatorname{tr}\varphi\mp2|$ since
$\det(\varphi\mp1)=2\mp\operatorname{tr}\varphi$. For $\varphi=L^aR^b=\begin{psmallmatrix}1+ab&a\\b&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ one has $\operatorname{tr}\varphi=ab+2$ and
\[
A_-\cong\mathbb{Z}_g\times\mathbb{Z}_{ab/g},\qquad g=\gcd(a,b).
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
$\varphi-1=\begin{psmallmatrix}ab&a\\b&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ has determinant $-ab$, and the greatest common divisor of its entries is $g$; these
are the product and the first of its two invariant factors.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:js}
Jeong--Sohn \cite{JS26} do not introduce $A_\pm$ or a linking form; they label vacua as their ansatz produces them, for $n=2$ by $\alpha_i$ (one per gauge node)
with spins $e^{2\pi i(\alpha_1^2/k_1+\alpha_2^2/k_2)}$, and by $\beta$ on a cyclic group. For $n=2$ with $k_1,k_2$ odd they also propose the full $S$ and $T$ \cite[(4.27)--(4.32)]{JS26}, checked
against the $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ relations, a positive row and integrality of the Verlinde coefficients. For $\varphi=ST^{k_1}ST^{k_2}$ one has
$\operatorname{coker}(1+\varphi)\cong\mathbb{Z}_{k_1}\times\mathbb{Z}_{k_2}$ and, for $k_1,k_2$ odd, $\operatorname{coker}(1-\varphi)$ cyclic of order $|k_1k_2-4|$, so for $n=2$ the labels by gauge node
\emph{are} the invariant groups. At $\vec k=(m,-m)$ the $\alpha$-form is $(\alpha_1^2-\alpha_2^2)/m$ on $\operatorname{coker}(1+\varphi)$, which is $A_-$ of $L^mR^m$ by the sign in
Section~\ref{sub:diagonal}. This is the hyperbolic form of Proposition~\ref{prop:linking}. For $n\ge3$ Jeong--Sohn label the vacua by $\mathbb{Z}^n/K_\pm[\vec k]$, with $K_\pm[\vec k]$ the cyclic tridiagonal matrix of \cite[(A.13)--(A.14)]{JS26}, $\det K_\pm[\vec k]=\operatorname{tr}\varphi\mp2(-1)^n$, and spins from the quadratic phase in \cite[(A.16)]{JS26}.
A computation for $n=3,4$ and $k_i\in\{\pm3,\pm5,7\}$ ($1500$ cases) gives $\operatorname{coker} K_\pm[\vec k]\cong\operatorname{coker}\bigl(1\mp(-1)^n\varphi\bigr)$ in every case. So their labels are the groups $A_\mp$, up to the parity sign $(-1)^n$.
What is new here is the linking form on $A_\mp$ for every word, defined without a presentation, and the completeness of the classes for words without a singleton run (Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:linking}
For every hyperbolic $\varphi\in SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ the formula $b(x,y)=x\wedge(1-\varphi)^{-1}y\bmod\mathbb{Z}$, with $x\wedge y=x_1y_2-x_2y_1$ the determinant pairing on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ representatives of classes of $A_-=\operatorname{coker}(1-\varphi)$ (a quotient of $\mathbb{Z}^2$, so with at most two generators), is a well-defined, symmetric and non-degenerate $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$-valued pairing on $A_-$. For $\varphi=L^mR^m$ with $m$ odd,
$A_-\cong\mathbb{Z}_m^2$ on the images of $e_1,e_2$ and
\[
b(x,y)=\frac{x_2y_2-x_1y_1}{m};
\]
this form is hyperbolic, and its quadratic refinement $q^{\mathrm{lk}}(x)=2^{-1}b(x,x)$, with $2^{-1}$ the inverse of $2$ modulo $m$, has Gauss sum
\[
\sum_{x\in A_-}e^{2\pi iq^{\mathrm{lk}}(x)}=+m .
\]
The same construction with $1+\varphi$ gives a symmetric linking form $b_+(x,y)=x\wedge(1+\varphi)^{-1}y$ on $A_+$, with refinement
$q^{\mathrm{lk}}(x)=2^{-1}b_+(x,x)$ when $N_+$ is odd. For $\varphi=L^mR^m$ with $m$ odd, $A_+\cong\mathbb{Z}_\mu$, $\mu=m^2+4$, on the image of $e_1$, with
$q^{\mathrm{lk}}(h)=sh^2/\mu$, $s\equiv-2^{-1}m\pmod\mu$, and Gauss sum $-\sqrt\mu$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ the identity $M^{\mathsf T}J=J\operatorname{adj}M$ for
$2\times2$ matrices ($J$ the matrix of $\wedge$) turns $b(x,y)-b(y,x)$ into
$x\wedge\bigl[(1-\varphi)^{-1}+(1-\varphi)/\det(1-\varphi)\bigr]y$; since $A+\operatorname{adj}A=(\operatorname{tr} A)\mathbf1$ and $\operatorname{tr}(1-\varphi)=\det(1-\varphi)$
on $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$, the bracket is $\mathbf1$ and the difference is $x\wedge y\in\mathbb{Z}$, so $b$ is symmetric modulo $\mathbb{Z}$. It depends only on the class of $y$, since
$b(x,(1-\varphi)y')=x\wedge y'\in\mathbb{Z}$, and by symmetry only on the class of $x$. It is nondegenerate: write $M=1-\varphi$; since $x\wedge M^{-1}y=(Mx)\wedge y/\det M$, if $b(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}$
for all $y$ then $Mx\in(\det M)\mathbb{Z}^2$, so $x\in\operatorname{adj}(M)\mathbb{Z}^2=(1-\varphi^{-1})\mathbb{Z}^2=(1-\varphi)\mathbb{Z}^2$, that is $x=0$ in $A_-$. For
$L^mR^m=\begin{psmallmatrix}m^2+1&m\\m&1\end{psmallmatrix}$, $(1-\varphi)^{-1}=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-1/m\\-1/m&1\end{psmallmatrix}$, giving
$b=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)/m$ modulo integers; and $x_2^2-x_1^2=(x_2-x_1)(x_2+x_1)$ is a hyperbolic plane over $\mathbb{Z}_m$, whose Gauss sum is $+m$.

For $A_+$ the same argument applies, since $\operatorname{tr}(1+\varphi)=\det(1+\varphi)$ and $\operatorname{adj}(1+\varphi)=\varphi^{-1}(1+\varphi)$. For $L^mR^m$ the entries of
$1+\varphi=\begin{psmallmatrix}m^2+2&m\\m&2\end{psmallmatrix}$ have greatest common divisor $1$, so $A_+$ is cyclic of order $\mu$; and
$(1+\varphi)^{-1}e_1=\mu^{-1}(2,-m)^{\mathsf T}$ has exact denominator $\mu$, so $e_1$ generates, with $b_+(e_1,e_1)=-m/\mu$. As $\mu\equiv1\pmod4$, the
Gauss sum of $sh^2/\mu$ is $(s/\mu)\sqrt\mu$, and $(s/\mu)=(-2/\mu)(m/\mu)=-1$, because $\mu\equiv5\pmod8$ and $(m/\mu)=(\mu/m)=(4/m)=1$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:lktop}
Up to sign, $b$ is the torsion linking form of the mapping torus $M_\varphi$ of $\varphi$ on the once-punctured torus $\Sigma$. Here
$H_1(M_\varphi)=\mathbb{Z}\oplus\operatorname{coker}(\varphi-1)$, the torsion being carried by curves in a fibre. For linking forms in general see
\cite{CFH16}. Let $x,y\in H_1(\Sigma)=\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $N=|\det(\varphi-1)|$, and put $w=N(\varphi-1)^{-1}x\in\mathbb{Z}^2$.
The cylinder swept by $w$ from the fibre at time $0$ to the fibre at time $1$ has boundary $\varphi(w)-w=Nx$. So it is a $2$-chain $S$
with $\partial S=Nx$. A curve representing $y$ in the fibre at time $\tfrac12$ meets $S$ in the intersection points of $w$ and $y$ in
$\Sigma$. Hence $\operatorname{lk}(x,y)=S\cdot y/N=\pm w\wedge y/N=\pm\bigl((\varphi-1)^{-1}x\bigr)\wedge y$, which is $b$ up to sign. The
elliptic involution $-1$ preserves $\Sigma$, and $\operatorname{coker}(-\varphi-1)=\operatorname{coker}(\varphi+1)$. So the same computation identifies $b_+$, up to
sign, with the torsion linking form of $M_{-\varphi}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{obs:untwisted}
Let $m$ be odd.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(A_-,q^{\mathrm{lk}})$ at $L^mR^m$ is the discriminant form of $\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z}_m)$.
\item[(ii)] Every quadratic form on $\mathbb{Z}_m\times\mathbb{Z}_m$ takes values in $\tfrac1m\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$, whereas a non-degenerate quadratic form on $\mathbb{Z}_{m^2}$ takes a value of order $m^2$.
So no metric group on $\mathbb{Z}_m\times\mathbb{Z}_m$ is isometric, or Galois conjugate, to one on $\mathbb{Z}_{m^2}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Part (i) is Proposition~\ref{prop:linking}: the hyperbolic form on $\mathbb{Z}_m^2$ is the discriminant form of $\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z}_m)$.
For (ii), on $\mathbb{Z}_m\times\mathbb{Z}_m$ the bilinear form $b(x,y)=q(x+y)-q(x)-q(y)$ satisfies $mb=0$. So $2q(x)=b(x,x)\in\tfrac1m\mathbb{Z}$, and $q(mx)=m^2q(x)=0$ gives $q(x)\in\tfrac1{m^2}\mathbb{Z}$.
Since $m$ is odd, $q(x)\in\tfrac1m\mathbb{Z}$. On $\mathbb{Z}_{m^2}$ write $q(1)=s/m^2$ modulo $\mathbb{Z}$; here $s\in\mathbb{Z}$, since $2s=m^2b(1,1)\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $m^2s=q(m^2)\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $m$ odd. Non-degeneracy makes $b(1,1)=2s/m^2$ of order $m^2$, so $q(1)$ has order $m^2$.
Galois conjugation preserves the order of a root of unity.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:twisted}
So $L^mR^m$ gives the metric groups of the $\omega=0$ member of the Evans--Gannon twisted family $\mathcal{D}^\omega\mathrm{Hg}_m$ of modular data \cite[\S3.2]{EG11}, namely $\mathbb{Z}_m\times\mathbb{Z}_m$ with the hyperbolic form and
$\mathbb{Z}_{m^2+4}$, whose group structure is seen in the fusion rules \cite[\S5.6]{EG20}. The block of \eqref{eq:GKT} with $k-2=9$ has spins $A^2/9$, which include primitive ninth roots of unity. By Proposition~\ref{obs:untwisted}(ii) it is not a Galois conjugate of a metric group on $\mathbb{Z}_3\times\mathbb{Z}_3$. So the folded $T$-spectra of $L^3R^3$ and $LR^9$ are
inequivalent. Gang--Kim's family at $k=4n^2+4n+3$ is a Galois conjugate of $\mathcal{D}^{\omega=2}\mathrm{Hg}_{2n+1}$ \cite[after (2.26)]{GK22}, \cite[(2.32)]{GKL23}, and realises
only $\omega=2$, so the untwisted Haagerup double is precisely the member it misses. The sentence of \cite{GKL23} after (2.32) recalls that $\mathcal{D}^{\omega=0}\mathrm{Hg}_3$ is the original Haagerup double. It is not an identification: \cite[\S4]{GKL23} place their family at $\omega=\pm2$, in line with (2.32) and with Proposition~\ref{obs:untwisted}(ii), which separates $\mathbb{Z}_9$ from $\mathbb{Z}_3\times\mathbb{Z}_3$. That the family misses $\omega=0$ is consistent with \cite[Table~1]{JS26} once its first entry is corrected; that entry
$(p;k_1,k_2)=(2;-3,-3)$ should read $(2;-3,3)$: the former has trace $7$ and groups of orders $9$ and $5$, the latter trace $-11$ and orders $9$
and $13$, as the pattern $(2;-2n-1,2n+1)$ of that table requires.
Each identification in that table holds up to a Galois conjugation $\mathrm{Gal}_p$, with $p=2$ for the untwisted rows. The table also matches two twisted members, both with $p=31$: $\mathcal{D}^{3}\mathrm{Hg}_9$ at $(k_1,k_2)=(-3,27)$ and $\mathcal{D}^{2}\mathrm{Hg}_9$ at $(5,17)$ \cite[Table~1]{JS26}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- observation-1: body_md -->
\label{obs:egconj}
Evans--Gannon \cite{EG17}, Conjecture~1, predict that the double of a Haagerup--Izumi fusion category
$\mathcal C(G;\pm,\omega,A)$ (here $\omega$ is a cube root of unity, not the twist of $\mathcal{D}^\omega\mathrm{Hg}_m$) with $|G|=m$ odd has its $\tfrac12(m^2+3)$ primaries of class~(iv)
parametrised by pairs $\pm l$, $l\ne0$, in an abelian group $H$ of order $\mu=m^2+4$ carrying a nondegenerate
bilinear form $\beta$, with
\[
w_l=e^{2\pi i\,\mathsf m\,\beta(l,l)},\qquad F_{l,l'}=\mp\tfrac2{\sqrt\mu}\cos\bigl(2\pi\beta(l,l')\bigr),
\]
and their Proposition~3 tabulates $(H,\beta)$ for the ten Q-systems known at odd $7\le m\le19$. Here $\mathsf m=(\mu-1)/2\equiv-\tfrac12\pmod\mu$ is the $m$ of \cite{EG17}, not $|G|$, which they write $\nu$. In the notation of \cite{GSY26} the twists are $e^{2\pi iq(l)}$ with $q=\mathsf m\beta$, the normalisation used in Observation~\ref{obs:gsy}. The conjecture, proved in \cite[Thm.~5.1]{GSY26}, asserts that such an $H$ and
$\beta$ exist; it does not say what they are. The pair $(A_+,b_+)$ of this paper constructs them from the word. Enumerating \emph{all}
conjugacy classes of trace $m^2+2$ and computing $(A_-,A_+,b_\mp)$ for each gives, for odd $7\le m\le19$:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ccccl}
\toprule
$m$ & trace & classes & distinct $(H,b_+)$ & realised \\
\midrule
$7$  & $51$  & $7$  & $1$ & $\mathbb{Z}_{53},\,ll'/53$ \\
$9$  & $83$  & $18$ & $2$ & $\mathbb{Z}_{85},\,ll'/85$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{85},\,12ll'/85$\\
$11$ & $123$ & $14$ & $2$ & $\mathbb{Z}_{125},\,ll'/125$ and $\mathbb{Z}_5{\times}\mathbb{Z}_{25},\,l_1l_1'/25+l_2l_2'/5$\\
$13$ & $171$ & $13$ & $1$ & $\mathbb{Z}_{173},\,ll'/173$\\
$15$ & $227$ & $45$ & $1$ & $\mathbb{Z}_{229},\,ll'/229$\\
$17$ & $291$ & $17$ & $1$ & $\mathbb{Z}_{293},\,ll'/293$\\
$19$ & $363$ & $38$ & $2$ & $\mathbb{Z}_{365},\,ll'/365$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{365},\,22ll'/365$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Nine of the ten entries of their Proposition~3 are reproduced as printed, group and form, up to the choice of generator. (Their labels
$j(m)$ and $j(m)'$ denote the first and second solutions at $m$.) The diagonal word $L^mR^m$ always gives the $j(m)$ entry, and their second solutions at $m=9,19$ are other words of the same trace (the classes split
$9+9$ and $19+19$ between the two forms, $\mathrm h(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{m^2+4}))=2$ in both cases). The count of distinct data is much smaller than the
count of classes, and it is a count of modular data, not of categories: Observation~\ref{obs:gsy} takes this up.

The tenth entry, $j(11)'$, is printed in \cite{EG17} with $H=\mathbb{Z}_{25}\times\mathbb{Z}_5$ and form $2l_1l_1'/25+2l_2l_2'/5$. Trace $123$ has $14$
conjugacy classes; three carry $A_+\cong\mathbb{Z}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_{25}$, and each gives the form $l_1l_1'/25+l_2l_2'/5$ --- the printed one
multiplied by $2^{-1}$, and $2$ is a non-residue modulo $5$, so the two are not isomorphic. The word data's form is the right one. The Gauss sum $\sum_id_i^2\theta_i=\dim\mathcal C$ of the Drinfeld centre, evaluated with the
dimensions of their (6.24), is satisfied by the word data's form and not by the printed one. Gannon--Schopieray--Yadav's independent
determination of $(H,q)$ from the HI matrix also agrees with the word data (Observation~\ref{obs:gsy}). So the table is reproduced ten times out
of ten. Here the word data's form is $q^{\mathrm{lk}}$, the normalisation of
the unitary double. The spin form $q_+=2^{-1}q^{\mathrm{lk}}$ of the $S$-fold is its Galois conjugate (Corollary~\ref{cor:galois}), and it is
isometric to the printed form, which differs from it by the square $4$.
<!-- end observation-1 -->
<!-- observation-2: body_md -->
\label{obs:gsy}
Gannon--Schopieray--Yadav \cite{GSY26}, Table~1, list every untwisted unitary Haagerup--Izumi category of Q-system type for
$\mathbb{Z}/m$, $m\le43$ odd, with the modular data of its centre written as a label $\mu^+_s$ for the cyclic metric group $\mathbb{Z}/\mu$ with
$q(h)=sh^2/\mu$, or an orthogonal sum of such labels. Their $q$ is the quadratic form of the twists, $q=\mathsf m\beta$ in the notation of
Observation~\ref{obs:egconj} (so $s\equiv-\tfrac12$ for the forms $ll'/\mu$). Enumerating all conjugacy classes of trace $m^2+2$ and
computing $(A_-,A_+,q)$ for each gives the table below. Here $q(x)=-2^{-1}\,x\wedge(\varphi+1)^{-1}x\bmod1$ on $A_+$, with $2^{-1}$ the
inverse of $2$ modulo $m^2+4$. This is isometric to $q^{\mathrm{lk}}$, since $-1$ is a square modulo $m^2+4$. Cyclic forms are compared by the
square class of $s$:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{ccc>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{6.2cm}}
\toprule
$m$ & classes & categories (data) & the data, all realised by words\\
\midrule
$3,5,7,13,17$ & $3,5,7,13,17$ & $1\ (1)$ & $13^+_6$, $29^+_{14}$, $53^+_{26}$, $173^+_{86}$, $293^+_{146}$\\
$9$ & $18$ & $2\ (2)$ & $85^+_{42}$, $85^+_6$\\
$11$ & $14$ & $2\ (2)$ & $125^+_{62}$, $25^+_{12}{\times}5^+_2$\\
$15,27,35,37$ & $45,81,105,111$ & $3\ (1)$ & $229^+_{114}$, $733^+_{366}$, $1229^+_{614}$, $1373^+_{686}$\\
$19,23,25$ & $38,46,50$ & $2\ (2)$ & $365^+_{182},365^+_{11}$; $533^+_{266},533^+_3$; $629^+_{314},629^+_3$\\
$31,41,43$ & $62,82,86$ & $2\ (2)$ & $965^+_{482},965^+_{11}$; $1685^+_{842},1685^+_{11}$; $1853^+_{926},1853^+_3$\\
$21$ & $84$ & $4\ (2)$ & $445^+_{222}$, $445^+_6$\\
$29$ & $63$ & $3\ (3)$ & $845^+_{422}$, $845^+_3$, $65^+_2{\times}13^+_2$\\
$33$ & $165$ & $5\ (1)$ & $1093^+_{546}$\\
$39$ & $195$ & $5\ (3)$ & $1525^+_{762}$, $1525^+_6$, $5^+_1{\times}5^+_1{\times}61^+_2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
At every odd $m\le43$ the set of distinct $(A_+,q)$ produced by the words of trace $m^2+2$ is \emph{exactly} the set of distinct
modular data in their table: every one of their labels is realised, and no word produces a form outside the list. The cyclic labels are
matched by the square class of $s$; the three non-cyclic ones, at $m=11,29,39$, by the multiset of values of $q$ and the Gauss sum.
Each form is moreover realised on every $A_-$-type of the trace, including the untwisted type $A_-\cong\mathbb{Z}_m\times\mathbb{Z}_m$. Two
things follow. First, their label $25^+_{12}\times5^+_2$ for the second $\mathbb{Z}/11$ category is $q=12l_1^2/25+2l_2^2/5=\mathsf m\beta$ for
$\beta=l_1l_1'/25+l_2l_2'/5$, the word data's form of Observation~\ref{obs:egconj}: their independent determination of
$(H,q)$ from the HI matrix (their Proposition~5.7) confirms the resolution of the $j(11)'$ entry reached there. Second, what the
words see is the modular data and not the category: at $m=15,21,27,33,35,37,39$ several categories share one datum (the three $\mathbb{Z}/15$ ones are Galois conjugates \cite[\S1.5]{GSY26}, pairwise
non-Morita-equivalent \cite[Cor.~5.9]{GSY26}), and the words produce that datum once per
$A_-$-type. The count of distinct data agrees with theirs at all twenty-one values of $m$; the count of categories is not a
question the Bethe equations can address.
<!-- end observation-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:Kformula}
Write the word cyclically as runs $L^{a_1}R^{b_1}\cdots L^{a_{n_R}}R^{b_{n_R}}$. For every hyperbolic word, the unique symmetric solution $K_{\mathrm{raw}}$ of $BK_{\mathrm{raw}}=A$ with
$\det K=2^r$ is given by $K=QK_{\mathrm{raw}} Q$ with
\begin{itemize}
\item each $R$-run of length $b$ a fan block $K_{ij}=2\min(i,j)$ within the run, $R$'s in different runs not coupling;
\item $L$ diagonal $4$, plus $2b$ for the first $L$ after an $R$-run of length $b$;
\item $L$--$L$ coupling $-2$ for each adjacency of cyclically consecutive $L$'s in the word with the $R$'s deleted: so $-4$ between the two
$L$'s when $\#L=2$, and $-4$ on the diagonal when $\#L=1$ (as for $LR^n$, giving $4+2n-4=2n$);
\item coupling $2j$ between the first $L$ after an $R$-run and the $j$-th $R$ of that run, so that these entries $2,4,\dots,2b$ increase linearly along the run (we call them the \emph{ramp}); and coupling $-2$ between the last $L$ before an $R$-run and every $R$ of it;
\end{itemize}
and the charge vector $c$, the primitive integer vector with $Q^{-1}c\in\ker B$ (which is one-dimensional), with its sign fixed by $c_{R_1}=1$, is $b$ at the first $L$ after an $R$-run of length $b$, $0$ at the other $L$'s, and $j$ at the $j$-th $R$ of each run. It is primitive because its entry at the first $R$ of each run is $1$.
Moreover $K$ is positive definite. The diagonal word $L^mR^m$ is the single-run case.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:closed}
For the diagonal words $\varphi=L^mR^m$, $K_{\mathrm{raw}}(m)\,P\,K_{\mathrm{raw}}(m)=P$, where $P=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&I\\I&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ is the permutation exchanging the $L$-sites with
the $R$-sites.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
One solution is described by four sets of variables: the Bethe shapes $x_b=z_b^{-Q_b}$ of \eqref{eq:bethex}; the Nahm variables $\delta_b=1-x_b$ and $d_b=\delta_b^{-1/2}$; and the chain variables $\hat d_b=s_b^{-1/2}$ of Section~\ref{sub:runchain}, with $s_b=x_b$ at an $L$-step and $s_b=1-x_b$ at an $R$-step, so that $\hat d_b=x_b^{-1/2}$ at an $L$-step and $\hat d_b=d_b$ at an $R$-step. Solutions are counted in the shapes: a solution $x$ of \eqref{eq:bethex} lifts to $2^{\#L}$ solutions $z$ of \eqref{eq:bethe}, the sign choices $z_L=\pm x_L^{-1/2}$. The positive vacuum $V^*$ is the all-plus lift ($z_a>1$ for all $a$) of the solution $x\in(0,1)^r$ of \eqref{eq:bethex}, which is unique (Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}). On this positive branch ($1-x_b>0$, $d_b>0$) Proposition~\ref{prop:bethenahm} makes a solution in one set of variables a solution in the others. Statements are made in the shapes $x$ unless they concern Nahm's equations.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:bethenahm}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word, $(K,Q)$ the pipeline output of Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula},
$K_{\mathrm{raw}}=Q^{-1}KQ^{-1}$, and
\[
\mathbf N:=2\bigl(I-QK^{-1}Q\bigr)=2\bigl(I-K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}\bigr).
\]
Under $\delta_b=1-x_b=d_b^{-2}$, on the positive branch (all $x_b\in(0,1)$, real logarithms), the undeformed Bethe equations \eqref{eq:bethe} and Nahm's ladder for $\mathbf N$ are the same system:
\begin{equation}
1-x_b=\prod_ax_a^{(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{ab}}
\iff
\log(1-\delta_b)=\sum_a\bigl(K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}\bigr)_{ba}\log\delta_a
\iff
d_b^2=1+\prod_ad_a^{\mathbf N_{ba}} .
\label{eq:bethenahm}
\end{equation}
Here the first form is the positive-root form of \eqref{eq:bethex} (for $Q_b=2$, \eqref{eq:bethex} reads $(1-x_b)^2=\cdots$), with $1-x_b>0$ and $d_b>0$. Moreover $\mathbf N$ is symmetric, because $K$ is.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Taking logarithms, the first equation reads $\log(1-x_b)=\sum_a(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{ab}\log x_a$. Substituting $\delta=1-x$ into the second and using the first,
\[
\sum_a\bigl(K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}\bigr)_{ba}\log(1-x_a)=\sum_a\bigl(K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}\bigr)_{ba}\sum_c(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{ca}\log x_c=\log x_b
\]
by symmetry of $K_{\mathrm{raw}}$, which is the second equation. For the third, $\delta_b=d_b^{-2}$ gives $\log\delta_a=-2\log d_a$ and
$\log(1-\delta_b)=\log(d_b^2-1)-2\log d_b$, so the second becomes $\log(d_b^2-1)=\sum_a\bigl[2\delta_{ba}-2(K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1})_{ba}\bigr]\log d_a$, which is the
third. Symmetry of $\mathbf N$ is symmetry of $K$, and $K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}=QK^{-1}Q$ by definition.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:twopoints}
The hyperbolic volume sum $\sum_iD(z_i)$ and the Nahm sum $\sum_iL(\delta_i)$ are one family of algebraic systems, specialised at
two different points: the completeness point, with $z_i\in\mathbb H$ and the Bloch--Wigner branch, and the flux point $(\mathfrak m,\nu)=(0,-1)$ of the twisted index (Section~\ref{sec:bethe}), with
$\delta_i\in(0,1)$ and the Rogers branch. Both $D$ and $L$ satisfy the same five-term functional equation --- $D$ the single-valued extension to $\mathbb{C}$,
$L$ the one to $(0,1)$ --- which is the mechanism behind Nahm's conjecture \cite{Nahm04,NRT92} and its refinements \cite{CGZ23}. This does \emph{not} give a numerical formula
$c_{\mathrm{eff}}=f(\mathrm{Vol})$, since among words with the same $\#L$, such as $LR^n$, the volume varies while $c_{\mathrm{eff}}=\#L$ does not. The relation is structural, with one variety and one functional
equation, and not numerical.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:nahmclosed}
For every $m\ge3$ the shape equations \eqref{eq:bethex} of $L^mR^m$ have exactly one solution $x\in(0,1)^{2m}$, whose all-plus lift is $V^*$, namely
\[
x_{L_j}=\frac{d^2}{\mathcal Q_j^2},\qquad x_{R_j}=\frac{\mathcal Q_{j-1}\mathcal Q_{j+1}}{\mathcal Q_j^2},\qquad j=1,\dots,m,
\]
where $L_j$ and $R_j$ denote the $j$-th $L$-site and the $j$-th $R$-site of the word, in the order the letters occur. Equivalently, by Proposition~\ref{prop:bethenahm}, the ladder equations have the unique solution $\delta=1-x$ in $(0,1)^{2m}$, $\delta_{L_j}=\mathcal Q_{j-1}\mathcal Q_{j+1}/\mathcal Q_j^2$ and $\delta_{R_j}=d^2/\mathcal Q_j^2$, so that $\delta=1-x=Px$ with $P$ the exchange of $L$- and $R$-sites of Proposition~\ref{prop:closed}. The $\mathcal Q_j$ are affine in $j$ and satisfy
$\mathcal Q_j^2-\mathcal Q_{j-1}\mathcal Q_{j+1}=d^2$ for all $j$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We verify the Bethe form $1-x_b=\prod_ax_a^{(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{ab}}$ for the stated $x$, using the blocks $C$, $F=2\min$, $V$ of \eqref{eq:Kdiag}. Summing by parts,
$\sum_{i=1}^m\min(i,j)\Delta^2\log\mathcal Q_i=\log \mathcal Q_0-\log \mathcal Q_j+j\log(\mathcal Q_{m+1}/\mathcal Q_m)$.

\emph{$R$-columns}: the fan gives $\mathcal Q_j^{-2}((d+1)/d)^{2j}$ and the couplings $(d/(1+d))^{2j}d^2$ (using $\mathcal Q_m=d^2$), so the right side is
$d^2/\mathcal Q_j^2=1-x_{R_j}$. \emph{Middle $L$-columns}: $(d^2/\mathcal Q_k^2)(\mathcal Q_{k-1}/d)(\mathcal Q_{k+1}/d)=\mathcal Q_{k-1}\mathcal Q_{k+1}/\mathcal Q_k^2=1-x_{L_k}$. \emph{$L_1$}: the corner
$(m+2)/2$ and the ramp give $(d/\mathcal Q_1)^{m+2}\cdot\mathcal Q_2\mathcal Q_m/d^2\cdot((d+1)/d)^m/d^2=\mathcal Q_2/\mathcal Q_1^2$. \emph{$L_m$}: the equation reduces to $\mathcal Q_1^2\mathcal Q_m=\mathcal Q_{m+1}^2$,
i.e.\ $(1+d)^2d^2=(d(d+1))^2$. All entries lie in $(0,1)$ since $\mathcal Q_j>d$ for $j\ge1$, and $K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}=QK^{-1}Q$ is positive definite (Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}), so the solution in $(0,1)^r$ of Nahm's equations for $\delta=1-x$ with matrix $K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}$ is unique \cite[\S2]{VZ11} (Proposition~\ref{prop:bethenahm}); this is the positive solution. Finally $\mathcal Q_j^2-\mathcal Q_{j-1}\mathcal Q_{j+1}=d^2$ gives $1-x_{R_j}=x_{L_j}$ and $1-x_{L_j}=x_{R_j}$, so $\delta=1-x=Px$; this is the relabelling $x\mapsto P\delta$ under which $K_{\mathrm{raw}}^{-1}=PK_{\mathrm{raw}} P$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:closed}) carries the Nahm system for $\delta$ to the Bethe system for $x$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:propagated}
Write the word as $\varphi=\ell_1\ell_2\cdots\ell_r$ with each $\ell_i\in\{L,R\}$. Let $\eta$ be the expanding left eigenvector, $\eta\varphi=\lambda\eta$,
and define the \emph{height} $h(v)=\langle\eta,v\rangle$ of a vector $v\in\mathbb{Z}^2$. At step $i$ the partial product $M_{i-1}=\ell_1\cdots\ell_{i-1}$ has
columns $(c_1,c_2)$, which are the two slopes of the Farey basis at that step (Section~\ref{sub:gluing}); the flip $\ell_i$ keeps one of them ---
$c_1$ if $\ell_i=L$, $c_2$ if $\ell_i=R$ ---, the \emph{kept slope} $a$ of the step (as in Section~\ref{sub:gluing}). Put $w=c_1+c_2$, the middle slope, and
$s_i=h(a)^2/h(w)^2$. Then
\begin{equation}
x_i=s_i\ \ (\ell_i=L),\qquad x_i=1-s_i=\frac{h(u)h(u')}{h(w)^2}\ \ (\ell_i=R),\quad u=w-a,\ u'=w+a,
\label{eq:propagated}
\end{equation}
solves the shape equations \eqref{eq:bethex} for every hyperbolic word. It is the unique solution with $x\in(0,1)^r$: with $x=e^{-t}$, such solutions are the critical points on $t>0$ of $\tfrac12t^{\mathsf T}K_{\mathrm{raw}} t+\sum_i\operatorname{Li}_2(e^{-t_i})$, which is strictly convex because $K_{\mathrm{raw}}$ is positive definite (Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}) \cite[\S II.3]{Zagier07}, \cite[\S2]{VZ11}; its all-plus lift is the positive vacuum $V^*$. The same formulae at the contracting
eigenvector $\eta'$, $\eta'\varphi=\lambda^{-1}\eta'$, give a second solution of the shape equations, the Galois conjugate of $x(V^*)$, whose all-plus lift is $\sigma V^*$. (In $z$, the Galois conjugate of the lift $V^*$ has $z_L=h'(w)/h'(a)$, which differs from the all-plus lift by a sign at every $L$-site, since this ratio is negative at every $L$-step (there $t\in(-1,0)$, Lemma~\ref{lem:crossings}); the sign of $W_c$ depends on the choice, $W_c^2$ does not.) In addition, within each run the kept slope $a$ is fixed and the middle slopes form a fan, $w_j=w_0+ja$, where $w_0$ is the slope dying at the first step of the run and $w_j$ the middle slope of its $j$-th step, so that at either eigenvector the signed heights satisfy $h(w_{j+1})=h(w_j)+h(a)$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} the equations are local in the runs. Within an $R$-run the kept slope $a$ is fixed and the middle slopes of the
successive steps form a fan, $w_j=w_0+ja$ for $j=0,1,\dots$, with $w_0$ the first column of the Farey basis on entering the run, the slope dying at its first step; likewise within an $L$-run, with $w_0$ the second column. With $X_a=x_a^{1/Q_a}$, so that $X=h(a)/h(w)$ at an $L$-step, each equation involves only a step and its
run neighbours. \emph{$R$-columns}: the fan block telescopes to $(h(w_0)/h(w_j))^2(h(w_{b+1})/h(w_b))^{2j}$; the last $L$ before the run contributes
$(h(a)/h(w_0))^2$ and the first $L$ after it $(h(w_b)/h(w_{b+1}))^{2j}$; the product is $h(a)^2/h(w_j)^2=1-x_{R_j}$. \emph{Middle $L$'s}:
$X_j^4X_{j-1}^{-2}X_{j+1}^{-2}=(h(w_{j-1})h(w_{j+1})/h(w_j)^2)^2=(1-x)^2$. \emph{Notation at a junction.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} the equation at an $L$-site $\ell$ is $(1-x_\ell)^2=\prod_aX_a^{K_{a\ell}}$.
We work on the developed word, the infinite periodic sequence of letters, so that the previous and next $L$-sites of $\ell$ and the
$R$-runs on either side of it are distinct sites; periodicity is used only at the end. Let $\rho$ be an $R$-run of length $b$, with kept slope
$q'$ and fan $w_j=p+jq'$, $j=0,\dots,b+1$, where $p$ is the slope kept by the $L$-run before $\rho$. Write $g_j=h(w_j)$, so that
$g_j=g_0+jh(q')$ and $X_{R_j}=g_{j-1}g_{j+1}/g_j^2$. Summation by parts gives
\[
\prod_{j=1}^bX_{R_j}=\frac{g_0g_{b+1}}{g_1g_b},\qquad \prod_{j=1}^bX_{R_j}^{\,j}=\frac{g_0\,g_{b+1}^{\,b}}{g_b^{\,b+1}} .
\]
The $L$-run before $\rho$ has kept slope $p$ and middle heights $h_i=h(q+ip)$, ending with $h_a=h(q')$. Its last site has $X=g_0/h_a$, and
$h_{a+1}:=h_a+g_0=g_1$. The $L$-run after $\rho$ has kept slope $w_b$ and middle heights $k_i=h(q'+iw_b)=k_0+ig_b$, with $k_0=h(q')$ and
$k_1=g_{b+1}$. Its first site has $X=g_b/k_1$.

\emph{First $L$ of a run of length $\ge2$.} Here $\ell=L^+(\rho)$. Its row has diagonal $4+2b$, the ramp $2j$ to $R_j$, and $-2$ to $L^-(\rho)$
and to the next $L$, whose $X$ is $g_b/k_2$. So the right side is
\[
\Bigl(\frac{g_b}{k_1}\Bigr)^{4+2b}\Bigl(\frac{h_a}{g_0}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(\frac{k_2}{g_b}\Bigr)^2\frac{g_0^2\,g_{b+1}^{2b}}{g_b^{2b+2}}
=\Bigl(\frac{k_0k_2}{k_1^2}\Bigr)^2 ,
\]
using $h_a=k_0$ and $k_1=g_{b+1}$. And $1-x_\ell=1-g_b^2/k_1^2=(k_1-g_b)(k_1+g_b)/k_1^2=k_0k_2/k_1^2$.

\emph{Last $L$ of a run of length $\ge2$.} Here $\ell=L^-(\rho)$. Its row has diagonal $4$, $-2$ to the previous $L$ (whose $X$ is $g_0/h_{a-1}$),
$-2$ to $L^+(\rho)$, and $-2$ to every $R$ of $\rho$. So the right side is
\[
\Bigl(\frac{g_0}{h_a}\Bigr)^4\Bigl(\frac{h_{a-1}}{g_0}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(\frac{g_{b+1}}{g_b}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(\frac{g_1g_b}{g_0g_{b+1}}\Bigr)^2
=\Bigl(\frac{h_{a-1}h_{a+1}}{h_a^2}\Bigr)^2 ,
\]
using $g_1=h_{a+1}$. And $1-x_\ell=(h_a-g_0)(h_a+g_0)/h_a^2=h_{a-1}h_{a+1}/h_a^2$.

\emph{A singleton $L$.} Here $\ell=L^+(\rho)$ and also $\ell=L^-(\rho')$ for the next $R$-run $\rho'$, of length $b'$. Its row has diagonal
$4+2b$, the ramp $2j$ to $\rho$, $-2$ to every $R$ of $\rho'$, and $-2$ to the previous and the next $L$. The run $\rho'$ has kept slope
$q'+w_b$ and fan heights $g'_j=g_b+jk_1$. So $\rho'$ contributes $(g'_1g'_{b'}/g'_0g'_{b'+1})^2$, and the next $L$ has $X=g'_{b'}/g'_{b'+1}$.
The right side is
\[
\Bigl(\frac{g_b}{k_1}\Bigr)^{4+2b}\frac{g_0^2\,g_{b+1}^{2b}}{g_b^{2b+2}}\Bigl(\frac{h_a}{g_0}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(\frac{g'_1}{g'_0}\Bigr)^2
=\Bigl(\frac{k_0k_2}{k_1^2}\Bigr)^2 ,
\]
since $g'_0=g_b$ and $g'_1=g_b+k_1=k_2$. This is $(1-x_\ell)^2$, as in the first case.

\emph{Wrap-around.} On the developed word every $X$ is a ratio of heights of slopes, and the slopes one period later are the images of the
earlier ones under $\varphi$. Since $h(\varphi v)=\lambda h(v)$, every $X$ is periodic, and the identities on the developed word are the
equations of the cyclic word. This covers $\#L=1$, where the single $L$ is its own previous and next $L$ and $\rho'=\rho$: the row becomes
$K_{LL}=2b$ and $K_{LR_j}=2j-2$. It also covers $\#L=2$, where the coupling $-4$ is the sum of the two adjacencies.

Heights are positive at $\eta$: $\varphi$ has positive entries, so $\eta>0$ by Perron--Frobenius, and the columns of $M_{i-1}$ are nonnegative and nonzero. So this
is the all-plus solution, with $x\in(0,1)^r$. At $\eta'$ the same identities hold: $\sigma(\eta)$ is a multiple of $\eta'$, the formulae are homogeneous of degree $0$ in $\eta$, and the shape equations have integer exponents.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{obs:stretch}
For a solution $z$ of the Bethe equations \eqref{eq:bethe} put $W_c:=\prod_az_a^{c_a}$, with $c$ the charge vector of Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}; it is the value of the Wilson line of gauge charge $c$ (Section~\ref{sec:bethe}). Then
$W_c(V^*)=\lambda(\varphi)$: the Wilson loop at the positive vacuum is the stretch factor of the monodromy.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
With $c$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}, and $h_j=h(w_j)$ for the fan $w_j$ of an $R$-run $\rho$ of length $b$, the factors $z_{R_j}^{\,j}$ multiply to $h_b^{\,b+1}/(h_{b+1}^{\,b}h_0)$ and the factor $z_{L^+(\rho)}^{\,b}$ is $(h_{b+1}/h_b)^b$, so $\rho$ contributes $h_b/h_0=h(c_1\text{ at run end})/h(c_1\text{ at run start})$ to $W_c(V^*)$. The $L$-runs leave $c_1$ fixed, so the product telescopes to $h(\varphi e_1)/h(e_1)=\lambda$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:rational}
Let $x$ be the solution \eqref{eq:propagated} given by the propagated eigenvector. Then $\sum_aL(\delta_a)/L(1)\in\mathbb{Q}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
This is the standard Bloch-group argument \cite{Nahm04,Zagier07}. All $\delta_a$ lie in $F=\mathbb{Q}(\lambda)=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{k^2-4})$ (see after Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}), which is real quadratic. Consider the element $\Delta=\sum_a[\delta_a]$ of the pre-Bloch group of $F$. Since $M=QK^{-1}Q$ is symmetric, $\sum_{a<b}(M_{ba}-M_{ab})(\delta_b\wedge\delta_a)=0$, and so $\sum_a\delta_a\wedge(1-\delta_a)=0$. The entries of $M$ are half-integers, so this relation holds in $\bigwedge^2F^\times\otimes\mathbb{Q}$, and a multiple of $\Delta$ lies in the Bloch group $B(F)$. This group is finite, since $F$ is totally real (Borel \cite{Borel77}, via \cite{Suslin91}). The Rogers sum of a torsion element is a rational multiple of $L(1)$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:friezedef}
Let $M\in SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, $w_j=M^jw_0$, let $h$ be any linear functional, and put $h_j=h(w_j)$, $\tau=\operatorname{tr} M$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] By the Cayley--Hamilton theorem $M^2=\tau M-1$, so $w_{j+1}=\tau w_j-w_{j-1}$ and $h_{j+1}=\tau h_j-h_{j-1}$. Hence $h_j^2-h_{j-1}h_{j+1}=h_j^2-\tau h_{j-1}h_j+h_{j-1}^2$ is independent of $j$: it is the $M$-invariant quadratic form evaluated at $(h_{j-1},h_j)$. The quantity $(h_{j-1}+h_{j+1})/h_j=\tau$ is also constant along the orbit.
\item[(ii)] Writing $\tau=2\cos\vartheta$ with $\tau\ne\pm2$, every solution of the recurrence over $\mathbb{C}$ with $h_j^2-h_{j-1}h_{j+1}\ne0$ is $h_j=A\sin(j\vartheta+\phi)/\sin\vartheta$ with constants $A,\phi\in\mathbb{C}$, and
$h_j^2-h_{j-1}h_{j+1}=A^2$; the remaining solutions $c\mu^{\pm j}$, $\mu+\mu^{-1}=\tau$, have $h_j^2-h_{j-1}h_{j+1}=0$, so they are not frieze rows. This is the trigonometric $Q$-recurrence for $|\tau|<2$, hyperbolic for $|\tau|>2$, and affine, $h_j=h_0+j\beta$ with
constant $\beta^2$, exactly at $\tau=\pm2$ (for $\tau=-2$ the affine solution is multiplied by $(-1)^j$).
\item[(iii)] Within a run of a word in $L,R$ the generator is $L$ or $R$, both \emph{parabolic}. Let $\ell=L$ or $R$ be the letter of the run, and $P$ the Farey basis on entering it. Then $w_j=P\ell^jP^{-1}w_0$, so $M=P\ell P^{-1}$ and $\tau=2$.
The kept slope $a$ is the fixed vector of $M$, and $\beta=h(a)$. Normalising by $\hat d_j=h_j/h(a)$ gives the $SL_2$-frieze relation
\begin{equation}
\hat d_j^2-\hat d_{j-1}\hat d_{j+1}=1 .
\label{eq:frieze}
\end{equation}
\item[(iv)] The passage $y_j=\hat d_{j-1}\hat d_{j+1}/\hat d_j^2$ gives $y_j=1-s_j$: the Bethe coordinate $x$ at an $R$-step, and $1-x$ at an $L$-step.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Proof.} (i) is $M^2=\tau M-I$ applied to $w_{j-1}$, and the conserved quantity is the substitution $h_{j+1}=\tau h_j-h_{j-1}$. (ii) solves the recursion.
(iii): $L$ and $R$ have trace $2$ and fixed vectors $e_1$, $e_2$; the kept slope of a run is that fixed vector, and $h_{j+1}-h_j=h(a)$, so
$\hat d_{j+1}=\hat d_j+1$ and $\hat d_j^2-(\hat d_j-1)(\hat d_j+1)=1$. (iv) is then $(\hat d_j^2-1)/\hat d_j^2=1-\hat d_j^{-2}=1-s_j$.

\emph{Frieze rows.} A sequence satisfying the \emph{frieze relation} \eqref{eq:frieze} satisfies
$\det\begin{psmallmatrix}\hat d_j&\hat d_{j+1}\\ \hat d_{j-1}&\hat d_j\end{psmallmatrix}=1$, the diamond rule of an $SL_2$-frieze \cite{CC73} with constant rows. We call such a sequence a
\emph{frieze row}, and the conserved quantity $\tau=(\hat d_{j-1}+\hat d_{j+1})/\hat d_j$ of (i) its \emph{frieze trace}: it is the trace of the transfer matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix}\tau&-1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}\in SL_2$ that advances the recurrence (i) by one step. For $i\hat d_j$ the relation \eqref{eq:frieze} is the exchange relation $x_{j-1}x_{j+1}=x_j^2+1$ of the Kronecker cluster algebra, and $y=\hat d_{j-1}\hat d_{j+1}/\hat d_j^2$
of (iv) equals $1-\hat d_j^{-2}$; the $y$-recursion is second order and algebraic, and the $Y$-side
periodicity theorems are not available (Section~\ref{sub:rogers}), while the $A$-side recursion (i) is linear. The $A$-side is available at all
only because $s$ is a \emph{square} of a height ratio, and that square is the charge $Q_L=2$: the $2^{\#L}$ vacua of a class in
Section~\ref{sec:bethe} are precisely the two values $z_L=\pm\hat d_L$, the square roots of $\hat d_L^2=x_L^{-1}$, at each $L$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:friezeall}
Let $\varphi$ be any hyperbolic word and let $z$ be \emph{any} solution of the undeformed Bethe equations \eqref{eq:bethe} with all coordinates in $\mathbb{C}^\times$, with $x_b=z_b^{-Q_b}$. Put $s_b=x_b$ at an
$L$-step and $s_b=1-x_b$ at an $R$-step. Then at every site $b$ interior to its run,
\begin{equation}
\Bigl(\frac{1-s_b}{s_b}\Bigr)^{\!2}=\frac1{s_{b-1}s_{b+1}},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \hat d_b^2\mp\hat d_{b-1}\hat d_{b+1}=1
\label{eq:friezeall}
\end{equation}
for $\hat d=s^{-1/2}$ on either branch. The same holds at a limit vacuum of the deformed system whose shapes $x_b$ at the sites of the run and their neighbours stay away from
$0$, $1$ and $\infty$; in general the polynomial form $s_{b-1}s_{b+1}(1-s_b)^2=s_b^2$ survives in the limit. In particular, for each run $\rho$ of length at least $3$, such a solution carries a frieze trace
$\tau_\rho:=(\hat d_{b-1}+\hat d_{b+1})/\hat d_b$ (Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}), the same at every interior site $b$ of the run, defined up to sign (Remark~\ref{rem:friezesign}), which need not equal $2$ away from $V^*$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
At a site $b$ interior to an $L$-run, Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} gives $K_{bb}=4$ and $K_{b\pm1,b}=-2$ with no other entry in that column, and
$Q_b=Q_{b\pm1}=2$, so $(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{bb}=1$ and $(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{b\pm1,b}=-\tfrac12$. The Bethe equation at $b$, in the shape form \eqref{eq:bethex} with $Q_b=2$, is therefore
$(1-x_b)^2=x_b^2/(x_{b-1}x_{b+1})$, which is \eqref{eq:friezeall}.

At a site $j$ interior to an $R$-run the column is not tridiagonal --- the fan block is $2\min(i,j)$ --- so combine three equations instead. Since
$Q=1$ on $R$-steps,
\[
\frac{(1-x_j)^2}{(1-x_{j-1})(1-x_{j+1})}=\prod_ax_a^{(2K_{aj}-K_{a,j-1}-K_{a,j+1})/Q_a}=\prod_ax_a^{-\Delta_j^2K_{aj}/Q_a} ,
\]
where $\Delta_j^2g(j)=g(j-1)-2g(j)+g(j+1)$ is the second difference in $j$. Now $-\Delta_j^2\bigl(2\min(a,j)\bigr)=2\delta_{aj}$ for $a$ in the same fan; the last $L$ before the run contributes the constant $-2$, and every other
run a constant, both annihilated by $\Delta_j^2$; and the first $L$ after the run contributes the ramp $2j$, affine in $j$, also annihilated. So the
right side is $x_j^2$, and with $s=1-x$ this reads $s_j^2/(s_{j-1}s_{j+1})=(1-s_j)^2$, i.e.\ \eqref{eq:friezeall}. The same holds for the deformed equations, since $c_b=0$ at middle $L$'s and $c$ is affine on $R$-runs, so the factor $(1+\epsilon)^{c}$ cancels; hence the relation holds at every limit vacuum whose run coordinates stay in $\mathbb{C}^\times$. For the conservation of $\tau_\rho$, choose the signs of the $\hat d_b$ so that the relation reads $\hat d_b^2-\hat d_{b-1}\hat d_{b+1}=1$ at every interior site. To do so, go through the interior sites in turn; where the relation at $i$ has the wrong sign, flip $\hat d_{i+1}$, which affects only the relation at $i+2$. Two consecutive relations then give $\hat d_j(\hat d_j+\hat d_{j+2})=\hat d_{j+1}(\hat d_{j-1}+\hat d_{j+1})$, that is, $\tau_j=\tau_{j+1}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:friezesign}
The sign sits on the product and not on the right-hand side: squaring
$(\hat d_b^2-1)^2=\hat d_{b-1}^2\hat d_{b+1}^2$ gives $\hat d_b^2-1=\pm\hat d_{b-1}\hat d_{b+1}$, and both
signs occur (at $L^3R^3$ both are found among the classes). Flipping the sign of $\hat d_b$ at alternate sites of a run preserves the relations and sends $\tau_\rho\mapsto-\tau_\rho$. Flipping it at a single site $b$ changes the sign of the relation at $b-1$ and $b+1$. So a run is determined, up to this sign, by its trace and its phase, or by two consecutive values.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:runreduce}
Let every run of $\varphi$ have length at least $2$. For a run of length $2$ put $\tau_\rho=(\hat d_1^2+\hat d_2^2-1)/(\hat d_1\hat d_2)$. Parametrise each run $\rho$ of length $n_\rho$ with $\tau_\rho\ne\pm2$ (the case $\tau_\rho=\pm2$ is the affine chain of Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}(ii), which contains $V^*$ and has one unknown, the anchor) by
\[
s_j=\frac{\sin^2\vartheta_\rho}{\sin^2(j\vartheta_\rho+\phi_\rho)},\qquad j=1,\dots,n_\rho ,
\]
with $\vartheta_\rho,\phi_\rho\in\mathbb{C}$, so that $\tau_\rho=2\cos\vartheta_\rho$; by Theorem~\ref{thm:friezeall} and Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}(ii) every solution has this form on such a run (the details are in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}). Write $r_b=(1-x_b)^{Q_b}/\prod_ax_a^{K_{ab}/Q_a}$ for the residual of \eqref{eq:bethe} at $b$. Then the
frieze relation \eqref{eq:friezeall} holds identically in $(\vartheta_\rho,\phi_\rho)$ at every site interior to a run; at an interior $L$-site it is
the Bethe equation $r_b=1$ (in which $Q_b=2$ already squares the coordinate), and at an interior $R$-site it is $r_j^2=r_{j-1}r_{j+1}$. For a word
with two runs the squared system $\{r_L=1,\ r_R^2=1\}$ therefore reduces to the four equations at the run ends, in the four unknowns $(\vartheta_L,\phi_L,\vartheta_R,\phi_R)$, up to an
$(n_\rho-1)$-st root of unity in $r_j^2$ at the interior $R$-sites; adding the equation at the second $R$-site removes it.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The frieze relation at an interior site is the product-to-sum identity
$\sin((j-1)\vartheta+\phi)\sin((j+1)\vartheta+\phi)=\sin^2(j\vartheta+\phi)-\sin^2\vartheta$. By the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:friezeall} it is $r_b=1$ at an
interior $L$-site, and at an interior $R$-site $r_j^2/(r_{j-1}r_{j+1})$ is the frieze relation, the product of the $x_a$ being $x_j^2$
identically. So along the $R$-run $(r_j)$ is geometric with ratio $\gamma$, say; $r_1^2=r_{n_\rho}^2=1$ gives $\gamma^{2(n_\rho-1)}=1$, and
$r_2^2=1$ gives $\gamma^2=1$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:runsharp}
The run-end equations, together with the equation at the second $R$-site of each run, are the quantisation. Take a two-run word with
both runs of length $\ge2$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} the non-degenerate solutions of the unsquared equations are exactly the
kernel-vector classes of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}, together with $V^*$ and $\sigma V^*$. The run-end equations alone would leave
spurious solutions, with $\gamma$ a nontrivial root of unity in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:runreduce}. The multiplier $\kappa$ of
Section~\ref{sub:runtraces} is therefore a property of this small system in the four run parameters, and not of the $r$-dimensional one. The sign flip of Remark~\ref{rem:friezesign} sends $\vartheta\mapsto\pi-\vartheta$ and
$j\mapsto N-j\equiv-(j+N)\pmod{2N}$, so the two square roots of $s$ along a run are the two labels $\{j,j+N\}$ of \eqref{eq:transN}. This is the pair
by which Corollary~\ref{cor:templatelabel} is taken modulo $\tfrac14$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:jsframe}
For $\varphi=L^2R^n$ the presentation used by Jeong--Sohn, with level matrix $K^{\mathrm{JS}}$ of \cite[(2.12)]{JS26}, has $r=n+2$ but charge vector $Q^{\mathrm{JS}}=(1,2,1,\dots,1)$ --- \emph{one} charge-$2$
field --- where Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} gives $Q=(2,2,1,\dots,1)$, two of them, and $\det K^{\mathrm{JS}}=2^{r-2}$ where the pipeline gives
$\det K=2^r$. The two are nevertheless one system. Writing $D$ for the map $e_1\mapsto2e_2$, $e_2\mapsto e_1$, $e_j\mapsto e_j$ ($j\ge3$), one has
\begin{equation}
K=D\,K^{\mathrm{JS}}D^{\mathsf T},\qquad QP=DQ^{\mathrm{JS}},\qquad \det D=-2,
\label{eq:jsframe}
\end{equation}
with $P$ the transposition of the first two sites, the two $L$-sites. For the first identity, order our sites as $L_1$ (the first $L$ after the
$R$-run), $L_2$, $R_1,\dots,R_n$. Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} gives $K_{L_1L_1}=2n+4$, $K_{L_2L_2}=4$, $K_{L_1L_2}=-4$, $K_{L_1R_j}=2j$,
$K_{L_2R_j}=-2$ and $K_{R_iR_j}=2\min(i,j)$. In $DK^{\mathrm{JS}}D^{\mathsf T}$ the row and column of $L_1$ are those of Jeong--Sohn's site $2$, those of
$L_2$ are twice those of their site $1$, and the $R$-block is unchanged; by \cite[(2.12)]{JS26} the entries are $2n+4$, $4\cdot1$, $2\cdot(-2)$,
$2j$, $2\cdot(-1)$ and $2\min(i,j)$, for every $n\ge1$. The second identity is $DQ^{\mathrm{JS}}=(2,2,1,\dots,1)=QP$. Hence
\[
QK^{-1}Q=P\,Q^{\mathrm{JS}}(K^{\mathrm{JS}})^{-1}Q^{\mathrm{JS}}P:
\]
the two presentations have the \emph{same} matrix $M=QK^{-1}Q$ up to relabelling $L_1\leftrightarrow L_2$, so the same Nahm ladder
$\mathbf N=2(I-M)$, the same positive solution and the same $c_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The Bethe equations are not literally the same. In the coordinates
$(z_{L_2}^2,z_{L_1},z_{R_1},\dots,z_{R_n})$ the pipeline equation at $L_2$, where $Q=2$, is the square of the equation at
site~$1$, where $Q=1$, of the system built from Jeong--Sohn's presentation \cite[(2.12)]{JS26}, and the other equations agree. So every solution of that system solves ours, but not conversely: numerically, one
of the three solutions found at $L^2R$, and three of the five at $L^2R^3$, give $-1$ in its site-$1$ equation. Since the matrices $M$ agree, Jeong--Sohn's ``$\varphi=L^2R^n$'' is the word
$L^2R^n$ in the sense of Section~\ref{sub:word}, and the positive solution of that system is the propagated eigenvector of
Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}, in the site order $d_1\mapsto L_2$, $d_2\mapsto L_1$, $d_{2+j}\mapsto R_j$; it is \eqref{eq:L2Rnclosed}.

What differs is the lattice, not the system. $D$ has elementary divisors $(1,\dots,1,2)$, so the pipeline's $U(1)^r$ charge lattice is an
index-two sublattice of Jeong--Sohn's, and $\det K/\det K^{\mathrm{JS}}=(\det D)^2=4$. The quantities that see $K$ and $Q$ separately rather than only
through $M$ therefore differ by that $\mathbb{Z}_2$: a class carries $2^{\#L}$ vacua in the pipeline presentation and $2^{\#L-1}$ in theirs, and the pipeline
system has the extra solutions just described. Since $\det K=2^r$ is the normalisation selected in Section~\ref{sub:charges}
(Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}), the pipeline presentation is the one attached to the layered triangulation, and the Jeong--Sohn presentation is its $\mathbb{Z}_2$
quotient. The torsion formula of Section~\ref{sec:torsion} and the Gauss-sum and spin computations of Section~\ref{sec:spins}, all of which turn on the
factor $2^{\#L}$, are statements in our unquotiented presentation.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:crossings}
For every hyperbolic word, along the orbit $t_0,t_1,\dots,t_r=t_0$ of the height ratio at the contracting eigenvector: every $L$-step has $t\in(-1,0)$ and every $R$-step has $t<-1$; an $L$ is followed by an $R$
iff $t\in(-1,-\tfrac12)$, and an $R$ by an $L$ iff $t\in(-2,-1)$. The downward crossings of $-1$ are exactly the last $L$ of each $L$-run, the upward
crossings exactly the last $R$ of each $R$-run, and the set of negative $R$-coordinates is the set $\mathcal E$ of last $R$'s of the $R$-runs.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
$t_i=h'(c_1)/h'(c_2)$, with $h'$ the height for the contracting eigenvector $\eta'=(\eta'_1,\eta'_2)$, is the orbit of the initial ratio
$t_0=\eta'_1/\eta'_2$ (the columns of $M_0=1$ being $e_1,e_2$) under the M\"obius maps $L:t\mapsto t/(1+t)$ and $R:t\mapsto t+1$, periodic because
$\eta'\varphi=\lambda^{-1}\eta'$. Since $\varphi$ has positive entries and $\lambda^{-1}<\varphi_{11}$, one has
$\eta'_1=\varphi_{21}/(\lambda^{-1}-\varphi_{11})<0$, so $t_0<0$. Both maps send $(0,\infty)$ into itself, so the orbit never becomes positive, or it
could not return to $t_0$. Hence an $L$ never occurs at $t<-1$ (it would land in $(1,\infty)$) and an $R$ never at $t\in(-1,0)$ (it would land in
$(0,1)$). An $L$ at $t\in(-1,-\tfrac12)$ lands below $-1$, where another $L$ is forbidden; at $t\in(-\tfrac12,0)$ it lands in $(-1,0)$, where an $R$ is
forbidden. Symmetrically an $R$ at $t\in(-2,-1)$ lands in $(-1,0)$, forcing an $L$, and at $t<-2$ lands below $-1$, forcing an $R$. Finally an $R$-step
coordinate is negative iff $t\in(-2,0)$, which, since every $R$-step has $t<-1$, means $t\in(-2,-1)$. The case splits are exhaustive: $t_0\in\mathbb{Q}(\lambda)\smallsetminus\mathbb{Q}$, since $\operatorname{tr}^2\varphi-4$ is not a square, and integral M\"obius maps preserve irrationality, so no $t_i$ equals $-1$, $-\tfrac12$ or $-2$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:ceff}
For every hyperbolic word, the Rogers identity $\sum_{\ell_i=L}L(s_i)=\sum_{\ell_i=R}L(s_i)$ holds at both eigenvectors (at the contracting
one with the extended dilogarithm, whose functional equations carry the defects above), and hence
\[
c_{\mathrm{eff}}=\#L .
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
At $V^*$ the identity is \eqref{eq:rogtel} with $t_r=t_0$. At the contracting eigenvector, by Lemma~\ref{lem:crossings} an $L$-step carries a defect $+\pi^2$ exactly when it is the last $L$ of an $L$-run, and an $R$-step a defect $-\pi^2$ exactly when it is the last $R$ of an $R$-run. Each run therefore contributes one defect, and since there are as many $L$-runs as $R$-runs they cancel. For $c_{\mathrm{eff}}$: in the Nahm
variables $\delta_b=1-x_b$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:bethenahm}, with $x=s$ at $L$-steps and $x=1-s$ at $R$-steps, the reflection identity
$L(1-y)=L(1)-L(y)$ on $(0,1)$, which holds for all real $y\ne0,1$ for the extended $L=\operatorname{Re}R$ since $\operatorname{Re}R(y)+\operatorname{Re}R(1-y)=\pi^2/6$, gives at $V^*$
\[
\sum_bL(\delta_b)=\sum_{\ell_i=L}\bigl(L(1)-L(s_i)\bigr)+\sum_{\ell_i=R}L(s_i)=\#L\,L(1),
\]
so $c_{\mathrm{eff}}=\#L$. The half-index is a Nahm sum in $Q\mathfrak m$ over the sublattice $Q\mathbb{Z}^r$ of index $2^{\#L}$. This does not change the exponential growth: the saddle-point analysis of Proposition~\ref{prop:vstar} works directly in $\mathfrak m$, and only the constant prefactor depends on the lattice. In the same way $\sum_bL(x_b)=\sum_{\ell_i=L}L(s_i)+\sum_{\ell_i=R}\bigl(L(1)-L(s_i)\bigr)=\#R\,L(1)$: the Rogers sum
$c_\alpha=\sum_bL(x_b)/L(1)$ of the class of $V^*$ is $\#R$, and, by the identity at the contracting eigenvector, so is that of the class of
$\sigma V^*$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:farey}
Assume the half-index dictionary of \cite{GKL23} as just stated, and input~(b): the unit lies in the class of $\sigma V^*$, with the unit taken
at $\sigma V^*$ itself, the vacuum selected by the flux rule (Proposition~\ref{prop:flux}; the only such vacuum for odd $m$). Then for every $m\ge3$ (the dominant saddle being $V^*$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:vstar}, with no assumption),
\[
\theta_{V^*}\equiv-\tfrac m4\pmod1,\qquad\text{hence}\quad c(L^mR^m)\equiv c_{\mathrm{eff}}+24\theta_{V^*}=m-6m=\#L-6\#R\ \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 24).
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Write $\mathcal F=\exp(-\Psi/2\pi i)$ as in \eqref{eq:Fdef} and use the Bethe equations in log form,
$Q_b\log(1-x_b)=-(KZ)_b+2\pi in_b$, the integers $n_b$ being those that make these the branches of $Z_b$ and $\log(1-x_b)$ used in evaluating $\Psi$ (Section~\ref{sec:bethe}). Changing $Z_b$ by $2\pi i$ changes the spin by an integer. The other choice of $\log(1-x)$ at $x>1$ changes $n_L$ by even integers and does not change $\theta$. Eliminating the quadratic form,
$\log\mathcal F=\tfrac i{2\pi}\sum_b\tilde L(x_b)+\tfrac12n\cdot Z$ with $\tilde L(x_b)=\operatorname{Li}_2(x_b)+\tfrac12\xi_b\log(1-x_b)$, $\xi_b=-Q_bZ_b$, so
$\arg\mathcal F=\tfrac1{2\pi}\operatorname{Re}\sum\tilde L+\tfrac12\operatorname{Im}(n\cdot Z)$.

At $V^*$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:nahmclosed}, all coordinates are real with $x\in(0,1)$, so $n=0$; they pair as $(x,1-x)$ and the reflection identity gives
$\sum L=m\pi^2/6$, so $\arg\mathcal F(V^*)=\pi m/12$. At the unit the coordinates again pair as $(x,1-x)$ --- the positive values are permuted by the Galois conjugation
$\sigma(\delta_{L_j})=\delta_{L_{m-j}}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:nahmclosed} --- one of these pairs being $(x_{R_m},x_{L_m})$, with $x_{R_m}<0$ the single negative coordinate of
Lemma~\ref{lem:crossings} and $x_{L_m}>1$. The branch integers are those of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:flux}, $n_L=(m,0,\dots,0)$, and at the
negative coordinate $n_{R_m}=\tfrac12K_{R_mR_m}=m$, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:fareygeneral} with $\mathcal E=\{R_m\}$; the
difference $\arg\mathcal F(V^*)-\arg\mathcal F(\text{unit})$ of the arguments at $V^*$ and at the unit then gives $\theta_{V^*}\equiv-m/4\pmod1$. With $c_{\mathrm{eff}}=m$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:ceff} and $c\equiv c_{\mathrm{eff}}+24\theta_{V^*}$, the
formula follows.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:vstar}
The function $\mathcal V$ has exactly one critical point with $Z>0$, and it is the maximum of $\mathcal V$ on $Z\ge0$. So the dominant saddle of
the half-index \eqref{eq:halfindex} exists, and it is the positive vacuum $V^*$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
With $q=e^{-\eta}$ and $Z_a=\eta\mathfrak m_a$, the leading derivative of the exponent of the summand of \eqref{eq:halfindex} is
$-(KZ)_a-Q_a\log(1-e^{-Q_aZ_a})$. So the saddle equations are $Q_a\log(1-x_a)=-(KZ)_a$ with $x_a=e^{-Q_aZ_a}$: the Bethe equations at $\nu=-1$ in
log form with every branch integer zero. The function $\mathcal V$ has Hessian $-K-\operatorname{diag}(Q_a^2x_a/(1-x_a))$, which is negative definite because $K$ is positive definite (Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}). So $\mathcal V$ is strictly concave on $Z>0$. It is continuous on $Z\ge0$, and $\mathcal V\to-\infty$ as $|Z|\to\infty$ in $Z\ge0$, because $K$ is positive definite and the $\operatorname{Li}_2$ terms are bounded. So $\mathcal V$ attains its maximum on $Z\ge0$. Its derivative in $Z_a$ tends to $+\infty$ as $Z_a\to0^+$, so the maximiser is interior. By strict concavity it is the unique critical point. Hence $z_a=e^{Z_a}>1$ and $x_a\in(0,1)$ for all $a$. The Bethe equations have a unique solution with all $x_a\in(0,1)$ (Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}), which is the positive class, and within the class $z_a>1$ selects exactly one vacuum. That the dominant saddle
governs the asymptotics is the standard saddle-point analysis of a Nahm sum with positive-definite $K$ \cite[\S3]{Nahm04}, \cite[Ch.~II]{Zagier07}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:flux}
\textup{(i)} Let $\varphi$ be any hyperbolic word and $V$ a Bethe vacuum. Let $n=n(V)$ be the vector of branch integers of the log-form Bethe equations $Q_b\log(1-x_b)=-(KZ)_b+2\pi in_b$ at $V$. It depends on the vacuum, not only on the word. Write $n_L$ and $c_L$ for the restrictions of $n$ and of the charge vector $c$ to the $L$-sites. The flip of the charge-$2$ coordinates in $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{\#L}$, the indicator of the flipped sites, changes the spin by $\tfrac18\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon+\tfrac12n_L\cdot\varepsilon\pmod1$, and
this equals the spin of the half-integer flux sector $s=\tfrac12\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon$ iff $n_L\equiv c_L\pmod2$.
\textup{(ii)} For $\varphi=L^mR^m$, $m\ge2$, the criterion holds at the all-plus vacuum of the class of $\sigma V^*$, and for odd $m$ the all-plus vacuum is the
only reference vacuum in the unit class for which it holds.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
(i) Flipping the charge-$2$ fields in $\varepsilon$ sends $Z_a\to Z_a+i\pi\varepsilon_a$ with $x$ unchanged. Using the Bethe log equations with branch
integers $n_b$, the fibering operator changes by $\Delta\log\mathcal F=i\pi\,\varepsilon\cdot n_L+\tfrac{i\pi}4\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon$,
where $K_{LL}$ is the $L$-block of $K$ (the submatrix on the $L$-sites), $n_L$ the restriction to the $L$-sites of the vector $n$ of branch
integers of the log-form Bethe equations, and $c_L$ that of the charge vector $c$,
so the flip spin is $\tfrac18\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon+\tfrac12n_L\cdot\varepsilon\pmod1$. For $\mathfrak m=s+k$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}^r_{\ge0}$, the exponent changes by $\tfrac12k^{\mathsf T}Kk+k^{\mathsf T}Ks+c\cdot k\in\mathbb{Z}$, since $K$ is even and $s\in\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}^r$. Every term of $I_s$ has nonnegative coefficients, and the factor $1/\prod_a(q)_{Q_a\mathfrak m_a}$ has constant term $1$, so nothing cancels. Hence the leading power of $I_s$ is $\equiv E(s)\pmod1$ wherever the minimum lies, with
$E(s)\equiv\tfrac18\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon+\tfrac12c_L\cdot\varepsilon\pmod1$. So the two agree for all $\varepsilon$ iff $n_L\equiv c_L\pmod2$.

(ii) At the all-plus unit of $L^mR^m$ only $Z_{R_m}$ and $\log(1-x_{L_m})$ are complex; the $L_1$ equation gives $n_{L_1}=m$ from $K_{R_mL_1}=2m$, the middle ones $0$,
and $L_m$ gives $0$, the $i\pi$ from $\log(1-d^2)$ cancelling $K_{R_mL_m}=-2$. So $n_L=(m,0,\dots,0)$, which is $c_L$ because $c$ is $m$ at the first $L$ after the $R$-run and $0$ at the other $L$'s (Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}); thus $n_L=c_L$ exactly. Any other reference, by $\varepsilon$, changes $n_L$ by $E_{LL}\varepsilon$, where $E_{LL}=\tfrac12K_{LL}$, which is nonzero modulo $2$ for
every $\varepsilon\ne0$ exactly when $E_{LL}$ is invertible over $\mathbb{F}_2$, that is, for odd $m$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:parity}).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:fluxall}
For every hyperbolic word, the branch integers $n_L$ of the log-form Bethe equations at $\sigma V^*$ (notation of Proposition~\ref{prop:flux}) equal the charge vector $c_L$ exactly.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
At $\sigma V^*$ the only complex coordinates are the $R$-run ends $\mathcal E$ of
Lemma~\ref{lem:crossings} ($z<0$) and the last $L$ of each $L$-run ($x'>1$, so $\log(1-x')$ carries $i\pi$). Fix an arbitrary $L$-site $p$. In its equation
$2\log(1-x_p)=-(KZ)_p+2\pi in_p$, with the branches $\operatorname{Im}\log(1-x'_p)=+\pi$ at the last $L$ of each $L$-run and $\operatorname{Im}Z_a=+\pi$ on $\mathcal E$, the imaginary parts are $2\pi[p\text{ last in its run}]$ on the left and $-\pi\sum_{a\in\mathcal E}K_{ap}+2\pi n_p$ on the right. Here $K_{ap}=2b$ if $p$ is the first $L$ after an $R$-run of length $b$ ending at $a$, and $K_{ap}=-2$ if $p$ is the last $L$ before that run; a singleton $L$-run has both. Hence
\[
n_p=[p\text{ last in its run}]+\tfrac12\sum_{a\in\mathcal E}K_{ap}=b\cdot[p\text{ first after a run of length }b]=c_p
\]
exactly, which is that criterion.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:fareygeneral}
Assume (a) the half-index dictionary of \cite{GKL23}, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:farey}, and (b) the vacuum input of Section~\ref{sub:status}:
that the Galois conjugate of $V^*$ lies in the unit class, the class of $\sigma V^*$, with the unit taken at $\sigma V^*$ itself (the vacuum of the unit
class selected by the flux rule, Proposition~\ref{prop:fluxall}; the only such vacuum when $\operatorname{tr}\varphi$ is odd, Lemma~\ref{lem:parity}). Then for
every hyperbolic word,
\[
c\equiv\#L-6\#R\pmod{24};
\]
here $c_{\mathrm{eff}}=\#L$ is proved for every hyperbolic word, without (a) and (b) (Theorem~\ref{thm:ceff}).
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} the Farey pipeline produces the run-structure $K$ and $c$. By Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated} the closed form is the
positive Nahm solution and, with the contracting eigenvector, gives $\sigma V^*$; the Rogers identity holds at both eigenvectors by
Theorem~\ref{thm:ceff}, so $c_{\mathrm{eff}}=\#L$. In the notation of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:farey}, $\operatorname{Re}\tilde L(x_b)=L(x_b)$ is the Rogers
dilogarithm, extended as in Theorem~\ref{thm:ceff} (at the negative coordinates $\tilde L$ also has an imaginary part, which the argument does not use), so $\operatorname{Re}\sum_b\tilde L(x_b)=\#R\,L(1)$ at both $V^*$ and $\sigma V^*$ by that theorem,
and $\theta_{V^*}$ is carried by the branch term $\tfrac12\operatorname{Im}(n\cdot Z)$ alone; at $V^*$ it vanishes, and at $\sigma V^*$ we take
$\operatorname{Im}Z_b=+\pi$ at the negative coordinates. By the run-end structure, at the last $R$ of a run of length $b$ one has $K_{bb}=2\min(b,b)=2b$ and runs do
not couple, so with $\mathcal E=\{\text{last }R\text{ of each }R\text{-run}\}$ the set of negative coordinates of Lemma~\ref{lem:crossings} and $K_{\mathcal E\mathcal E}$ the
block of $K$ on those sites, $\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}K_{\mathcal E\mathcal E}\mathbf1=2\#R$ exactly; hence
$\sum_{b\in\mathcal E}n_b=\tfrac12\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}K_{\mathcal E\mathcal E}\mathbf1=\#R$ (the $L$-coordinates have real $Z$, so they do not
enter the imaginary part), giving $\theta_{V^*}\equiv-\tfrac1{2\pi}\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\pi\#R=-\#R/4$ and $c\equiv\#L+24(-\#R/4)=\#L-6\#R$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Let $D=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(Q_a^2x_a/(1-x_a)\bigr)$, the diagonal by which the Hessian of the twisted superpotential
differs from $K$, with blocks $D_R$, $D_L$ on the $R$- and $L$-sites. By \eqref{eq:Habelian}, $\mathcal H=W_c^2\det(K+D)\prod_a(1-x_a)$, and
$W_c(V^*)=\lambda$ (Proposition~\ref{obs:stretch}). By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} the block $K_{RR}$ is the direct sum over the $R$-runs of
the fans $F_b=(2\min(i,j))_{i,j=1}^b$. Eliminating the $R$-sites gives $\det(K+D)=\det(K_{RR}+D_R)\det S$, where
\[
S=(K+D)_{LL}-(K+D)_{LR}(K_{RR}+D_R)^{-1}(K+D)_{RL}
\]
is the \emph{$L$-Schur complement}. It is a \emph{periodic Jacobi matrix} of order $n=\#L$: $S_{ii}=d_i$, $S_{i,i+1}=S_{i+1,i}=\beta_i$
(indices modulo $n$, entries added when positions coincide), and all other entries zero. The couplings are $-2$ inside the $L$-runs and,
across the $q$-th $R$-run, of length $b$,
\[
\beta_q=-2-\mathsf r^{\mathsf T}(F_b+D_R)^{-1}s,\qquad \mathsf r=2(1,\dots,b)^{\mathsf T},\ s=-2\cdot\mathbf1,
\]
the ramp $\mathsf r$ being the column of $K$ that couples the run to the first $L$ after it, and $s$ the column that couples it to the last $L$ before it. The \emph{transfer matrix} of $S$ is
$T=T_n\cdots T_1$ with $T_i=\begin{psmallmatrix}-d_i/\beta_i&-\beta_{i-1}/\beta_i\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$. Each factor has determinant $\beta_{i-1}/\beta_i$, so the product $T$ has determinant $1$. Its
eigenvalues $\Lambda^{\pm1}$ are the \emph{Floquet multipliers}, and $\operatorname{tr} T-2$ is the \emph{Floquet discriminant}. Hill's formula
(\cite{Hill}; the discrete form used here is that of \cite{vM76}) reads
\[
\det S=(-1)^n\prod_{i=1}^n\beta_i\,(\operatorname{tr} T-2).
\]
The torsion formula splits into two halves, both at $x=V^*$:
\begin{align}
&\det S=(-1)^{\#L}\textstyle\prod_i\beta_i\,((\operatorname{tr}\varphi)^2-4),\tag{A}\\
&\det(K_{RR}+D_R)\textstyle\prod_a(1-x_a)\,(-1)^{\#L}\prod_i\beta_i=2^{\#L}/\lambda .\tag{B}
\end{align}
Multiplied together with $W_c(V^*)^2=\lambda^2$ they give the formula. Half (A) says that the Floquet discriminant of $S$ is $(\operatorname{tr}\varphi)^2-4$:
a Floquet solution with multiplier $\lambda^{-2}$ is written down explicitly, as a limit of the universal Floquet vector of
Lemma~\ref{lem:floqvec}, and Hill's formula then gives $\det S$. Half (B) reduces to one identity per $R$-run, Lemma~\ref{lem:perrun}, which
holds for every frieze row and is used again at the general classes in Section~\ref{sub:hillgen}. Both halves, and the two lemmas, are proved
in Appendix~\ref{app:torsion}. The theorem below assembles them and obtains $\mathcal H(\sigma V^*)$ by Galois conjugation; the remark after
the theorem records what the formula says about input~(b).
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:torsion}
For every hyperbolic word, with $V^*$ the positive vacuum \eqref{eq:propagated},
\[
\mathcal H(V^*)=2^{\#L}\lambda\,|A_-||A_+|,\qquad \mathcal H(\sigma V^*)=2^{\#L}\lambda^{-1}|A_-||A_+|,
\]
where $|A_-||A_+|=|\det(\varphi-1)\det(\varphi+1)|$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
$\mathcal H(V^*)=W_c(V^*)^2\det(K+D)\prod(1-x)$ with $W_c(V^*)=\lambda$ by Proposition~\ref{obs:stretch}. At $V^*$ all heights are positive, so $D_R>0$,
the $R$-blocks are positive definite and $\det(K+D)=\det(K_{RR}+D_R)\det S$; the couplings $\beta$ are nonzero, since the right side of \eqref{eq:perrun} in Lemma~\ref{lem:perrun} is positive at $V^*$. (A) gives
$\det S=(-1)^{\#L}\prod\beta_i|A_-||A_+|$, and (B), by Lemma~\ref{lem:perrun}, gives
$\det(K_{RR}+D_R)\prod(1-x)(-1)^{\#L}\prod\beta_i=2^{\#L}/\lambda$; multiplying, $\det(K+D)\prod(1-x)=2^{\#L}|A_-||A_+|/\lambda$. All quantities lie in
$\mathbb{Q}(\lambda)$ and $x(\sigma V^*)=\sigma(x(V^*))$, so the second formula is the Galois conjugate of the first.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:internal}
Theorem~\ref{thm:torsion} also tests input (b) for $LR^n$, for every $n$, through the dictionary \eqref{eq:dict}: $S_{00}=a_0$, with $a_0$ as in \eqref{eq:as}, gives
$\mathcal H(\text{unit})=a_0^{-2}=\mathcal H(\sigma V^*)$. Here $S_{00}=a_0$ is the value of $|Z_{S^3_b}|$ in the degenerate limit \cite[(2.11), (3.107)]{GKLSY21}, also used by Gang--Kim \cite{GK22}. This is agreement, not a proof of (b). For general words it shows that (b) implies that the unit's $\mathcal H$ is $2^{\#L-1}a_0^{-2}$, and conversely when no degenerate class has
that value (for words with no singleton run the non-degenerate classes are those of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} by Theorem~\ref{thm:complete}, and under the non-degeneracy condition they have rational $\mathcal H$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall}). Since $a_0/a_3=\lambda(\varphi)$ identically (as noted after Proposition~\ref{obs:stretch}), this condition is equivalent to
$|S_{0V^*}/S_{00}|=1/\lambda$. Input (b) is stated in Section~\ref{sub:status}.

Gang--Kim's consistency conditions include one meant to identify the vacuum among the Bethe vacua,
$\bigl|\sum_\alpha\mathcal H_\alpha^{-1}\mathcal F_\alpha\bigr|=\mathcal H_{\alpha=0}^{-1/2}$, besides $\sum_\alpha\mathcal H_\alpha^{-1}=1$ and
$|\mathcal F_\alpha|=1$ for every $\alpha$ \cite[(2.17)]{GK22}. For modular data the left side is $\bigl|\sum_\alpha S_{0\alpha}^2\theta_\alpha\bigr|$, the modulus of a Gauss
sum divided by the global dimension, which is $S_{00}$. So the criterion holds automatically, and what it records is the value of $|S_{00}|$.
On their data this value is $a_0$, never $a_3$, for $k=5,7,\dots,15$; this is a numerical check. Theorems~\ref{thm:torsion} and~\ref{thm:Hall} give, for every
word and up to the factor $2^{\#L-1}$, the $\mathcal H$-values (not their multiplicities) of the Gang--Kim template, Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} at the classes of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} under the non-degeneracy condition; the modular data \eqref{eq:GKT} with $k=\operatorname{tr}\varphi$. So for every word whose modular
data is the template, the first paragraph places the unit in the class of $\sigma V^*$, provided no degenerate class has the same $\mathcal H$.
Whether the spins match the template is taken up in Section~\ref{sub:template}.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:Hspectrum}
Let $m\ge3$ be odd. Each class carries $2^m$ vacua, and:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] the identity classes, of $V^*$ and of $\sigma V^*$, have $\mathcal H=2^m\lambda^{\pm1}m^2(m^2+4)$;
\item[\textup{(ii)}] every $A_+$ class of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} satisfying the hypothesis $\det(F+D_R)\ne0$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} has
$\mathcal H=2^m(m^2+4)=2^{\#L}|A_+|$, and the classes of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} are all the non-degenerate non-identity classes;
\item[\textup{(iii)}] if, in addition, the $A_-$ sector consists of $\tfrac{m^2-1}2$ classes with $\mathcal H=2^mm^2=2^{\#L}|A_-|$ and the $A_+$ sector
of $\tfrac{m^2+3}2$ non-identity classes, each with $\mathcal H=2^m(m^2+4)$, and there are no other classes, then the handle-gluing operator takes four values, three up to Galois conjugation, on $m^2+3$ classes and
$2^m(m^2+3)$ vacua, and the sum rule over the vacua closes identically:
\[
\sum_\alpha\frac1{\mathcal H_\alpha}=\frac{m^2-1}{2m^2}+\frac{m^2+3}{2(m^2+4)}+\frac{\lambda+\lambda^{-1}}{m^2(m^2+4)}=1 .
\]
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The $2^m$ vacua of a class are the sign choices of Section~\ref{sec:bethe}. (i) is Theorem~\ref{thm:torsion}. (ii) is Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall},
with Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} for completeness, every run of $L^mR^m$ having length $m\ge2$. For $m$ a prime power every nonzero kernel vector of the
$A_-$ sector is degenerate. Indeed, the kernel vectors are $v=m v'$ with $v'\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^2$, and $\langle v,e\rangle/m^2=\langle v',e\rangle/m$. The
middle slopes of the $L$-run are $(i,1)$ and those of the $R$-run are $(1+im,i)$, $i=1,\dots,m$ (proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:lines}). So
$\langle v',e\rangle\equiv0\pmod m$ is solvable on the $L$-run if $v'_2$ is prime to $m$, and on the $R$-run if $v'_1$ is. Otherwise the prime $p$
of $m=p^e$ divides both; then $v'=pv''$ and the same argument applies to $v''$ modulo $m/p$. So the non-degenerate non-identity classes all lie in $A_+$. This fails for other $m$: at $m=15$, $8$ of the $112$ classes of $A_-$ are non-degenerate, and at $m=21$, $12$ of $220$. (iii) is arithmetic, with $\lambda+\lambda^{-1}=m^2+2$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:sumrule}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word of odd trace $k$, and suppose $\mathcal H$ takes the three values $2^{\#L}|A_-|$, $2^{\#L}|A_+|$ and
$2^{\#L}\lambda^{\pm1}|A_-||A_+|$ on the classes, with multiplicities $\#(A_-/\!\pm)-1$, $\#(A_+/\!\pm)-1$ and $1,1$. Then
\[
\sum_\alpha\frac1{\mathcal H_\alpha}=1 .
\]
For even $k$ with $A_-$ and $A_+$ cyclic, the same hypotheses give $1+k/(k^2-4)$ instead.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Each class carries $2^{\#L}$ vacua, so the factor $2^{\#L}$ cancels and the sum over vacua is the sum over classes of the reciprocals of $|A_-|$,
$|A_+|$ and $\lambda^{\pm1}|A_-||A_+|$. With $|A_\mp|=k\mp2$ and $\lambda+\lambda^{-1}=\operatorname{tr}\varphi=k$, and $\#(A/\!\pm)=(|A|+1)/2$ for odd order,
\[
\sum_\alpha\frac1{\mathcal H_\alpha}=\frac{k-3}{2(k-2)}+\frac{k+1}{2(k+2)}+\frac k{(k-2)(k+2)}=1 .
\]
For even $k$ and cyclic $A_\mp$ one has $\#(A/\!\pm)=|A|/2+1$ instead, and the first two terms become $\tfrac12$ each,
leaving the excess $k/(k^2-4)$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- observation-3: body_md -->
\label{obs:spectrumgen}
\emph{Harvesting} the Bethe classes of a word means solving the deformed system of Section~\ref{sec:bethe} numerically from many random
starting points at a fixed small $\epsilon$ and collecting the distinct classes reached. Harvesting $LR^3$, $LR^5$ and $L^2RLR$ at
$\epsilon=10^{-3}$ reproduces the three-value structure with the predicted multiplicities, the even-trace word $L^2RLR$ giving the sum
$1+k/(k^2-4)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:sumrule}.
<!-- end observation-3 -->
<!-- observation-4: body_md -->
\label{obs:tauquant}
At every non-identity Bethe class $\alpha$ of every word tested, the run traces are
\begin{equation}
\tau_\rho=2\cos\frac{j_\rho\pi}{N_\alpha},\qquad j_\rho\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad N_\alpha=|A_-|\ \text{or}\ |A_+|\ \text{by sector},
\label{eq:tauquant}
\end{equation}
and
\[
\mathcal H_\alpha=2^{\#L}N_\alpha :
\]
\emph{the quantisation modulus of the frieze trace is the value of the handle-gluing operator.} At the two identity classes $j_\rho=0$ in every run and
$\mathcal H=2^{\#L}\lambda^{\pm1}|A_-||A_+|$. The harvests record indices only on runs of length at least $3$, so on a word with short runs fewer indices are visible.
<!-- end observation-4 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:tworun}
Let $\varphi=L^aR^b$ with $a,b$ odd, $N=ab+4$, and $\kappa=\tfrac12(N-a)$, an integer with $2\kappa\equiv-a$ and $b\kappa\equiv2\pmod N$. For every $j$
with $\gcd(j,N)=1$ put $\vartheta=j\pi/N$ and
\[
z_{L_i}=\varepsilon_i\,\frac{\sin((i+\kappa)\vartheta)}{\sin\vartheta}\ (1\le i\le a),\qquad
z_{R_i}=\Bigl(1-\frac{\sin^2(\kappa\vartheta)}{\sin^2((i\kappa-1)\vartheta)}\Bigr)^{-1}\ (1\le i\le b),
\]
with $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}^a$.
Then $z$ solves the Bethe equations \eqref{eq:bethe}. The solutions for $j$ and $N-j$ coincide, so these are $\tfrac12\phi(N)$ classes of
$2^a$ vacua ($\phi$ Euler's function), one for each $\pm j\in(\mathbb{Z}/N)^\times/\!\pm$; the run traces of the class $\pm j$ are
\[
\tau_L=2\cos\frac{j\pi}N,\qquad \tau_R=2\cos\frac{\kappa j\pi}N ,
\]
so its index vector is $(j,\kappa j)$, with $\kappa\equiv-2^{-1}a$ the multiplier; and it is the index vector
\eqref{eq:ellrho} of the kernel vector $v=(-\kappa j,j)\in\mathcal K_+$, since $\iota_L(v)=j$ and $\iota_R(v)=-\kappa j-aj\equiv \kappa j$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
This is the case $v=(-\kappa j,j)$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} below, whose proof does not use the present statement. Starting from the basis $(e_1,e_2)$ the $L$-run has kept slope $e_1$ and
middle slopes $e_2+ie_1$, with $\langle v,e_1\rangle=-j$ and $\langle v,e_2+ie_1\rangle=-(i+\kappa)j$, so $f(e_1)^2/f(e_2+ie_1)^2=
\sin^2\vartheta/\sin^2((i+\kappa)\vartheta)$; the $R$-run has kept slope $e_2+ae_1$ and middle slopes $e_1+i(e_2+ae_1)$, with
$\langle v,e_2+ae_1\rangle=-(a+\kappa)j\equiv \kappa j$ and $\langle v,e_1+i(e_2+ae_1)\rangle\equiv(i\kappa-1)j$. No denominator vanishes:
$\sin((i+\kappa)\vartheta)=0$ needs $i+\kappa\equiv0\pmod N$, and $\kappa+1\le i+\kappa\le \kappa+a<N$; $\sin((i\kappa-1)\vartheta)=0$ needs $i\equiv \kappa^{-1}\equiv2^{-1}b=\tfrac12(N+b)>b+1$.
And $v\in\mathcal K_+$:
$(\varphi+1)v=\begin{psmallmatrix}2+ab&a\\b&2\end{psmallmatrix}\begin{psmallmatrix}-\kappa j\\j\end{psmallmatrix}\equiv
\begin{psmallmatrix}(2\kappa+a)j\\(2-b\kappa)j\end{psmallmatrix}\equiv0\pmod N$. The run traces are read off the chains.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:allwords}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word of length $r$, let $N=|A_\mp|$ be the order of the sector $A_\mp$ in which we work, and let $v\in\mathcal K_\mp$, i.e.\ $(\varphi\mp1)v\equiv0\pmod N$. Put
\[
f(e)=\sin\frac{\pi\langle v,e\rangle}N\qquad(e\in\mathbb{Z}^2),
\]
and suppose $f(\mathsf m_t)\ne0$ for the middle slope $\mathsf m_t$ of every tetrahedron $\Delta_t$, $t=1,\dots,r$. Then, with $\mathsf k_t$ the kept slope
of $\Delta_t$,
\[
x_t=\frac{f(\mathsf k_t)^2}{f(\mathsf m_t)^2}\ \ (L\text{-flip}),\qquad x_t=1-\frac{f(\mathsf k_t)^2}{f(\mathsf m_t)^2}\ \ (R\text{-flip}),\qquad t=1,\dots,r,
\]
with $z_t=x_t^{-1/Q_t}$ on either branch, solves the Bethe equations \eqref{eq:bethe} at $\epsilon=0$. Along a run of length $a$ with kept
slope $p$, entered from a basis $\{p,q\}$, the coordinates are $f(p)^2/f(q+ip)^2$, $i=1,\dots,a$; on an $R$-run these are the frieze coordinates $1-x$. So the run's frieze trace is
$2\cos(\pi\langle v,p\rangle/N)$ and its index is $\iota_\rho(v)$ of \eqref{eq:ellrho}, up to sign: the index vector of the class is the index vector of
$v$ up to sign. Theorem~\ref{thm:tworun} is the case $\varphi=L^aR^b$, $v=(-\kappa j,j)$. The solution is a Bethe class with $\mathcal H\ne0$ under the non-degeneracy condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall}, which gives its value of $\mathcal H$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Three facts about $f$. (a) \emph{Ptolemy}: for any $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, $f(a+b)^2-f(a)^2=f(b)f(2a+b)$ and $f(a+b)^2-f(b)^2=f(a)f(a+2b)$, by
$\sin^2X-\sin^2Y=\sin(X-Y)\sin(X+Y)$. So at an $L$-flip $1-x_t=f(b)f(2a+b)/f(a+b)^2$ and at an $R$-flip $x_t=f(a)f(a+2b)/f(a+b)^2$: every
shape is a ratio of two opposite-edge products. (b) \emph{Periodicity}: $\langle v,\varphi e\rangle=\langle\varphi^{-1}v,e\rangle$ and
$\varphi^{-1}v\equiv\pm v\pmod N$, so $f(\varphi e)=\pm f(e)$ up to a sign $(-1)^{\langle w,e\rangle}$, $Nw=\varphi^{-1}v\mp v$; on the
squares $f(e)^2$ and on the opposite-edge products $f(b)f(2a+b)$, $f(a)f(a+2b)$ the sign is $+$, since $\langle w,b\rangle+\langle
w,2a+b\rangle$ is even. Hence the shapes $x_t$ are well defined on the cyclic word. (c) Every entry of $K$ is even
(Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}), so \eqref{eq:bethe} reads $(1-x_b)^{Q_b}=\prod_ax_a^{Q_b(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{ab}}$ and involves the $L$-coordinates only
through $z_L^2=1/x_L$; where a half-integer power $x_L^{-1/2}$ appears below it stands for $f(\mathsf m_t)/f(\mathsf k_t)$ with its sign (and $x_L^{1/2}$ for its inverse), and only
its square matters.

Now fix an $L$-run of length $a$ with kept slope $p$, entered from the basis $(p,q)$, so that its tetrahedra have middle slopes
$c_i=q+ip$ and $x_{L_i}=f(p)^2/f(c_i)^2$; let the $R$-run following it have length $b$, kept slope $c_a$ and middle slopes
$g_j=p+jc_a$ ($g_0=p$, $g_1=c_{a+1}$), so $x_{R_j}=1-f(c_a)^2/f(g_j)^2=f(g_{j-1})f(g_{j+1})/f(g_j)^2$; and let the $R$-run preceding it
have length $b'$, kept slope $q$ and middle slopes $e_j=p'+jq$ with $e_{b'}=p$, $e_{b'+1}=c_1$, so that the last $L$ before that run has
$x=f(p')^2/f(q)^2$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula} the entries of $K_{\mathrm{raw}}=Q^{-1}KQ^{-1}$ are: $(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{L_iL_i}=1$ and
$(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{L_iL_{i\pm1}}=-\tfrac12$ at an interior $L_i$; at the first $L$ of the run, $(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{L_1L_1}=1+\tfrac{b'}2$, $-\tfrac12$ to $L_2$
and to the last $L$ of the preceding $L$-run, and the ramp $(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{L_1R'_j}=j$ to the $j$-th $R$ of the preceding run; at the last $L$,
$(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{L_aL_a}=1$, $-\tfrac12$ to $L_{a-1}$ and to the first $L$ of the following $L$-run, and $(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{L_aR_j}=-1$ to every $R$ of the
following run; and $(K_{\mathrm{raw}})_{R_iR_k}=2\min(i,k)$ within a run.

\emph{Interior $L$-sites:} $(1-x_i)^2=x_i^2/(x_{i-1}x_{i+1})$ is the square of $f(c_{i-1})f(c_{i+1})/f(c_i)^2$ by $f(c_{i-1})f(c_{i+1})=f(c_i)^2-f(p)^2$, which is (a).

\emph{$R$-sites:} summation by parts gives
\[
\prod_ix_{R_i}^{2\min(i,k)}=\Bigl(\frac{f(g_0)}{f(g_k)}\Bigr)^{2}\Bigl(\frac{f(g_{b+1})}{f(g_b)}\Bigr)^{2k},
\]
so the equation at $R_k$, $1-x_{R_k}=x_{L'_1}^k\,x_{L_a}^{-1}\prod_ix_{R_i}^{2\min(i,k)}$ with $L'_1$ the first $L$ of the next run, reads
$f(c_a)^2=x_{L_a}^{-1}f(g_0)^2\bigl[x_{L'_1}(f(g_{b+1})/f(g_b))^2\bigr]^k$. Both brackets are identities: $x_{L_a}=f(p)^2/f(c_a)^2$ and
$g_0=p$; and $L'_1$ is the $L$-flip at the basis $(g_b,c_a)$, so $x_{L'_1}=f(g_b)^2/f(g_{b+1})^2$.

\emph{The last $L$ of a run:} $(1-x_{L_a})/x_{L_a}=f(c_{a-1})f(c_{a+1})/f(p)^2$ by (a); the right side of the equation is
\[
x_{L_{a-1}}^{-1/2}x_{L'_1}^{-1/2}\prod_jx_{R_j}^{-1}=\frac{f(c_{a-1})}{f(p)}\cdot\frac{f(g_{b+1})}{f(g_b)}\cdot\frac{f(g_1)f(g_b)}{f(g_0)f(g_{b+1})}
=\frac{f(c_{a-1})f(g_1)}{f(p)^2},
\]
and $g_1=c_{a+1}$.

\emph{The first $L$ of a run:} $(1-x_{L_1})/x_{L_1}=f(c_0)f(c_2)/f(p)^2$; the right side is the product
$x_{L_1}^{b'/2}x_{L_2}^{-1/2}x_{L_{\mathrm{prev}}}^{-1/2}\prod_jx_{R'_j}{}^{j}$, where
\[
\prod_jx_{R'_j}{}^{j}=\Bigl(\frac{f(e_{b'+1})}{f(e_{b'})}\Bigr)^{b'}\frac{f(e_0)}{f(e_{b'})}
\]
by the same summation by parts; $x_{L_1}^{b'/2}(f(e_{b'+1})/f(e_{b'}))^{b'}=(f(p)/f(c_1))^{b'}(f(c_1)/f(p))^{b'}=1$, and what is left is
$\frac{f(c_2)}{f(p)}\cdot\frac{f(q)}{f(p')}\cdot\frac{f(p')}{f(p)}=\frac{f(q)f(c_2)}{f(p)^2}$, with $c_0=q$.

(For a run of length $1$ the first and last $L$ coincide; its equation carries both the ramp and the $-1$ couplings, and the two
