computations combine: the right side is $\frac{f(p')}{f(p)}\cdot\frac{f(q)}{f(p')}\cdot\frac{f(g_{b+1})}{f(g_b)}\cdot\frac{f(g_1)f(g_b)}{f(g_0)f(g_{b+1})}
=\frac{f(q)f(c_2)}{f(p)^2}$ again.) Every equation is therefore an identity between values of $f$ on slopes of the cyclic word, and the only place the hypothesis on $v$
enters is (b), which makes $f$ single-valued on the slopes when the word closes up. The run traces are read off $f(c_i)=\sin(\pi(\langle
v,q\rangle+i\langle v,p\rangle)/N)$, and $\langle v,p\rangle$ is the coordinate of $v$ in the basis $(p,q)$ that the $L$-flip $(p,q)\mapsto(p,p+q)$
leaves invariant.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- observation-5: body_md -->
\label{obs:kervec}
\textup{(i)} For every non-identity Bethe class $\alpha$ of the sector $A_\mp$, of order $N=|A_\mp|$, there is a kernel vector $v_\alpha\in\mathcal K_\mp$ with
\[
j_\rho(\alpha)\equiv\pm\,\iota_\rho(v_\alpha)\pmod N\qquad\text{for every run $\rho$ carrying an index.}
\]
\textup{(ii)} Where $N$ is a prime power and the sector is cyclic, $v_\alpha$ is determined up to sign and $\alpha\mapsto\pm v_\alpha$ is
injective; in every sector whose harvest is complete (all its classes found) it is a bijection onto $(\mathcal K_\mp\smallsetminus0)/\!\pm$, the identity class taking $v=0$.
\textup{(iii)} The spins of the vacua of the class, defined by \eqref{eq:spindef} through the fibering operator, agree modulo $\tfrac14$. Modulo $\tfrac14$ they are given by a quadratic form in $v_\alpha$: with $v_\alpha$ lifted to $\mathbb{Z}^2$, for every vacuum $V$ of the class,
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{spin}(V)\equiv\pm\frac{v_\alpha\wedge\varphi v_\alpha}{4N^2}+q_\mp^{*}\pmod{\tfrac14},
\label{eq:kerspin}
\end{equation}
with $N=|A_\mp|$ as above and $q_\mp^{*}$ the spin of $V^*$, resp.\ $\sigma V^*$, for the sector, so that \eqref{eq:kerspin} holds at $v=0$ too, and with
the sign $-$ on $A_+$ and $+$ on $A_-$. Formula \eqref{eq:kerspin} is a property of the spin, not its definition.

\textup{Status.} At the non-degenerate classes the following are proved.
Part (i) holds for words with no singleton run: by Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} every non-degenerate class is a class of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}, whose index vector is that of its kernel vector. Conversely, every non-degenerate kernel vector occurs, by Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}.
In (ii), injectivity holds for words with no singleton run, since Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} determines $v$ up to sign.
Part (iii) holds for odd trace, by Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers} together with the reduction after Observation~\ref{obs:basevac}.
The rest of (ii), and (i) and (iii) at the degenerate classes, are numerical.
<!-- end observation-5 -->
<!-- observation-6: body_md -->
\label{obs:basevac}
Let $\operatorname{tr}\varphi$ be odd. \textup{(i)} \textup{(}Proved.\textup{)} $E_{LL}=\tfrac12K_{LL}$ is invertible over $\mathbb{F}_2$ for every word of odd trace and singular for
every word of even trace (Lemma~\ref{lem:parity}), so the base Bethe vacuum $V_{\varepsilon_0}$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:spinq} is defined in every class
of every word of odd trace. (It is the Bethe vacuum of the class from which the spin function is exactly $q$.) \textup{(ii)} At the class of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} with kernel vector $v\in\mathcal K_\mp$,
$N=|A_\mp|$ and $w=(\varphi\mp1)v/N\in\mathbb{Z}^2$,
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{spin}(V_{\varepsilon_0})\equiv\frac{\#R}{24}\pm[4^{-1}]_N\,\frac{v\wedge w}{N}\pmod1,
\label{eq:basevac}
\end{equation}
where $[4^{-1}]_N$ is the inverse of $4$ modulo $N$ and the sign is $+$ on $\mathcal K_-$ and $-$ on $\mathcal K_+$; so the spin function on the whole class is
$\#R/24\pm[4^{-1}]_N\,v\wedge w/N+q(\varepsilon+\varepsilon_0)$.
<!-- end observation-6 -->
<!-- observation-7: body_md -->
\label{obs:strata}
Continuing each harvested $A_-$ class from $\epsilon=10^{-3}$ to $10^{-5}$ and fitting the exponents $p_b$ of $z_b=C_b\epsilon^{p_b}(1+o(1))$, one finds
integer exponents (to $10^{-3}$) with the following pattern. Below, the exponent vector $(p_b)$ and the limit $z$ are listed site by site. A vertical bar $|$ separates the $L$-sites, listed before it, from the $R$-sites, listed after it; on each side the sites are in their order in the word.
For example $(-2\,|\,{-1},-1,2)$ at $LR^3$ means $p=-2$ at the single $L$-site and $p=-1,-1,2$ at the three $R$-sites.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] \emph{Most classes are not degenerate.} At $L^2R^3$ one of the two $A_-$ classes found has every $p_b=0$, with
limit $z=(\pm\tfrac12,\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\,|\,-\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,4)$ exactly, the class of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} at $v=(2,3)$, $N=6$; at $L^2RLR^3$ six of the seven found are finite. Those classes need no
leading-order analysis: they are ordinary solutions of the undeformed system, and the closed form of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} applies to
them directly.
\item[\textup{(ii)}] \emph{In the degenerate classes reached, the $R$-coordinates degenerate on one $R$-run only, except for the $L^3R^3$ classes of Observation~\ref{obs:l3r3minus}}: in that run, of length $b$, the exponents are
\[
(p_1,\dots,p_b)=(-1,\,0,\dots,0,\,-1,\,2)
\]
up to a cyclic rotation of the run --- $(-1,-1,2)$ at $b=3$, $(-1,0,-1,2)$ at $b=4$, $(-1,0,0,-1,2)$ at $b=5$, $(-1,0,0,0,-1,2)$ at $b=6$.
Among the classes reached, on a word with a single $R$-run every $L$-site has exponent $-2$ as well, $(-2\,|\,{-1},-1,2)$ at $LR^3$ and $(-2,-2,-2\,|\,{-1},-1,2)$ at
$L^3R^3$ --- but not among all degenerate classes: the complete $A_-$ sector of $L^3R^3$ (Observation~\ref{obs:l3r3minus}) also contains
classes with a single degenerate $L$-site, of the placement types of Section~\ref{sec:lines}; on a word with two $R$-runs the $L$-sites stay finite and only one run degenerates, the degenerate class of $L^2RLR^3$ having
$(0,0,0\,|\,0,-1,2,-1)$. Here the three $L$-sites are finite; the first $R$-site is the run $R$ of length $1$, which stays finite; and the run $R^3$ has $(-1,2,-1)$, a cyclic rotation of $(-1,-1,2)$.
\item[\textup{(iii)}] A single word therefore carries classes of both kinds; at $L^2R^3$ the two $A_-$ classes found are one of each.
\end{enumerate}
This was measured on seven words with $R$-runs of lengths $3$ to $6$, among them the four named above. The harvest is at a fixed $\epsilon$, so
which classes it reaches is biased towards the finite ones, and the counts above are of classes found rather than of classes.
<!-- end observation-7 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:wcmono}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word and let $\tilde v\in\mathbb{Z}^r$ be the run vector
\[
\tilde v_b=\begin{cases}
j, & b\ \text{the }j\text{-th }L\text{ of its run,}\\
a, & b\ \text{the first }R\text{ of a run preceded by an }L\text{-run of length }a,\\
0, & b\ \text{any other }R .
\end{cases}
\]
Then $K\tilde v=2c$, so $c$ lies in the image of $K$ over $\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$. Consequently, at any solution of
the deformed equations \eqref{eq:bethe} (with right side $(1+\epsilon)^{c_b}$),
\begin{equation}
W_c^2=(1+\epsilon)^{\tilde v\cdot c}\prod_b(1-x_b)^{-\tilde v_bQ_b}
=(1+\epsilon)^{\tilde v\cdot c}\prod_{L\text{-runs}}\ \prod_{j=1}^{a}(1-x_{L_j})^{-2j}
\cdot\prod_{R\text{-runs}}(1-x_{R_1})^{-a},
\label{eq:wcmono}
\end{equation}
which at $\epsilon=0$ is a monomial with integer exponents read off the run structure.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
$K\tilde v=2c$ is checked row by row against Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}. Let an $L$-run of length $a$ be
preceded by an $R$-run of length $b'$, which is preceded by an $L$-run of length $a'$, and followed by an $R$-run of length $b$.
At an interior $L_i$: $4i-2(i-1)-2(i+1)=0$. At $L_1$ ($a\ge2$): the diagonal $4+2b'$, the coupling $-2$ to $L_2$, the coupling $-2$
to the last $L$ of the previous run (where $\tilde v=a'$) and the ramp $+2\cdot1$ to the first $R$ of the preceding run (where
$\tilde v=a'$) give $(4+2b')-4-2a'+2a'=2b'$. At $L_a$ ($a\ge2$): $4a-2(a-1)-2\cdot1-2a=0$, the last two terms being the coupling to
the first $L$ of the next run ($\tilde v=1$) and the $-2$ to the first $R$ of the following run ($\tilde v=a$). At a singleton $L$ the
two computations add: $(4+2b')-2a'+2a'-2-2=2b'$, and the case $\#L=1$ ($LR^n$) is this with $a'=1$ and both $-2$'s on the
diagonal. At the $j$-th $R$ of a run preceded by an $L$-run of length $a$: $2\min(j,1)\,a+2j-2a=2j$. In every case the result is $2c$.

The first part is what makes $W_c^2$ computable. The exponent of $W_c^2=e^{2c\cdot Z}$ is $2c\cdot Z=\tilde v\cdot KZ$, and the Bethe
equations express $KZ$ through the logarithms $\log(1-x_b)$. In detail, in log form \eqref{eq:bethe} reads $\sum_aK_{ab}Z_a=2\pi in_b-Q_b\log(1-x_b)+c_b\log(1+\epsilon)$, so, using $K=K^{\mathsf T}$,
\[
2\log W_c=\sum_a2c_aZ_a=\sum_a(K\tilde v)_aZ_a
=\sum_b\tilde v_b\Bigl(2\pi in_b-Q_b\log(1-x_b)+c_b\log(1+\epsilon)\Bigr),
\]
and $\tilde v\cdot n\in\mathbb{Z}$ kills the first term. The displayed form is $Q=2$ on $L$-sites and $Q=1$ on $R$-sites.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:wcboundary}
In the frieze variable $\hat d_b=s_b^{-1/2}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:friezeall} the monomial collapses. On an $L$-step $1-x_b=1-s_b$ and
$1-s_b=(\hat d_b^2-1)/\hat d_b^2$, so the signed form $\hat d_b^2\mp\hat d_{b-1}\hat d_{b+1}=1$ of \eqref{eq:friezeall} gives
$1-s_b=\pm\hat d_{b-1}\hat d_{b+1}/\hat d_b^2$ at every site interior to the run. Substituting, the
exponent of $\hat d_k$ in $\prod_j(\hat d_{j-1}\hat d_{j+1}/\hat d_j^2)^{-2j}$ is
\[
\underbrace{+4k}_{j=k}\ \underbrace{-2(k+1)}_{j=k+1}\ \underbrace{-2(k-1)}_{j=k-1}\ =\ 0
\]
identically. So every interior site cancels and $W_c^2$ depends only on the two ends of each run and
their neighbours: \emph{$W_c(\alpha)^2=1$ off the identity classes is a boundary identity, not a bulk
one}, and the same holds for the statement $\Lambda_\alpha\in\{\lambda,-\lambda^{-1}\}$ about the Floquet multiplier of $S_\alpha$: both reduce to the junctions.
What is left is the junction between consecutive runs, which Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} evaluates.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:Hall}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word and $\alpha$ the Bethe class of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} at $v\in\mathcal K_\mp$, with
$f(\mathsf m_t)\ne0$ for every tetrahedron and $\det(F+D_R)\ne0$ on every $R$-run. The last is the \emph{non-degeneracy condition}; it holds in every case computed. Then, with the upper sign on $A_-$ and the lower on $A_+$,
\[
W_c(\alpha)^2=1,\qquad \Lambda_\alpha=\pm\lambda^{\pm1},\qquad \Delta_\alpha=\pm|A_\mp|,\qquad P_\alpha=\pm2^{\#L},\qquad
\mathcal H_\alpha=2^{\#L}\,|A_\mp| .
\]
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:tworunH}
At every class of Theorem~\ref{thm:tworun} satisfying the non-degeneracy condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} (automatic when $b=1$),
\[
W_c(\alpha)^2=1,\qquad \Lambda_\alpha=-\lambda^{-1},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad\Delta_\alpha=-N,\qquad P_\alpha=-2^a,\qquad
\mathcal H_\alpha=2^{\#L}|A_+| .
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:count}
Let $\varphi\in SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ be hyperbolic with $k=\operatorname{tr}\varphi\ge3$. The $\varphi$-fixed points of the reducible locus of the $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ character variety of
$\Sigma_{1,1}$ are the union of the images of
\[
A_-/\!\pm\quad\text{and}\quad A_+/\!\pm,\qquad A_\mp=\operatorname{coker}(\varphi\mp1),
\]
which for odd $k$ meet only in the trivial character. Counting the trivial character in both sectors, the count is $\#(A_-/\!\pm)+\#(A_+/\!\pm)$, which is $k+1$ for odd $k$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
A reducible $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ representation of $F_2$ is, up to semisimplification and conjugation, diagonal, i.e.\ a character
$\chi\in\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(\Sigma),\mathbb{C}^\times)$ with $H_1(\Sigma)=\mathbb{Z}^2$; by Goldman's criterion \cite{Goldman09} these are exactly the points with $\operatorname{tr}[a,b]=2$. A
point of the character variety remembers $\chi$ only up to the Weyl involution $\chi\mapsto\chi^{-1}$, so it is $\varphi$-fixed iff
$\chi\circ\varphi=\chi$ or $\chi\circ\varphi=\chi^{-1}$, i.e.\ iff $\chi$ is trivial on $\operatorname{im}(\varphi-1)$, respectively on
$\operatorname{im}(\varphi+1)$. Thus $\chi\in\operatorname{Hom}(A_\mp,\mathbb{C}^\times)\cong A_\mp$, both finite since $\det(\varphi\mp1)=2\mp\operatorname{tr}\varphi\ne0$.
Quotienting by the Weyl involution gives the two orbit sets; the two conditions hold simultaneously iff $\chi^2=1$ and $\chi\circ\varphi=\chi$, which for
$|A_\pm|$ odd forces $\chi=1$. For $A$ of odd order $n$, $\#(A/\!\pm)=(n+1)/2$. For $A$ of even order, $\#(A/\!\pm)=(|A|+|A[2]|)/2$, where $A[2]$ is the subgroup of elements of order at most $2$; for $A$ cyclic this is $n/2+1$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:sine}
For $A,B\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\sin A\sin B\sin(A+B)\ne0$ write $r_1=\sin B/\sin A$,
$r_2=\sin(A+B)/\sin A$. Then $\cos A=(r_1^2+r_2^2-1)/2r_1r_2$; if $r_1,r_2$ are known only up to sign, so is $\cos A$.
Hence the triple $(\sin A:\sin B:\sin(A+B))$, known up to a common factor and up to the sign of each entry,
determines $(A,B)$ up to $(A,B)\mapsto(-A,-B)$ and shifts by $\pi$ in each entry. And a triple of the form $(h_1:h_2:h_1+h_2)$,
the values of a linear function, has $r_1^2+r_2^2-1=2r_1r_2$, hence $\cos A=\pm1$, $\sin A=0$: a sine triple is never
proportional to a linear one.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
From $\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B$ one gets $\cos B=r_2-r_1\cos A$, and $\sin B=r_1\sin A$. Substituting in
$\cos^2B+\sin^2B=1$ gives $1-r_2^2+2r_1r_2\cos A-r_1^2=0$, which is the formula for $\cos A$. With $\cos A$ known up to sign, $r_1$
determines $\sin B/\sin A$ and hence $B$ given $A$ up to $B\mapsto\pi-B$ and shifts by $\pi$. The alternative $\pi-B$, that is $-B$ modulo $\pi$, is compatible with $\cos B=r_2-r_1\cos A$ only if $\cos A=0$ or $\cos B=0$, and there it is the ambiguity $(A,B)\mapsto(-A,-B)$. For a linear triple, $r_1=h_2/h_1$ and $r_2=(h_1+h_2)/h_1$
give $r_1^2+r_2^2-1=2r_1r_2$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:complete}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word in which every run has length at least $2$, and let $x$ be a non-degenerate solution of
\eqref{eq:bethex} at $\epsilon=0$. Then either $x$ is the class of $V^*$ or of $\sigma V^*$, or $x$ is the class of
Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} at a vector $v\in\mathcal K_\mp\smallsetminus0$, $N=|A_\mp|$, in one of the two sectors; and
$v$ is determined by $x$ up to sign. In particular the non-degenerate classes of such a word are in bijection with
$\{V^*,\sigma V^*\}\sqcup\bigl(\mathcal K_-^{\mathrm{nd}}\smallsetminus0\bigr)/\!\pm\ \sqcup\ \bigl(\mathcal K_+^{\mathrm{nd}}\smallsetminus0\bigr)/\!\pm$,
where $\mathcal K^{\mathrm{nd}}_\mp$ is the set of kernel vectors with no vanishing $f(\mathsf m_t)$.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:singleton}
This remark uses the notation of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:complete} in Appendix~\ref{app:complete}: $(R_k)$, $(L_a)$, $(L'_1)$ are the
Bethe equations at the sites of an $R$-run and at the $L$-sites on either side of it, and $\rho_e$, $\varsigma_e$ are the ratios of the
rows of adjacent runs on a shared slope $e$.
For eight words with singleton runs ($LR^2$, $LR^3$, $LR^4$, $LRLR^2$, $L^2RLR$, $L^2RLR^2$, $LRL^2R^2$, $L^2R^2LR$) the number of solutions, computed exactly, is the number given by the bijection of the theorem. The argument has to be modified: a run of
length $1$ carries one coordinate while a row has two parameters, so the run-end equations fix the junction ratios only after the free
parameter is chosen. For a singleton $R$-run between $L$-runs of length $\ge2$, choose the free value
$F_R(p)$ with $\rho_p^2=\rho_{q'}^2$. Then the three equations $(R_1)$, $(L_a)$, $(L'_1)$ read
$(\rho_{q'}/\rho_p)^2=(\rho_{c_{a+1}}/\rho_p)^2=(\varsigma_{g_1}/\varsigma_{g_2})^2$ and $\varsigma_{q'}^2=\varsigma_{g_1}^2$, which are the full junction conditions; a singleton $L$-run between $R$-runs of length $\ge2$ is the same
computation with the roles exchanged. Words with consecutive singleton runs, such as $LRLR\cdots$, have not been written out.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:exclusion}
Let $\varphi=LR^3$ or $L^3R^3$, and $k=\operatorname{tr}\varphi$. The Jacobian determinants $\det(I-d\varphi|_T)$ (the adjoint torsions) at the $\varphi$-fixed points on the Markov locus $\operatorname{tr}\partial=-2$,
counted with multiplicity, do not contain the rational values $\pm(k-2)$ and $\pm(k+2)$ with the multiplicities $\tfrac{k-3}2$ and $\tfrac{k+1}2$ that Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} gives at the non-degenerate classes, and that the moduli \eqref{eq:as} of the template require through $\mathcal H_\alpha=1/S_{0\alpha}^2$, in the class-level normalisation $\mathcal H/2^{\#L}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall}. (The two identity classes, with $\mathcal H/2^{\#L}=(k^2-4)\lambda^{\pm1}$, are
not needed for the exclusion.)
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The modular data require the rational values $k-2$ and $k+2$, up to sign (the comparison with the torsion is up to sign), with multiplicities $\tfrac{k-3}2$ and $\tfrac{k+1}2$. Let $I\subset\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]$ be the ideal of the $\varphi$-fixed points on $\operatorname{tr}\partial=-2$, so that
$\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]/I$ is the coordinate ring of the fixed-point scheme, and let $\det(I-d\varphi|_T)$ be the Jacobian determinant of $\varphi$ on the surface,
whose value at a fixed point is its adjoint torsion, i.e.\ the $\mathcal H$ that the class would have. Explicitly the function is $J=3-\operatorname{tr}d\varphi$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$. At a smooth point it equals $\det(I-d\varphi|_T)$, because $\det d\varphi=1$ and $dF\circ d\varphi=dF$ for the defining function $F$ of the surface. At the singular points, the origin (the quaternionic character, with $J=3$) among them, $J$ is the extension by this formula. The eigenvalues of multiplication by this
function on $\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]/I$ are its values at the fixed points, with multiplicity, so the roots of its characteristic polynomial are the
torsion values the locus offers. It factors over $\mathbb{Q}$ as
\begin{align}
LR^3,\ \operatorname{tr}\partial=-2:&\quad (t-3)^2\bigl(t^4+30t^3+356t^2+1394t+2091\bigr),\\
L^3R^3,\ \operatorname{tr}\partial=-2:&\quad (t-7)^2(t-3)^2\bigl(t^4+106t^3+3604t^2+43190t+90699\bigr)^2 .
\end{align}
The quartic factors are irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, so the torsion values they give (four distinct values, each repeated when the quartic is squared) are Galois-conjugate algebraic numbers of degree four, and
irrational; they can equal none of the required rational values. The only rational roots are $3$ (twice) at $LR^3$ and $7$, $3$ (twice each) at $L^3R^3$.
Now the required values are $(k-2,k+2)=(3,7)$ with multiplicities $(1,3)$ at $LR^3$ and $(9,13)$ with multiplicities $(4,6)$ at $L^3R^3$. At $LR^3$ neither $7$ nor $-7$ is
a root; at $L^3R^3$ none of $\pm9$, $\pm13$ is. So the required multiplicities ($3$ at $LR^3$, and $4$ and $6$ at $L^3R^3$) cannot be attained.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:jacfixed}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word of odd trace $k$. Every non-trivial $\varphi$-fixed character on the reducible surface $\operatorname{tr}\partial=+2$ is
a smooth point of the surface and a simple fixed point, and the Jacobian determinant of $\varphi$ on the surface there is
\[
\det(I-d\varphi|_T)=\begin{cases}\det(I-\varphi)=-(k-2)=-|A_-|&\text{on the }A_-\text{ sector},\\
\det(I+\varphi)=k+2=|A_+|&\text{on the }A_+\text{ sector}.\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The reducible surface is the image of the torus $\operatorname{Hom}(H_1(\Sigma),\mathbb{C}^\times)=(\mathbb{C}^\times)^2$ of abelian characters under the
quotient by the Weyl involution $\iota:\chi\mapsto\chi^{-1}$, and $\varphi$ acts on the torus by $\chi\mapsto\chi\circ\varphi$, which in the
logarithmic coordinates of the Lie algebra $\mathbb{C}^2$ is the linear map $\varphi^{\mathsf T}$. A point of the surface is $\varphi$-fixed iff
$\chi\circ\varphi=\chi$ (the $A_-$ sector) or $\chi\circ\varphi=\chi^{-1}$ (the $A_+$ sector), as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:count}. The
involution $\iota$ acts freely away from the four characters with $\chi^2=1$, and the quotient map is \'etale there. For odd $k$ the orders
$|A_\mp|=k\mp2$ are odd, so a non-trivial fixed $\chi$ has $\chi^2\ne1$ and is such a point. On the $A_-$ sector the action of $\varphi$ on the
surface near the image of $\chi$ lifts to the action of $\varphi$ on the torus, which fixes $\chi$, so
$\det(I-d\varphi|_T)=\det(I-\varphi^{\mathsf T})=1-k+1$. On the $A_+$ sector it lifts to $\iota\circ\varphi$, which fixes $\chi$ and has
differential $-\varphi^{\mathsf T}$, so $\det(I-d\varphi|_T)=\det(I+\varphi)=k+2$. Neither value is $0$, so the fixed point is simple.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:thirteenth}
The quaternionic character is a candidate extra class, read through (F1). Its peripheral holonomy is central, the kind of flat connection
that the ideal-triangulation construction may fail to realise: \cite[\S2, footnote~1]{DGG11} note that ``almost all flat connections can be realized as (possibly degenerate)
hyperbolic metrics''. At $L^3R^3$ and $L^5R^5$ the
numerical harvest finds $96$ Bethe vacua ($12$ classes) and $896$ ($28$ classes), and on them $\sum1/\mathcal H=1$ exactly, the sum running over
the vacua. The sum rule is a consistency condition of the TQFT, not a consequence of the Bethe equations. If the TQFT satisfies it, a further
class with positive $1/\mathcal H$ would push the sum above $1$; so under that proviso the quaternionic character is excluded at these two words.
The argument does not show that the harvest is exhaustive.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:interpretation}
Assume \textup{(F1)}. Then for every hyperbolic word the Bethe classes of the topologically twisted $S$-fold theory correspond to the $\varphi$-fixed reducible
characters of the fibre, on the surface $\operatorname{tr}\partial=+2$; these are the restrictions to the fibre of the fibre-abelian flat $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$
connections on $M_\varphi$. The quaternionic character is a further abelian $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$ connection, and its exclusion is argued, assuming the sum rule and on numerical harvests, only at $L^3R^3$ and $L^5R^5$ (Remark~\ref{rem:thirteenth}). The complete hyperbolic structure is not among them. In it the peripheral loop $\partial$ has parabolic, hence non-trivial, holonomy,
whereas on a flat connection abelian on the fibre $\rho(\partial)=\rho([a,b])$ is trivial in $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$. At $LR^3$ and $L^3R^3$, given the
modular data \eqref{eq:GKT}, the classes do not lie on the Markov locus $\operatorname{tr}\partial=-2$ \textup{(}Proposition~\ref{prop:exclusion}\textup{)}.
They are counted by $\#(A_-/\!\pm)+\#(A_+/\!\pm)$ \textup{(}Theorem~\ref{thm:count}\textup{)}. At the non-identity classes the handle-gluing operators are, up to the factor $2^{\#L}$ and up to sign, the adjoint torsions
$\det(I-d\varphi|_T)$ of the fixed points, namely $|A_\mp|$ in absolute value: the value $\mathcal H_\alpha=2^{\#L}|A_\mp|$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} is $2^{\#L}$ times the absolute value of the Jacobian
determinant of Proposition~\ref{prop:jacfixed}. At the two identity classes, over the trivial character, they are the Floquet discriminant
$|A_-||A_+|$ times $\lambda^{\pm1}$ \textup{(}Theorem~\ref{thm:torsion}\textup{)}. Finally, under the half-index dictionary and input~(b), the
central charge of the resulting TQFT satisfies $c\equiv\#L-6\#R\pmod{24}$ \textup{(}Theorems~\ref{thm:farey}, \ref{thm:fareygeneral}\textup{)}.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:signsum}
For odd $m$, on the $2^m$ vacua of a class of $L^mR^m$ the spin is, up to a translation (the choice of base vacuum), the quadratic form, restricted to the $2$-primary part, of the discriminant group of
$K_{LL}$, all of whose entries are even,
\[
q(\varepsilon)=\tfrac18\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon
=\tfrac12\Bigl[\sum_a\varepsilon_a-\sum_a\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_{a+1}\Bigr]+\frac{m\varepsilon_1}4\pmod1,\qquad\varepsilon\in(\mathbb{Z}/2)^m,
\]
well defined because $K_{LL}$ is even, and $\tfrac14\mathbb{Z}$-valued with the quarter-values occurring exactly at $\varepsilon_1=1$. It splits orthogonally
\[
\bigl((\mathbb{Z}/2)^m,q\bigr)\cong\bigl(\mathbb{Z}/2,\tfrac m4\bigr)\oplus\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dec}},\qquad |\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dec}}|=2^{m-1},\ q|_{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dec}}}\subset\tfrac12\mathbb{Z},
\]
where $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dec}}$, the \emph{decoupled factor}, is the orthogonal complement of the all-flip $w=(1,\dots,1)$, for which $q(w)=m/4$ (the
$U(1)_{\pm2}$ generator). The Gauss sum of $q$ is
\[
\sum_\varepsilon e^{2\pi iq(\varepsilon)}=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((1+i)^m\bigr)(1+i^m)=\sqrt{2^m}\,e^{2\pi im/8},
\]
so the signature is $\equiv m\pmod8$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
That the spin is $q$ up to translation is Proposition~\ref{prop:flux}(i) together with the completion of the square in Proposition~\ref{prop:spinq}(ii) below; here we compute $q$. Write $K_{LL}=2E_{LL}$, so that $E_{LL}=\tfrac12K_{LL}$ is the integral form of the $L$-block (every entry of $K$ being even); at $L^mR^m$ it is
the cyclic tridiagonal $(-1,2,-1)$ plus $m$ at the $(1,1)$ entry, so
$\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon=4[\sum\varepsilon_a-\sum\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_{a+1}]+2m\varepsilon_1$, which is the displayed form; only
the last term is not in $\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$, and it is nonzero exactly when $\varepsilon_1=1$. All row sums of $E_{LL}$ vanish except the first, which is $m$,
so $q(w)=2m/8=m/4$; for odd $m$ that is a primitive quarter, $b(w,w)=m/2\ne0$, and $q$ is half-integral on $\ker b(w,\cdot)$, of order $2^{m-1}$, so the
splitting is the standard orthogonal one. For the Gauss sum, write
$e^{2\pi iq(\varepsilon)}=i^{m\varepsilon_1}\prod_{a=1}^m(-1)^{\varepsilon_a}(-1)^{\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_{a+1}}$, indices modulo $m$. The product is a
sum over a closed chain of binary variables with nearest-neighbour weights, so it is a trace of a transfer matrix: with
$M_{\varepsilon\varepsilon'}=(-1)^{\varepsilon}(-1)^{\varepsilon\varepsilon'}$, i.e.\ $M=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ in the order
$\varepsilon=0,1$, one has $\sum_\varepsilon\prod_a(-1)^{\varepsilon_a}(-1)^{\varepsilon_a\varepsilon_{a+1}}=\operatorname{tr} M^m$, and the sums restricted to
$\varepsilon_1=0$ and to $\varepsilon_1=1$ are the two diagonal entries $(M^m)_{00}$ and $(M^m)_{11}$. The eigenvalues of $M$ are $1\pm i$, so
$\operatorname{tr} M^m=(1+i)^m+(1-i)^m=2\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^m)$; and $(M^m)_{00}=(M^m)_{11}$ because $\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)M^m)=0$: $M=\sqrt2\,R_{-\pi/4}$ is a
multiple of a rotation, so $M^m=2^{m/2}R_{-m\pi/4}$ has equal diagonal entries. Hence each $\varepsilon_1$-sector contributes
$\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^m)$, the sector $\varepsilon_1=1$ carrying the extra factor $i^m$, and
$\sum_\varepsilon e^{2\pi iq(\varepsilon)}=\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^m)(1+i^m)$, of modulus $\sqrt{2^m}$ and argument $2\pi m/8$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:arf}
For odd $m$ the Gauss sum of $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dec}}$ has modulus $\sqrt{2^{m-1}}$ and signature
\[
\sigma(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dec}})\equiv\begin{cases}m-1&m\equiv1\pmod4\\ m+1&m\equiv3\pmod4\end{cases}\pmod8,
\]
so $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{dec}}$ is Arf-odd \textup{(}$\sigma\equiv4$\textup{)} exactly when $m\equiv\pm3\pmod8$, and Arf-even \textup{(}$\sigma\equiv0$\textup{)} exactly when
$m\equiv\pm1\pmod8$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Divide the Gauss sum of Proposition~\ref{prop:signsum} by that of the orthogonal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ factor, which is $1+i^m$: of modulus $\sqrt2$ and signature
$+1$ for $m\equiv1\pmod4$, $-1$ for $m\equiv3\pmod4$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:parity}
For every hyperbolic word, $\det E_{LL}\equiv\operatorname{tr}\varphi\pmod2$. Hence $E_{LL}$ is invertible over $\mathbb{F}_2$ precisely when $\operatorname{tr}\varphi$ is odd.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}, modulo $2$ the matrix $E_{LL}=\tfrac12K_{LL}$ on the $\#L$ $L$-sites in cyclic order has diagonal entry $b$ at the first
$L$ after an $R$-run of length $b$ and $0$ at the other $L$'s, and off-diagonal entry $1$ for each adjacency of cyclically consecutive $L$'s; for
$\#L=2$ the two adjacencies cancel and for $\#L=1$ the matrix is $(b)$. For a cyclic tridiagonal matrix with unit off-diagonals, Hill's formula
(Section~\ref{sec:torsion}) reads $\det=(-1)^n(\operatorname{tr}\prod_iT_i-2)$ with $T_i=\begin{psmallmatrix}-d_i&-1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, so
$\det E_{LL}\equiv\operatorname{tr}\prod_iT(d_i)\pmod2$ with $T(d)=\begin{psmallmatrix}d&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$; the cases $\#L=1,2$ give $b$ and
$d_1d_2$, which the same expression gives. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ one has $L^2=R^2=I$, $T(0)=LRL$ and $T(1)=L\,T(0)$, so an $L$-run of length $a$ after an
$R$-run of length $b$ contributes $T(b)T(0)^{a-1}=L^{b+1}R^aL$, and the cyclic product over the runs is, up to conjugation,
$L^{b_n}R^{a_1}L^{b_1}R^{a_2}\cdots L^{b_{n-1}}R^{a_n}$. This is the word $\varphi=L^{a_1}R^{b_1}\cdots L^{a_n}R^{b_n}$ with the letters $L$ and $R$ interchanged (each run $L^{a_i}$ becomes a run $R^{a_i}$ and each run $R^{b_i}$ a run $L^{b_i}$), read cyclically from the run $L^{b_n}$, and it is
conjugate to $\varphi$ by $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ and so has the same trace.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:spinq}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word and $V$ a Bethe vacuum with branch integers $n$, that is, the integers $n_b$ in the log-form Bethe equations $Q_b\log(1-x_b)+(KZ)_b=2\pi in_b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:flux}). For $\varepsilon\in(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\#L}$ let $V_\varepsilon$ be
the vacuum obtained by flipping the charge-$2$ coordinates in $\varepsilon$; put $q(\varepsilon)=\tfrac18\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon$
and $E_{LL}=\tfrac12K_{LL}$, as in Proposition~\ref{prop:signsum} for $L^mR^m$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] $\operatorname{spin}(V_\varepsilon)-\operatorname{spin}(V)\equiv q(\varepsilon)+\tfrac12n_L\cdot\varepsilon\pmod1$.
\item[\textup{(ii)}] $E_{LL}$ is invertible over $\mathbb{F}_2$ iff $\operatorname{tr}\varphi$ is odd (Lemma~\ref{lem:parity}).
When it is, $\varepsilon_0:=E_{LL}^{-1}n_L\bmod2$ exists and is unique, and
\[
\operatorname{spin}(V_\varepsilon)=\operatorname{spin}(V_{\varepsilon_0})+q(\varepsilon+\varepsilon_0)\pmod1 :
\]
measured from $V_{\varepsilon_0}$, the spin function on the $2^{\#L}$ vacua of the class is exactly $q$.
\item[\textup{(iii)}] For $\varphi=L^mR^m$ with $m$ odd and $V=\sigma V^*$ (the all-plus vacuum of its class), $E_{LL}\mathbf1=c_L=n_L$ as integer vectors, so $\varepsilon_0=\mathbf1$. The base vacuum is the all-flip of
$\sigma V^*$, and $q(\mathbf1)=m/4$.
\item[\textup{(iv)}] For odd trace, the sign-sum of the class is $e^{2\pi i\operatorname{spin}(V_{\varepsilon_0})}$ times the Gauss sum of $q$, so the $\mu_8$ property
follows from Milgram's formula \cite{MH73}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
(i) is the computation in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:flux}. The flip sends $Z_a\mapsto Z_a+i\pi\varepsilon_a$ with $x$ fixed and changes
$\log\mathcal F$ by $i\pi\,\varepsilon\cdot n_L+\tfrac{i\pi}4\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}K_{LL}\varepsilon$, i.e.\ the spin by $\tfrac12n_L\cdot\varepsilon+q(\varepsilon)$. At a degenerate class the spin is defined along the continuation in $\epsilon$; there the deformation term changes under the flip by $-i\pi\log(1+\epsilon)\,c\cdot\varepsilon\to0$, so (i) holds in the limit.

(ii) The class of $n_L$ modulo $2$ does not depend on the branches: $Z_b\mapsto Z_b+2\pi i$ moves $n$ by a column of $K$, which is even, and the other branch of $\log(1-x_L)$ moves $n_L$ by $Q_L=2$. The general statement is Lemma~\ref{lem:parity}. For $L^mR^m$ directly: modulo $2$, $E_{LL}$ is $C+m\,e_1e_1^{\mathsf T}$ with $C$ the adjacency matrix of the $m$-cycle. The rows of $C$ sum to $0$ modulo $2$, so
$\det C\equiv0\pmod2$, which settles even $m$. For odd $m$, the determinant is linear in the $(1,1)$ entry, so
$\det E_{LL}\equiv\det C+m\det C'\equiv\det C+\det C'\pmod2$, where $C'$ is the matrix obtained by deleting the first row and column of $C$, the adjacency matrix of the path on the $m-1$
vertices $2,\dots,m$. The path determinants satisfy $p_n=-p_{n-2}$, $p_1=0$, $p_2=-1$, so $p_{m-1}$ is odd. Hence $E_{LL}$ is invertible over
$\mathbb{F}_2$ iff $m$ is odd. The bilinear form of $q$ is $b(\varepsilon,\varepsilon')=q(\varepsilon+\varepsilon')-q(\varepsilon)-q(\varepsilon')=
\tfrac12\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}E_{LL}\varepsilon'\bmod1$, so $\tfrac12n_L\cdot\varepsilon\equiv b(\varepsilon,\varepsilon_0)$ and (i) reads
$\operatorname{spin}(V_\varepsilon)-\operatorname{spin}(V)\equiv q(\varepsilon+\varepsilon_0)-q(\varepsilon_0)$. Taking $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0$
and subtracting gives the display, since $q(2\varepsilon_0)=0$.

(iii) The row sums of $E_{LL}$ are $(m,0,\dots,0)$ (proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:signsum}), and $n_L=c_L=(m,0,\dots,0)$ at $\sigma V^*$
(proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:flux}); so $E_{LL}\mathbf1=n_L$ and $\varepsilon_0=\mathbf1$, with $q(\mathbf1)=m/4$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:signsum}.

(iv) By (ii), $\sum_\varepsilon e^{2\pi i\operatorname{spin}(V_\varepsilon)}=e^{2\pi i\operatorname{spin}(V_{\varepsilon_0})}\sum_\varepsilon e^{2\pi iq(\varepsilon)}$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{prop:suslin}
Let $m$ be odd, $\zeta_m$ a primitive $m$-th root of unity, $F=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)^+=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m+\zeta_m^{-1})\subset\mathbb{R}$ its maximal real subfield, and let $\xi=\sum_an_a[x_a]\in B(F)$ with all $x_a\in F\setminus\{0,1\}$. Here $B(F)$ is the Bloch group (as in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:rational}), the subgroup of the pre-Bloch group of $F$ cut out by the condition $\sum_an_a\,x_a\wedge(1-x_a)=0$, and $\mathfrak p(\mathbb{R})$ below is the pre-Bloch group of $\mathbb{R}$. For a field $k$ the pre-Bloch group $\mathfrak p(k)$ is generated by the symbols $[x]$, $x\in k\smallsetminus\{0,1\}$, modulo Suslin's five-term relation
\[
[x]-[y]+\Bigl[\frac yx\Bigr]-\Bigl[\frac{1-x^{-1}}{1-y^{-1}}\Bigr]+\Bigl[\frac{1-x}{1-y}\Bigr]=0\qquad(x\ne y).
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] $B(F)$ is finite cyclic of order $\tfrac14\operatorname{lcm}(24,m)=6m/\gcd(3,m)$.
\item[\textup{(ii)}] Extend the Rogers dilogarithm to $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,1\}$ in the standard way, by $\widetilde L(x)=L(x)-L(1)$ for $0<x<1$,
$\widetilde L(x)=-\widetilde L(1/x)$ for $x>1$, and $\widetilde L(x)=-L(1)+\widetilde L(1/(1-x))$ for $x<0$. Then $\xi\mapsto\sum_an_a\widetilde L(x_a)$ is a well-defined homomorphism
$\widetilde L:\mathfrak p(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{R}/\pi^2\mathbb{Z}$.
\item[\textup{(iii)}] $\operatorname{Gal}(F/\mathbb{Q})$ acts on $B(F)$ as follows: the automorphism $\sigma_k$, $k\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times/\!\pm1$, $\zeta_m\mapsto\zeta_m^k$, acts by multiplication by $a^2$, for some $a$ depending on $k$. Therefore $\widetilde
L(\sigma_k\xi)=a^2\widetilde L(\xi)$ in $\mathbb{R}/\pi^2\mathbb{Z}$. By (iv), $c(\sigma_k\xi)\equiv a^2c(\xi)\equiv k^2c(\xi)\pmod1$, for $c(\xi)=\sum_an_aL(x_a)/L(1)$.
\item[\textup{(iv)}] $c(\xi)\bmod1$ lies in $\tfrac6{|B(F)|}\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$, i.e.\ $\tfrac m{\gcd(3,m)}c(\xi)\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
For (i): $K_3(F)$ is the third algebraic $K$-group of $F$ and $K_3^M(F)\subset K_3(F)$ the image of the Milnor $K$-group, the part generated by symbols; write $K_3(F)_{\mathrm{nd}}=K_3(F)/K_3^M(F)$ for the indecomposable part, the quotient that symbols do not see, as in \cite{Suslin91}. Borel's rank computation \cite{Borel77} gives $K_3(F)_{\mathrm{nd}}\otimes\mathbb{Q}=0$ for $F$ totally real; the torsion of
$K_3(F)_{\mathrm{nd}}$ is cyclic of order $w_2(F)$, the largest $N$ for which $\operatorname{Gal}(F(\mu_N)/F)$ has exponent dividing $2$
\cite{MS90,Levine89}; Suslin's exact sequence $0\to\operatorname{Tor}(\mu(F),\mu(F))^\sim\to K_3(F)_{\mathrm{nd}}\to B(F)\to0$
\cite[Thm.~5.2]{Suslin91}, in which the first term is the nontrivial extension of $\operatorname{Tor}(\mu(F),\mu(F))$ by $\mathbb{Z}/2$ and has order $4$ for $F\subset\mathbb{R}$, gives $|B(F)|=w_2(F)/4$; and for $F=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)^+$ with $m$ odd,
$\operatorname{Gal}(F(\mu_N)/F)\subset(\mathbb{Z}/N)^\times$ has exponent dividing $2$ exactly for $N\mid\operatorname{lcm}(24,m)$, so
$w_2(F)=\operatorname{lcm}(24,m)$. For (ii), that $\widetilde L$ vanishes modulo $\pi^2$ on every real five-term relation is \cite[\S2.3.1]{Kirillov95}; the value there is $0$ or $-\pi^2$. For (iii), $K_3(F)_{\mathrm{nd}}$ is identified Galois-equivariantly with $H^0(F,\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}(2))$ \cite{MS90,Levine89}, on which $\sigma_k$ acts by the square of the cyclotomic character, and Suslin's sequence is natural. So $\sigma_k$ acts on $B(F)$ by $a^2$.
Here $a$ is $k$ itself when $k$ is prime to $6$. In general $a$ is any integer with $a\equiv\pm k\pmod m$ and $\gcd(a,6)=1$, which exists by the Chinese remainder theorem since $m$ is odd and $k$ is prime to $m$. As $a^2\equiv k^2\pmod m$ and $a^2\equiv1$ modulo $2$ and $3$, the class of $a^2$ modulo $|B(F)|$ does not depend on the choice. Then $\widetilde L(\sigma_k\xi)=a^2\widetilde L(\xi)$ because $\widetilde L$ is a homomorphism. Part (iv) follows from (i) and (ii). Part (iv) sharpens the naive denominator $24$ of $c\bmod1$ to $m/\gcd(3,m)$, and this denominator is sharp: $\xi_1=\sum_{b=2}^{(m-1)/2}[x_b]$ lies in $B(F)$, since its image in $\wedge^2F^\times$ telescopes to $0$, and $c(\xi_1)=1-3/m$ has exact order $m/\gcd(3,m)$ modulo $1$, by \eqref{eq:Smk}.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:disc}
Let $\mathbb L_\varphi=(\mathbb{Z}^2,S_\varphi)$ with $S_\varphi=J\varphi+(J\varphi)^{\mathsf T}=J(\varphi-\varphi^{-1})$. Then $\mathbb L_\varphi$ is even and indefinite, and its
discriminant form is isometric to $(A_-,q_-)\perp(A_+,-q_+)$. In particular $q_\mp$ are well-defined nondegenerate quadratic forms, and
$\gamma_-=\gamma_+$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
$S_\varphi$ has diagonal $(2c,-2b)$ and $\det S_\varphi=-(k^2-4)<0$. Its discriminant form is $y\mapsto\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}S_\varphi^{-1}y$ on
$\mathbb{Z}^2/S_\varphi\mathbb{Z}^2$; substituting $u=Jy$ and using $JS_\varphi=-(\varphi-\varphi^{-1})$, a direct computation turns it into
the form $u\mapsto-\Phi(u)/N_-N_+$ on $\mathbb{Z}^2/(\varphi^2-1)\mathbb{Z}^2$. As $\gcd(N_-,N_+)=1$, the $N_\mp$-primary part is $(\varphi\pm1)\mathbb{Z}^2/(\varphi^2-1)\mathbb{Z}^2$, identified
with $A_\mp$ by $x\mapsto(\varphi\pm1)x$. From $\varphi^{\mathsf T}J=J\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi^2=k\varphi-1$,
\[
(\varphi\pm1)^{\mathsf T}J\varphi(\varphi\pm1)=\pm J(\varphi\pm1)^2=\pm(k\pm2)\,J\varphi ,
\]
so $\Phi((\varphi+1)x)=N_+\Phi(x)$ and $\Phi((\varphi-1)x)=-N_-\Phi(x)$, and the two parts carry $-\Phi/N_-$ on $A_-$ and $\Phi/N_+$ on $A_+$. Since
$4[4^{-1}]_N\equiv1$, these are $q_-(2x)$ and $-q_+(2x)$, and $x\mapsto2x$ is an automorphism of each group. The discriminant form of an even
lattice is nondegenerate, and Milgram's formula \cite{MH73} gives $G(q_-)\overline{G(q_+)}=\sqrt{N_-N_+}\,e(\operatorname{sign}\mathbb L_\varphi/8)=\sqrt{N_-N_+}$.
Hence $\gamma_-\bar\gamma_+=1$ with $|\gamma_\mp|=1$, that is, $\gamma_-=\gamma_+$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:rogers}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word of odd trace, and let $\xi$ be the non-degenerate class of $v=\operatorname{adj}(\varphi\mp1)u\in\mathcal K_\mp$. Then
\[
c_\xi\equiv\#R-6\,\frac{\Phi(u)}{N_\mp}\pmod 6 .
\]
Consequently every one of the $2^{\#L}$ vacua of $\xi$ has spin $\equiv\#R/24-\Phi(u)/4N_\mp\pmod{\tfrac14}$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1: reduction to principal real parts.} For real $s\notin\{0,1\}$ the reflection formula for $\operatorname{Li}_2$ gives $L(1-s)=L(1)-L(s)$. Hence, exactly,
\begin{equation}
c_\xi=\#R+\frac6{\pi^2}\,\Sigma,\qquad \Sigma:=\sum_{L\text{-steps}}\operatorname{Re}R(s_t)-\sum_{R\text{-steps}}\operatorname{Re}R(s_t).
\label{eq:Sigma}
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 2: a primitive.} Put $\vartheta(e)=\pi\langle v,e\rangle/N_\mp$ for $e\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, with $v=\operatorname{adj}(\varphi\mp1)u$ as an integer vector, the lift used in Step~4; $\vartheta$ is linear. At step $t$
let $(c_1,c_2)$ be the Farey basis and $(\alpha,\beta)=(\vartheta(c_1),\vartheta(c_2))$; an $L$-step replaces it by $(c_1,c_1+c_2)$ and has
$s=\sin^2\alpha/\sin^2(\alpha+\beta)$, an $R$-step by $(c_1+c_2,c_2)$ with $s=\sin^2\beta/\sin^2(\alpha+\beta)$. Define
\[
z(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{e^{2i\alpha}-1}{e^{2i(\alpha+\beta)}-1}=\frac{\sin\alpha}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}\,e^{-i\beta},\qquad
1-z=\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}\,e^{i\alpha},
\]
\[
\mathcal G(\alpha,\beta)=2\operatorname{Re}R(z)+\alpha\arg z+\beta\arg(1-z).
\]

\emph{Step 3: the step identities.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:steps} (Appendix~\ref{app:steps}),
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Re}R\bigl(\tfrac{\sin^2\alpha}{\sin^2(\alpha+\beta)}\bigr)-\mathcal G(\alpha,\beta)+\mathcal G(\alpha,\alpha+\beta)\in\pi^2\mathbb{Z},\qquad
-\operatorname{Re}R\bigl(\tfrac{\sin^2\beta}{\sin^2(\alpha+\beta)}\bigr)-\mathcal G(\alpha,\beta)+\mathcal G(\alpha+\beta,\beta)\in\pi^2\mathbb{Z}
\label{eq:steps}
\end{equation}
wherever the arguments are defined. These are the step identities.

\emph{Step 4: telescoping.} Non-degeneracy gives $f\neq0$, with $f(e)=\sin(\pi\langle v,e\rangle/N)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}, on every kept, dying, middle and newborn slope (proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall}, Appendix~\ref{app:Hall}), that
is $\sin\alpha,\sin\beta,\sin(\alpha+\beta)$ and $\sin(2\alpha+\beta)$ (resp.\ $\sin(\alpha+2\beta)$) are nonzero at every step, so \eqref{eq:steps}
applies at every step. Consecutive steps share a basis, so
\[
\Sigma\equiv \mathcal G\bigl(\vartheta(e_1),\vartheta(e_2)\bigr)-\mathcal G\bigl(\vartheta(\varphi e_1),\vartheta(\varphi e_2)\bigr)\pmod{\pi^2},
\]
the final basis being the columns of $\varphi$. Write $\varphi\mp1=\varphi-\upsilon$ with $\upsilon=\pm1$. Then $\det(\varphi-\upsilon)=-\upsilon N_\mp$, and
$\varphi^{-1}v=\upsilon v+N_\mp\tilde w$ with $\tilde w=\varphi^{-1}u$, because $\varphi^{-1}v-\upsilon v=-\upsilon\varphi^{-1}(\varphi-\upsilon)\operatorname{adj}(\varphi-\upsilon)u$.
Hence $\vartheta(\varphi e)=\upsilon\vartheta(e)+\pi\langle\tilde w,e\rangle$. Put $(\alpha_0,\beta_0)=(\vartheta(e_1),\vartheta(e_2))$ and
$(p_1,p_2)=(\langle\tilde w,e_1\rangle,\langle\tilde w,e_2\rangle)$. Since $z$ is $\pi$-periodic in each variable and
$z(-\alpha,-\beta)=\overline{z(\alpha,\beta)}$, the final $z$ is $z_0$ or $\bar z_0$; $\operatorname{Re}R$ agrees on the two, and the arg-terms give
\[
\Sigma\equiv-\upsilon\pi(p_2\alpha_0-p_1\beta_0)=-\frac{\upsilon\pi^2}{N_\mp}\langle v,\tilde w\rangle\pmod{\pi^2}.
\]
Finally $\upsilon\langle v,\tilde w\rangle=\upsilon\,u^{\mathsf T}J(\varphi-\upsilon)\varphi^{-1}u=-u^{\mathsf T}J\varphi^{-1}u=\Phi(u)$, using
$\operatorname{adj}(M)^{\mathsf T}J=JM$, $u^{\mathsf T}Ju=0$ and $\varphi^{-1}=k-\varphi$. So $\Sigma\equiv-\pi^2\Phi(u)/N_\mp\pmod{\pi^2}$, and \eqref{eq:Sigma} gives the
congruence.

\emph{Step 5: spins.} At a non-degenerate class all Bethe coordinates are real and $x_L=s_t>0$ at the charge-$2$ sites, so
$\operatorname{Im}Z_a\in\pi\mathbb{Z}$ for every $a$ and in \eqref{eq:Fphase} the factor $e^{n\cdot Z/2}$ lies in
$\{\pm1,\pm i\}$; hence every vacuum of the class has spin $\equiv c_\xi/24\pmod{\tfrac14}$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{obs:kirillov}
For odd $m$ and $\gcd(k,m)=1$, $mS(m,k)\equiv-6k^2\pmod m$.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- observation-8: body_md -->
\label{obs:e1even}
Let $N$ be odd. Writing $A=2a$ and $A=2a+1$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{gathered}
\frac{A^2}{4N}=\frac{a^2}N\quad(A\ \text{even},\ a=1,\dots,\tfrac12(N-1)),\\
\frac{A^2}{4N}=\frac{a^2+a}N+\frac1{4N}\quad(A\ \text{odd},\ a=0,\dots,\tfrac12(N-3)),
\end{gathered}
\label{eq:parsplit}
\end{equation}
so the template multiset splits by the parity of $A$; $a^2/N$ and $(a^2+a)/N$ are quadratic refinements of the same bilinear form $2ab/N$ on
$\mathbb{Z}/N$, and the even half, with the $\pm$-doubled weighting proper to a form on $A_-$ and the term $a=0$ included, has Gauss modulus $\sqrt N$, the modulus of the quadratic
Gauss sum. The two halves are translates of one another: for $A$ even, $(A+N)^2/4N=A^2/4N+A/2+N/4\equiv A^2/4N+N/4\pmod1$, and $A\mapsto A+N$ carries
the even labels in $[2,N-1]$ to the odd labels in $[N+2,2N-1]$. The symmetry $A\mapsto2N-A$, under which $(2N-A)^2/4N\equiv A^2/4N\pmod1$, carries these to the odd labels in $[1,N-2]$. So
\begin{equation}
\{A^2/4N:A\ \text{odd}\}=\{A^2/4N:A\ \text{even}\}+\tfrac N4\pmod 1
\label{eq:transN}
\end{equation}
as multisets. All of this is elementary. The empirical part is the identification of the shift $N/4$ as the semion of the sign group. At
$\varphi=LR^n$, where a class has exactly two vacua, $K_{LL}=2n$ and $q(1)=K_{LL}/8=n/4\equiv N/4\pmod1$ in both sectors ($N=n$ or $n+4$). For the general case it was checked by computer on all $427$ cyclic
words of length at most $11$ with $\operatorname{tr}\varphi>2$, the whole range checked and nothing is claimed beyond it, that $q$ attains $\pm N/4$, Among the $103$ words of odd trace, both values occur at $95$ words, only $+N/4$ at $LR$, $LR^3$, $LR^5$, $LR^7$, $LR^9$ and $LR^3LR^3$, and only $-N/4$ at $LRLR$ and $LRLR^5$.
<!-- end observation-8 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:templatelabel}
Let $\varphi$ have odd trace, let $A_\mp$ be cyclic of order $N$, and let $\rho$ be a run with kept slope $p_\rho$. On the non-degenerate
classes of $A_\mp$, with $v=\operatorname{adj}(\varphi\mp1)u$ and index $j_\rho=\langle v,p_\rho\rangle$ \textup{(}Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}\textup{)},
\[
-\Phi(u)\equiv c_\rho\,j_\rho^2\pmod N
\]
for a constant $c_\rho$ independent of the class, whenever the index of a generator is prime to $N$. Hence every vacuum of the class has spin
$\equiv\#R/24+c_\rho j_\rho^2/4N\pmod{\tfrac14}$. For $\varphi=LR^n$ and $\rho$ the $R$-run, $c_\rho=1$ in both sectors. On $A_+$ this gives
\[
\operatorname{spin}\equiv\frac{\#R}{24}+\frac{j^2}{4N}\pmod{\tfrac14},
\]
so the template label of Gang--Kim on the $(k+2)$-block is $B=j$. The $A_-$ sector of $LR^n$ is degenerate, and there the same spin formula is observed
numerically at the harvested classes.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
In a cyclic sector $u=tu_0$, so $v=tv_0$, $\Phi(u)=t^2\Phi(u_0)$ and $j_\rho=t\langle v_0,p_\rho\rangle$; put $c_\rho=-\Phi(u_0)\langle v_0,p_\rho\rangle^{-2}$.
The spin is Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers}. For $LR^n$, $\Phi(u)=nu_1^2-nu_1u_2-u_2^2$ and $p_\rho=e_1+e_2$. On $A_-$ ($N=n$),
$v=(-u_2,\,n(u_2-u_1))$ and $j\equiv-u_2$, so $j^2\equiv-\Phi(u)$. On $A_+$ ($N=n+4$), $v=(2u_1-u_2,\,-nu_1+(n+2)u_2)$ and
$j\equiv-2u_1+u_2$, so $j^2=4u_1^2-4u_1u_2+u_2^2\equiv-\Phi(u)$, since $n\equiv-4$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:lines}
With $m$, $\varphi$ and the pairs $(j,k)$ as just described:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] the leading data $(j,k)$ are the closed form of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} at the kernel vector $v=m(jk,k)$ (at $v=m(k,0)$ for
the fixed type) on every site where its denominator is nonzero. For $j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}$ the degenerate sites are exactly those where the denominator vanishes, together with their
neighbours. For the type $0$ the denominator vanishes only at $L_m$, and every $R$-coordinate tends to $1$. For the fixed type the numerator vanishes on the $L$-run, and every $L$-coordinate tends to $0$; the corresponding point of $A_-$ is $u=k(1,j)$, respectively $u=(0,k)$, and $v\equiv-\operatorname{adj}(\varphi-1)u$, which is $\operatorname{adj}(\varphi-1)u$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers} up to sign, $v$ mattering only up to sign;
\item[\textup{(ii)}] the placement types are the points of $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb{F}_m)$: the type $j\in\mathbb{F}_m$ is the line of $A_-$ spanned by $(1,j)$, and the fixed type is the point $\infty$, the line spanned by $(0,1)$; and $(j,k)\mapsto\pm u$ is a bijection onto $(A_-\smallsetminus0)/\!\pm$, the Galois index $k$ running over the $\tfrac12(m-1)$ antipodal pairs on each line;
\item[\textup{(iii)}] for every vacuum of a solution with these leading data that is real-analytic in $\epsilon$ for $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$ with real coordinates (the coordinates are then meromorphic at $\epsilon=0$), such as the solutions of Theorem~\ref{thm:exist}, the component in $\tfrac1m\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$ of its spin is $q_-(u)$, with $q_-$ the form
\eqref{eq:qform}. Equivalently, the $\theta$-exponent of the class, the residue $e\in\mathbb{Z}/m$ with $e/m\equiv$ that component, is $(j^2-1)(k/2)^2$, and $(k/2)^2$ for the fixed type.
\end{enumerate}
Here a class means its leading data; which of them are limits of exact solutions is Theorem~\ref{thm:aminus}.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
\textup{(i)} For $v=m(v_1,v_2)$, $\langle v,e\rangle/m^2=(v_1e_2-v_2e_1)/m$. In the layered triangulation of $L^mR^m$, as in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:tworun}, the $L$-run has kept slope $e_1$ and middle slopes $(i,1)$, and the $R$-run has kept slope $(m,1)$ and middle slopes
$(1+im,i)$, $i=1,\dots,m$. At $v=m(jk,k)$, with $\vartheta=k\pi/m$, the formula of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} gives
$x_{L_i}=\sin^2\vartheta/\sin^2((i-j)\vartheta)$ and $1-x_{R_i}=\sin^2(j\vartheta)/\sin^2((ij-1)\vartheta)$: the chains of
Section~\ref{sec:leading} at zero phase. The denominator vanishes exactly at $L_{j}$ and at $R_p$, $p=j^{-1}$; at $L_{j\pm1}$ the formula
gives $x=1$ and at $R_{p\pm1}$ it gives $x=0$, which is the pattern of the type $j$. At $v=m(0,k)$ the only vanishing denominator is at $L_m$ and every
$x_R=1$: the type $0$. At $v=m(k,0)$, $f$ vanishes on the kept slope of the $L$-run, so every $x_L=0$, and on the middle slope of $R_m$; the
$R$-coordinates are $1-\sin^2\vartheta/\sin^2(i\vartheta)$: the fixed type. Finally $(\varphi-1)\mathbb{Z}^2=m\mathbb{Z}^2$, and
$\operatorname{adj}(\varphi-1)=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-m\\-m&m^2\end{psmallmatrix}$ sends $k(1,j)$ to $-m(jk,k)$ and $(0,k)$ to $-m(k,0)$ modulo $m^2$.
\textup{(ii)} Every nonzero $u\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^2$ lies on exactly one line through the origin, spanned by $(1,j)$ or by $(0,1)$, and the
$\tfrac12(m-1)$ antipodal pairs on a line are the multiples $\pm k$, $k\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times\!/\!\pm$.
\textup{(iii)} With $\varphi=\begin{psmallmatrix}1+m^2&m\\m&1\end{psmallmatrix}$, $\Phi(u)=m(u_1^2-u_2^2)-m^2u_1u_2$, so
$q_-(u)=-[4^{-1}]\Phi(u)/m^2\equiv[4^{-1}](u_2^2-u_1^2)/m$, which is $(j^2-1)(k/2)^2/m$ at $u=k(1,j)$ and $(k/2)^2/m$ at $(0,k)$. That this is
the spin is the following computation.

Put $\vartheta=k\pi/m$. First let $j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}$ and $p=j^{-1}\bmod m$. At the class
$(j,k)$ the finite $L$-coordinates are $\sin^2\vartheta/\sin^2(n\vartheta)$, $n=2,\dots,m-2$, the values of \eqref{eq:closedform}. By (T5) of
Lemma~\ref{lem:telescope} the finite $R$-coordinates satisfy $1-x_{R_i}=\sin^2(j\vartheta)/\varsigma_i^2$ with $\varsigma_i=\sin((ij-1)\vartheta)
=\pm\sin((i-p)j\vartheta)$, since $(pj-1)\vartheta\in\pi\mathbb{Z}$; over the arc $i-p=2,\dots,m-2$ these are the values of \eqref{eq:closedform} at
the Galois index $jk$. The remaining coordinates tend to $0$, $1$ or $\infty$ and contribute integers to $c_\alpha$, which vanish after
multiplication by $m$ modulo $m$. With the reflection identity $L(x)+L(1-x)=L(1)$ (modulo $\pi^2$ for the extended $L$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:suslin}(ii)) and Proposition~\ref{obs:kirillov} at $k$ and at $jk$,
\[
mc_\alpha\equiv mS(m,k)-mS(m,jk)\equiv-6k^2+6(jk)^2=6k^2(j^2-1)\pmod m ,
\]
and $24\theta\equiv c_\alpha$, which holds at every vacuum of the class by \eqref{eq:theta24}, turns this into $4e\equiv k^2(j^2-1)$, dividing by $6$, which is invertible modulo $m$ since $m\ge5$.

At the type $0$ every $R$-coordinate tends to $1$ and contributes an integer, and the finite $L$-coordinates are the chain at $k$. So $mc_\alpha\equiv mS(m,k)\equiv-6k^2$, and $e\equiv-(k/2)^2$, which is $(j^2-1)(k/2)^2$ at $j=0$. At the fixed type every $L$-coordinate tends to $0$ and contributes an integer. The finite $R$-coordinates satisfy $1-x_{R_i}=\sin^2\vartheta/\sin^2(i\vartheta)$, $i=2,\dots,m-2$, so by the reflection identity $mc_\alpha\equiv-mS(m,k)\equiv6k^2$, and $e\equiv(k/2)^2$. For these two types no solution is constructed, so there (iii) describes the spin of a solution if one exists.

The relation \eqref{eq:theta24} was derived for solutions with finite coordinates. At a degenerate class it is applied along the
continuation in $\epsilon$, which is how the fibering operator of such a class is defined (Section~\ref{sec:bethe}). The existence of the continuation is Theorem~\ref{thm:exist}, proved in Appendix~\ref{app:existence}, which does not use the present theorem. For $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$ the solution
of that theorem is real-analytic in $\epsilon$ with real data. Hence all its coordinates are finite, nonzero and real, and
$\operatorname{Im}Z_a\in\{0,\pi\}$. The deformed log-form Bethe equations differ from the undeformed ones by the term $c_b\log(1+\epsilon)$.
This adds to $\log\mathcal F$ a term proportional to $\log(1+\epsilon)\,c\cdot Z$, which tends to $0$ with $\epsilon$ since
$Z_a=O(\log\epsilon)$. Hence \eqref{eq:theta24} holds at every $\epsilon$ up to a term that vanishes in the limit, and both sides are continuous
along the continuation, $c_\alpha$ with $L=\operatorname{Re}R$, so that $L-L(1)$ is the function $\widetilde L$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:suslin}(ii).

Distinct pairs $(j,k)$ give distinct classes, because the leading data differ. Two classes with different $j$ have different sets of degenerate coordinates, hence different placement types. Two classes with the same $j$ and
$k\ne\pm k'$ have different $x_b$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:exhaustive}
Theorem~\ref{thm:lines} says the closed-form family has $|A_-\smallsetminus0|/2$ distinct members. That the family is \emph{all} of the $A_-$ sector then
follows if the sector has that many classes, which is Theorem~\ref{thm:count} read through localisation, and if every class has leading data of this list. The second condition is a classification of the possible degenerate classes, and it is not proved. So the labelling is proved and the count is arithmetic. Exhaustiveness needs F1 (Section~\ref{sub:F1}) and the classification. Nothing else in this part depends on them.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{prop:shifts}
Both chains satisfy their recurrences for \emph{every} phase: $\mathcal Q_n=\sin(n\vartheta+\alpha)/\sin\vartheta$ satisfies $\mathcal Q_n^2-\mathcal Q_{n-1}\mathcal Q_{n+1}=1$ identically in
$\alpha$, and with $\varsigma_i=\sin((ij-1)\vartheta+\beta)$ the products of $w_i=\varsigma_i^2/(\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_{i+1})$ telescope identically in $\beta$. The
degenerate coordinates are exactly the zeros of the unshifted chains --- $\mathcal Q_0=0$ at the small $L$, $\varsigma_p=0$ at the middle of the triple, $p=j^{-1}$
--- and taking the phases of the two chains of order $\epsilon$, $\alpha=a\epsilon$ and $\beta=b\epsilon$ with $a,b$ the unknown \emph{shift
coefficients}, resolves them, giving the degenerate coefficients explicitly in terms of $a$ and $b$:
\[
C_s=\frac{a^2}{\sin^2\vartheta},\qquad c_\pm=\pm2a\cot\vartheta,\qquad s=-\frac{b^2}{\sin^2(j\vartheta)},\qquad
A_{\mathrm l,\mathrm r}=\mp\frac{\sin^2(j\vartheta)}{\sin(2j\vartheta)\,b}.
\]
Hence, for $j\ne1$, the leading data carry two free parameters $(a,b)$: by Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction} (Appendix~\ref{app:existence}), for $\alpha,\beta=O(\epsilon)$ one has $\Lambda,\Xi=1+O(\epsilon)$, so the leading-order equations hold for all $(a,b)$.
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
For the $L$-chain, with $\psi=n\vartheta+\alpha$, $\sin^2\psi-\sin(\psi-\vartheta)\sin(\psi+\vartheta)=\sin^2\vartheta$ gives $\mathcal Q_n^2-\mathcal Q_{n-1}\mathcal Q_{n+1}=1$ for every $\alpha$. For the $R$-chain, the telescoping of the products of the $w_i$ is the content of the identities (T1)--(T5) of Lemma~\ref{lem:telescope}, which hold for arbitrary $\beta$. For the coefficients, put $\alpha=a\epsilon$, $\beta=b\epsilon$ and expand to leading order. At the small $L$, $C_s\epsilon^2=\mathcal Q_0^2=\sin^2(a\epsilon)/\sin^2\vartheta$, and at its neighbours $\sin^2(\pm\vartheta+a\epsilon)/\sin^2\vartheta=1\pm2a\epsilon\cot\vartheta+O(\epsilon^2)$. At the centre of the triple, $\varsigma_p=\sin\beta\approx b\epsilon$ and $\varsigma_{p-1}\varsigma_{p+1}=\sin(\beta-j\vartheta)\sin(\beta+j\vartheta)\approx-\sin^2(j\vartheta)$, so $w_p\approx-b^2\epsilon^2/\sin^2(j\vartheta)$. At its neighbours $w_{p\pm1}=\varsigma_{p\pm1}^2/(\varsigma_p\varsigma_{p\pm2})\approx\pm\sin^2(j\vartheta)/(b\epsilon\sin(2j\vartheta))$, so $w_{p-1}=A_{\mathrm l}/\epsilon$ and $w_{p+1}=A_{\mathrm r}/\epsilon$ with the values in the display.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:exist}
Let $m\ge3$ be odd, $k,j\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$ and $\vartheta=k\pi/m$. There are $\epsilon_0>0$ and real-analytic $\alpha(\epsilon),\beta(\epsilon)$, real for real $\epsilon$, on
$|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0$, vanishing at $\epsilon=0$ and nonzero for $\epsilon\ne0$, such that for $0<|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0$ the shifted chains of
Section~\ref{sec:leading} with phases $\alpha(\epsilon),\beta(\epsilon)$ solve the deformed Bethe system of $L^mR^m$ exactly, with the leading
data of type $j$ and Galois index $k$. Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] for $j\ne1$, $\alpha=-\tfrac\epsilon2\cot\vartheta+O(\epsilon^2)$ and $\beta=\tfrac\epsilon2\cot(j\vartheta)+O(\epsilon^2)$;
\item[\textup{(ii)}] for $j=1$, $\alpha=-\tfrac\epsilon2\cot\vartheta+O(\epsilon^2)$ and $\alpha+\beta=-\epsilon^2\cos\vartheta/(4\sin^3\vartheta)+O(\epsilon^3)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:corank}
Let $m\ge5$ be prime, $k\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$, and let $j\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$ be a placement. At $j=1$, $\operatorname{corank}\hat J_0=2$. At $j\ne1$,
$\operatorname{corank}\hat J_0=1+\operatorname{corank}M''$, where $M''$ is the block of $\hat J_0$ on all sites other than the small $L$ and its two
neighbours; the finite block of $M''$ is nonsingular when $\mathsf P(j^{-1})\not\equiv0\pmod m$, so $\operatorname{corank}\hat J_0\le4$; and
by a floating-point computation, $\operatorname{corank}\hat J_0=2$ at every placement of every prime $m\le43$.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
\emph{The case $j=1$.} We show $\operatorname{corank}\hat J_0=2$. Recall the construction of $\hat J_0$ at the start of this section. Read $\psi^{\mathsf T}\hat J_0=0$ column by column. The two $1+c\epsilon$ columns are multiples of $e_{L_2}$ and $e_{L_m}$, so $\psi_{L_2}=\psi_{L_m}=0$. The
finite-$L$ columns are $L_3,\dots,L_{m-1}$; each is tridiagonal in $L$ alone, and since $L_1,L_m$ are not among them the system closes on
$\psi_{L_3},\dots,\psi_{L_{m-1}}$ with the boundary values already $0$. Its matrix is the finite-$L$ block, nonsingular by
the \hyperref[prop:lblock]{$L$-block lemma}, so $\psi_{L_n}=0$ for $2\le n\le m$.

Every $R$-column gives $2i\psi_{L_1}-2\psi_{L_m}+\sum_l2\min(i,l)\psi_{R_l}+D_i\psi_{R_i}=0$, with $D_i$ the diagonal. Second differences in $i$
annihilate $2i\psi_{L_1}$ and $-2\psi_{L_m}$ and reduce $\sum_l2\min(i,l)\psi_{R_l}$ to $-2\psi_{R_i}$, giving
$d_{i-1}\psi_{R_{i-1}}-(2+2d_i)\psi_{R_i}+d_{i+1}\psi_{R_{i+1}}=0$ for $2\le i\le m-1$, with $d_i$ as in the
\hyperref[prop:arc]{arc-continuant lemma}. Since $D_2=D_m=0$ the chain breaks at both ends of the triple,
and $i=3,\dots,m-1$ is a closed system on the finite $R$-sites: the arc matrix, nonsingular by the \hyperref[prop:arc]{arc-continuant lemma}. Hence $\psi_{R_i}=0$ for
$3\le i\le m-1$, and the broken relation at $i=2$ reads $-\psi_{R_1}-2\psi_{R_2}=0$.

Three unknowns remain, $\psi_{L_1},\psi_{R_2},\psi_{R_m}$, and the columns $L_1$, $R_m$ and $R_2$ all give $\psi_{L_1}+\psi_{R_m}=0$, while the column
$R_1$ is satisfied identically on substituting $\psi_{R_1}=-2\psi_{R_2}$ and $\psi_{R_m}=-\psi_{L_1}$. So the solution space is free in $\psi_{L_1}$ and
$\psi_{R_2}$, of dimension exactly $2$.

\emph{The case $j\ne1$.} In $\hat J_0$ the columns of the two neighbours $L_{j\pm1}$ are nonzero multiples of $e_{L_{j\pm1}}$ (nonzero because $c_\pm=\mp\cot^2\vartheta\ne0$ on the solutions of Theorem~\ref{thm:exist}),
so a left kernel vector $\psi$ has $\psi_{L_{j\pm1}}=0$ and the corank of $\hat J_0$ is that of the block $M'''$ on the other $2m-2$ sites. In
$M'''$ the row and column of the small $L_j$ vanish: its diagonal is $4+D_{L_j}=4-4=0$ and its only couplings are to $L_{j\pm1}$. Hence
$\operatorname{corank}\hat J_0=1+\operatorname{corank}M''$ with $M''$ the block on the finite $L$-sites and all $m$ $R$-sites, and the theorem asks
for $\operatorname{corank}M''=1$. The finite block $B$ of the \hyperref[thm:modp]{finite-block lemma} is $M''$ with the three sites of the triple removed, so
$\det B\ne0$ gives $\operatorname{corank}M''\le3$, with equality to $1$ if and only if the $3\times3$ Schur complement of $B$ in $M''$ has rank $2$. The
reduction modulo $\mathfrak p$ cannot decide this last step: modulo $\mathfrak p$ the entries of $M''$ are those of the \hyperref[prop:modp]{reduction lemma}
extended to the triple ($D=0$ at its ends and $-1$ at its centre are the values of $(i-p)^2-1$ there), and the corank of the reduced $M''$ is
not $1$ (by exact computation over $\mathbb{F}_m$ it is $3$ at every placement $j\ne1$ for primes $m\le61$); the exact corank is decided at higher $\mathfrak p$-adic order, as the arc continuant of
the \hyperref[prop:arc]{arc-continuant lemma} is. It was computed in floating point for every placement $j\ne1$ and every $k$ of every prime $5\le m\le43$ ($3720$
placements): $\hat J_0$ has two singular values below $10^{-15}$ times the largest and the third at least $4\cdot10^{-8}$ of the largest, so
$\operatorname{corank}\hat J_0=2$ there. A proof uniform in $m$ would need the closed form of the Schur complement, as in the \hyperref[prop:arc]{arc-continuant lemma}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
At $j=1$ the block splits as $L\oplus R$ and both factors have closed forms, but their determinants have positive $\mathfrak p$-adic valuation (Appendix~\ref{sub:continuants}, the \hyperref[prop:lblock]{$L$-block} and \hyperref[prop:arc]{arc-continuant} lemmas), so the reduction modulo $\mathfrak p$ is singular and gives no information. At $j\ne1$ the block is
coupled, the splitting is unavailable, and the $\mathfrak p$-adic reduction of the finite block is a unit. Neither route covers a single placement the
other does; together they cover the finite block at all of them except the placements with $\mathsf P(p)\equiv0\pmod m$ discussed above.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:aminus}
Let $m\ge5$ be prime.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] \emph{Labelling and spins.} The $\tfrac12(m^2-1)$ leading data of Section~\ref{sec:leading} correspond bijectively to
$(A_-\smallsetminus0)/\!\pm$ through their kernel vectors, and the $\tfrac1m\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$-component of the spin of every vacuum of a real-analytic real solution with the leading data at $\pm u$ is $q_-(u)$.
\item[\textup{(ii)}] \emph{Existence.} For every placement $j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}$ and every $k$, the leading data $(j,k)$ are the limit as
$\epsilon\to0$ of an exact solution of the deformed Bethe system. These are $\tfrac12(m-1)^2$ distinct $A_-$ classes: all but the $m-1$ of
the types $0$ and $\infty$.
\item[\textup{(iii)}] \emph{Rank of the linearisation.} That solution is the only one with these leading data on the shifted-chain family. The leading-order Jacobian has
corank exactly two at $j=1$; at $j\ne1$ its finite block is nonsingular when $\mathsf P(j^{-1})\not\equiv0\pmod m$, and for every $j$ when $m<260$,
and, numerically, the corank is two at every placement of every prime $m\le43$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
\textup{(i)} is Theorem~\ref{thm:lines}, and \textup{(ii)} is Theorem~\ref{thm:exist}; the classes are distinct because their leading data are.
\textup{(iii)} Uniqueness on the family is the implicit function theorem of Theorem~\ref{thm:exist}. The corank at $j=1$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:corank};
the finite block is the \hyperref[thm:modp]{finite-block lemma} and the evaluation recorded after it; the corank for $m\le43$ is the computation in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:corank}
(Section~\ref{sub:corankproof}).
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:aminusgaps}
\textup{(i)} The types $0$ and $\infty$, together $m-1$ classes. Their leading data and kernel vectors are those of Theorem~\ref{thm:aminus}(i). Existence is not proved; at the type $0$ the shifted chains cannot satisfy the $R$-equations (see after Theorem~\ref{thm:exist}). If such solutions exist and are real-analytic with real data, Theorem~\ref{thm:lines}\textup{(iii)} gives their spin components.
\textup{(ii)} Isolatedness of the solutions of Theorem~\ref{thm:exist} in the full system, at every placement: the bifurcation equations of the
Lyapunov--Schmidt reduction begin at second order in $\epsilon$ (Section~\ref{sub:uniqueness}). The corank statement itself is proved only at $j=1$,
and verified for $m\le43$ otherwise.
\textup{(iii)} That these classes, with the $m-1$ of \textup{(i)}, are the whole sector rests on (F1) and on a classification of the possible degenerate leading data, which is not proved (Remark~\ref{rem:exhaustive}); at $m=5,7,11$ the
numerically harvested sectors are complete.
\textup{(iv)} At $m=3$ Theorem~\ref{thm:exist} gives the classes with $j=1,2$, but the division by $6$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:lines} fails and the
spins rest on Observation~\ref{obs:l3r3minus}.
\textup{(v)} The handle-gluing operator at these classes. They are $A_-$ classes in the sense of Section~\ref{sub:degenerate}, by their kernel
vectors; the value $\mathcal H=2^mm^2$ is observed at $m=5,7,11$ and is not computed here, Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} not reaching degenerate
classes. Corollary~\ref{cor:diagonal} obtains the corresponding moduli from the fusion rules instead.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:F}
The TQFT factorises as $\mathrm{TFT}_0\boxtimes\mathcal P$, with $\mathcal P$ pointed on the sign group $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\#L}$ and $\mathrm{TFT}_0$ a
modular category whose simple objects are $o$ (the unit, denoted $0$ in \eqref{eq:dict}), $b$, $a_g$ for $g\in(A_-\smallsetminus0)/\!\pm$ and $c_l$ for
$l\in(A_+\smallsetminus0)/\!\pm$, the two identity classes corresponding to $o,b$ in some order and the kernel-vector classes of
$A_\mp$ to the $a_g$, $c_l$, the class of the kernel vector $\operatorname{adj}(\varphi-1)g$ to $a_g$ and that of
$\operatorname{adj}(\varphi+1)l$ to $c_l$. With $X=b+\sum_ga_g+\sum_lc_l$, the fusion rules are those of the grafting. The fusion rules of the Haagerup double were computed in \cite[\S4.3.1]{EP06} and \cite[\S3.2]{EG11}; the grafted form is \cite[\S5.6]{EG20}:
\[
b\otimes b=o+X,\quad b\otimes a_g=X+a_g,\quad b\otimes c_l=X-c_l,\quad a_g\otimes c_l=X,
\]
\[
a_g\otimes a_{g'}=X+a_{g+g'}+a_{g-g'},\qquad c_l\otimes c_{l'}=X-c_{l+l'}-c_{l-l'},
\]
with the conventions $a_0=o+b$ and $c_0=b-o$.\footnote{In \cite{EG20} the convention printed as $d_0=0-b$ should read $d_0=b-0$; this is the convention $c_0=b-o$ used here.} The dictionary \eqref{eq:dict} holds: $S_{0\alpha}^2=\mathcal H_\alpha^{-1}$, and the spins are read off the fibering operator, $T_{\alpha\alpha}/T_{00}=\mathcal F_\alpha/\mathcal F_0$.
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:T}
Under Assumption~\ref{ass:F}, the spins of $\mathrm{TFT}_0$, relative to the unit, are $\theta_o=\theta_b=0$, $\theta_{a_g}=q_-(g)$ at every
non-degenerate class of $A_-$, and $\theta_{c_l}=q_+(l)$ at every non-degenerate class of $A_+$; the $T$-eigenvalues are $e(\theta)$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
The global dimension of $\mathrm{TFT}_0$ is $1/S_{00}^2=\lambda^{\mp1}N_-N_+$, of norm $(N_-N_+)^2$. By the Cauchy theorem for spherical fusion
categories \cite[Thm~3.9]{BNRW16}, every rational prime dividing the order of $T$ divides $N_-N_+$; so every twist has odd order. The pointed
factor has spins in $\tfrac14\mathbb{Z}$, since a quadratic form on an elementary abelian $2$-group takes values in $\tfrac14\mathbb{Z}$. Hence the twist of
a class is determined by the spins of its vacua modulo $\tfrac14$, which an element of odd order determines uniquely. At the identity classes
the Rogers sum is $c_\alpha=\#R$ exactly (Theorem~\ref{thm:ceff}). By \eqref{eq:Fphase} this fixes their spins modulo $\tfrac18$, which also determines an element of odd order, so $\theta_o=\theta_b$. At a non-degenerate class, Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers} gives the spin modulo
$\tfrac14$ relative to the identity classes as $-\Phi(u)/4N_\mp$, and the unique element of odd order in that class is $-[4^{-1}]_{N_\mp}\Phi(u)/N_\mp=q_\mp(u)$,
since $4[4^{-1}]_N-1\in N\mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
\label{prop:S}
Let $\mathrm{TFT}_0$ be as in Assumption~\ref{ass:F}, with spins $\theta_o=\theta_b=0$, $\theta_{a_g}=q_-(g)$, $\theta_{c_l}=q_+(l)$ for
nondegenerate quadratic forms $q_\mp$ on $A_\mp$, and vacuum column with moduli \eqref{eq:moduli}. The overall sign of $S$ is not fixed by these data (Remark~\ref{rem:Ssign}); normalise $s_o>0$. Then
\[
s_b>0,\qquad s_{a_g}=\frac1{\sqrt{N_-}}\ \text{for all }g,\qquad s_{c_l}=\frac{\operatorname{sgn}(s_b-s_o)}{\sqrt{N_+}}\ \text{for all }l,
\]
and the unit is the identity class with $s_o^2=\lambda/N_-N_+$ if and only if $\gamma_-=\gamma_+$, and the one with $s_o^2=1/\lambda N_-N_+$ if
and only if $\gamma_-=-\gamma_+$. In either case $S$ is the Evans--Gannon grafting \cite[\S3.3]{EG11} of $(A_-,q_-)$ and $(A_+,q_+)$, whose fusion rules \cite[\S5.6]{EG20} are those of Assumption~\ref{ass:F}, in the frame fixed by the unit
\textup{(}$s_o^2=\lambda/N_-N_+$ or $1/\lambda N_-N_+$\textup{)}.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
The balancing equation in a modular category reads $S_{ij}=\bar t_i\bar t_j\sum_kN_{ij}^kt_ks_k$, with $t_i=e(\theta_i)$ the $T$-eigenvalues relative to the unit (the objects are
self-dual). Put
$P=s_b+\sum_gt_{a_g}s_{a_g}+\sum_lt_{c_l}s_{c_l}$, $p_x=t_{a_x}s_{a_x}$ on $A_-$ with $p_0=s_o+s_b$, and $p_y=t_{c_y}s_{c_y}$ on
$A_+$ with $p_0=s_b-s_o$. The fusion rules give
\[
S_{bb}=s_o+P,\quad S_{ba}=\bar t_aP+s_a,\quad S_{bc}=\bar t_cP-s_c,\quad S_{ac}=\bar t_a\bar t_cP,
\]
\[
S_{a_ga_{g'}}=\bar t_g\bar t_{g'}\bigl(P+p_{g+g'}+p_{g-g'}\bigr),\qquad S_{c_lc_{l'}}=\bar t_l\bar t_{l'}\bigl(P-p_{l+l'}-p_{l-l'}\bigr).
\]
(i) $P=0$. Otherwise reality of $S_{ac}$ for all $c$ forces $e(q_+(l)-q_+(l'))=\pm1$, so $q_+$ is constant, say $\equiv\varrho$, on
$A_+\smallsetminus0$, $N_+$ being odd, and $q_+(2l)=4q_+(l)$ gives $3\varrho\equiv0$. Then $|G(q_+)|^2=|1+(N_+-1)e(\varrho)|^2$ is $N_+^2$
if $\varrho=0$ and $N_+^2-3N_++3$ otherwise, whereas a nondegenerate form on a group of odd order has $|G(q_+)|^2=N_+$; neither is
possible for $N_+=k+2\ge7$.

(ii) With $P=0$, orthogonality of the rows $o$ and $b$ reads $2s_os_b+\tfrac12(N_+^{-1}-N_-^{-1})=0$, so $s_os_b=1/N_-N_+>0$ and $s_b>0$. By
\eqref{eq:moduli}, in both cases $s_o+s_b=N_-^{-1/2}$ and $|s_o-s_b|=N_+^{-1/2}$.

(iii) Let $B_-$ be the bilinear form of $q_-$. As $t_{a_{g\pm g'}}=t_gt_{g'}e(\pm B_-(g,g'))$,
\[
S_{a_ga_{g'}}=e(B_-(g,g'))\,s_{a_{g+g'}}+e(-B_-(g,g'))\,s_{a_{g-g'}}\qquad(s_{a_0}:=s_o+s_b),
\]
and reality forces $s_{a_{g+g'}}=s_{a_{g-g'}}$ whenever $B_-(g,g')\neq0$, since $B_-\notin\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}$ for odd $N_-$. Taking $g=g'$: $s_{a_{2g}}=s_o+s_b=N_-^{-1/2}$ whenever $q_-(g)\ne0$, which covers every non-isotropic element.
For isotropic $x\ne0$ choose a non-isotropic $y$ and $g=(x+y)/2$, $g'=(x-y)/2$; then $B_-(g,g')=-q_-(y)/2\ne0$, so $s_{a_x}=s_{a_y}$. Thus
$s_{a_g}=N_-^{-1/2}$ for all $g$. The same argument on $A_+$, with the sign of the $c$-block, gives $s_{c_l}=s_b-s_o$ for all $l$.

(iv) Now $\sum_gt_{a_g}=(G(q_-)-1)/2$, so $P=0$ reads
$s_b+\tfrac12(\gamma_--N_-^{-1/2})+\tfrac12(s_b-s_o)(\sqrt{N_+}\gamma_+-1)=0$. If $s_o^2=\lambda/N_-N_+$ then $s_b=\tfrac12(N_-^{-1/2}-N_+^{-1/2})$
and $s_b-s_o=-N_+^{-1/2}$, and the equation is $\gamma_-=\gamma_+$; if $s_o^2=1/\lambda N_-N_+$ it is $\gamma_-=-\gamma_+$. All entries of $S$ are now
determined by the balancing equation, and they are those of the grafting.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:Ssign}
The data of Assumption~\ref{ass:F} determine $S$ only up to $S\mapsto-S$. Both signs give $S^2=1$ and the same Verlinde coefficients. With $T_{oo}=1$, the relation $(ST)^3=e(c/8)S^2$ changes $c$ by $4$ modulo $8$ under this sign. So the sign is fixed by the central charge, and the representative with $s_o>0$ need not be the right one.

This can be tested on the full set of vacua, without Assumption~\ref{ass:F}. Put $G=\sum_\alpha(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{unit}}/\mathcal H_\alpha)\,e(\theta_\alpha)$, where $\theta_\alpha$ is the spin relative to the unit. Then $|G|^2=\sum_\alpha\mathcal H_{\mathrm{unit}}/\mathcal H_\alpha$, and $G/|G|=\operatorname{sgn}(S_{oo})\,e(c/8)$.

We computed $G$ numerically for the six words of Remark~\ref{rem:scope}, from the $\mathcal H_\alpha$ and spins of all vacua, with $c=\#L-6\#R$. In each case $\sum_\alpha\mathcal H_\alpha^{-1}=1$ and $G/|G|=\pm e(c/8)$. The sign is $-$ for $L^2RLR^2$, $L^2R^2LR$ and the two words of length $10$, and $+$ for $L^2RLRLR^2$ and $L^2R^2LRLR$. This confirms the congruence of Theorem~\ref{thm:fareygeneral} modulo $4$ independently of the fusion rules, given input~(b). Modulo $8$ it shows that $S_{oo}<0$ for the first four words. For $L^mR^m$ with $m$ odd the comparison can be made for $\mathrm{TFT}_0$ alone. The pointed factor $\mathcal P$ has spins, measured from the unit, with Gauss sum $\sqrt{2^m}\,e(-m/8)$ (Propositions~\ref{prop:signsum} and~\ref{prop:spinq}(iii)), so its central charge is $c_{\mathcal P}\equiv-m\pmod8$. Hence $c(\mathrm{TFT}_0)\equiv c-c_{\mathcal P}\equiv-5m+m\equiv4\pmod8$. The grafting with $s_o>0$ has central charge $0$ modulo $8$ (computed for $m=3,5,7,9$), so the offset is again $4$, and $S_{oo}<0$.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let $\varphi$ be a hyperbolic word of odd trace $k\ge5$. Assume Assumption~\ref{ass:F}, the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall}, and that every nonzero kernel vector of $\varphi$ is non-degenerate.
Then the modular data of $\mathrm{TFT}_0$ are determined: $T$ is given by the forms $q_\mp$ of \eqref{eq:qform}, the unit is $\sigma V^*$, and
$S$ is the Evans--Gannon grafting of $(A_-,q_-)$ and $(A_+,q_+)$ in the frame $s_o^2=\lambda/N_-N_+$, up to the overall sign of Remark~\ref{rem:Ssign}. Since $\gamma_-=\gamma_+$, no unitary
grafting has these forms \textup{(}Proposition~\ref{prop:S}\textup{)}; for $L^mR^m$, Corollary~\ref{cor:galois} identifies the unitary data of
which these are a Galois conjugate.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Corollary~\ref{cor:T} gives $T$; Lemma~\ref{lem:disc} gives $\gamma_-=\gamma_+$; Proposition~\ref{prop:S} then gives $S$ and places the unit at
the identity class with $\mathcal H=2^{\#L}\lambda^{-1}N_-N_+$, which is $\sigma V^*$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:torsion}).
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:galois}
Let $\varphi=L^mR^m$ with $m$ odd, and let $\sigma_\ell$ be the automorphism $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^\ell$ of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{N_-N_+})$ with
$\ell\equiv2^{-1}\pmod{N_-N_+}$. The modular data of Proposition~\ref{prop:S} with the spins $q_\mp$ and $s_o>0$ --- the form that Theorem~\ref{thm:main}
gives to the modular data of $\mathrm{TFT}_0$, up to the sign of $S$ --- are the image under $\sigma_\ell$ of the unitary Evans--Gannon grafting of $(A_-,q^{\mathrm{lk}})$
and $(A_+,q^{\mathrm{lk}})$, the forms of Proposition~\ref{prop:linking}.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:linking}, the forms $q^{\mathrm{lk}}$ have $\gamma_-=+1$ and $\gamma_+=-1$, so by Proposition~\ref{prop:S} their grafting has
its unit at $s_o^2=1/\lambda N_-N_+$, which is the unitary frame. Its entries, listed in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:S}, lie in
$\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{N_-N_+})$, since $N_-=m^2$ and $N_+=\mu\equiv1\pmod4$. The automorphism $\sigma_\ell$ sends $e(q^{\mathrm{lk}})$ to $e(2^{-1}q^{\mathrm{lk}})=e(q_\mp)$
(Section~\ref{sec:metric}) and $\cos2\pi B^{\mathrm{lk}}$ to $\cos2\pi B_\mp$, where $B$ denotes the bilinear form of each quadratic form. It
fixes $m$, and it sends $\sqrt\mu$ to $(\ell/\mu)\sqrt\mu=(2/\mu)\sqrt\mu=-\sqrt\mu$, as $\mu\equiv5\pmod8$. Hence it exchanges the values
$\tfrac12(m^{-1}\mp\mu^{-1/2})$ of $s_o$ and $s_b$, which gives $s_o^2=\lambda/N_-N_+$, and it changes the sign of $s_{c_l}=s_b-s_o$. These are
the data of Proposition~\ref{prop:S} with the spins $q_\mp$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:diagonal}
Let $\varphi=L^mR^m$ with $m\ge5$ prime and $\mu=m^2+4$ prime, for instance $m=5,7,13,17,37,47$, and assume Assumption~\ref{ass:F}. Suppose that the $m-1$ classes of $A_-$ of types $0$ and
$\infty$ exist as solutions real-analytic in $\epsilon$ with real coordinates, with the leading data of Theorem~\ref{thm:aminus}\textup{(i)} \textup{(}Remark~\ref{rem:aminusgaps}\textup{(i)}\textup{)}. Then
the unit is $\sigma V^*$, and $S$ is, up to the sign of Remark~\ref{rem:Ssign}, the grafting of $(A_-,q_-)$ and $(A_+,q_+)$ in the frame $s_o^2=\lambda/N_-N_+$: by
Corollary~\ref{cor:galois}, the image under $\sigma_\ell$, $\ell\equiv2^{-1}$, of the modular data of the double of every pseudo-unitary untwisted Haagerup--Izumi category of $\mathbb{Z}_m$ \cite[Thm.~A(2)]{GSY26}.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
First, every nonzero $A_+$ kernel vector is non-degenerate. Since $\mu$ is prime, $\mathcal K_+$ is a line over $\mathbb{F}_\mu$, so $\langle v,e\rangle\equiv0\pmod\mu$ with $v\in\mathcal K_+\smallsetminus0$ forces $e\in\mathcal K_+$, i.e.\ $(\varphi+1)e\equiv0\pmod\mu$.
The middle slopes are $e=(i,1)$ and $e=(1+im,i)$, $1\le i\le m$ (proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:lines}). The second coordinate of $(\varphi+1)e$ is $mi+2$, resp.\ $m-2i$ modulo $\mu$. It vanishes only at $i\equiv-2m^{-1}$, resp.\ $i\equiv m/2$, and both residues equal $\tfrac12(m^2+m+4)$, which lies strictly between $m$ and $\mu$. So no middle slope is degenerate, and Corollary~\ref{cor:T} gives $\theta_{c_l}=q_+(l)$. On $A_-$,
Theorem~\ref{thm:aminus}\textup{(i)} gives the $\tfrac1m\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$-component of the spin as $q_-$, and under Assumption~\ref{ass:F} that component is
the whole twist: by the Cauchy argument of Corollary~\ref{cor:T} every twist has order prime to $6$ ($3\nmid m^2(m^2+4)$), while
$24\theta\equiv c_\alpha\in\tfrac1m\mathbb{Z}$. The moduli $s_{a_g}^2=1/N_-$ of \eqref{eq:moduli}, which Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} does not give at these
degenerate classes, are forced by Assumption~\ref{ass:F}: the dimensions $d_\alpha=s_\alpha/s_o$ form a character of the fusion ring, and
