$a_g\otimes c_l=X=b\otimes a_g-a_g=b\otimes c_l+c_l$ gives $d_{a_g}=d_b+1$ and $d_{c_l}=d_b-1$ for all $g,l$, dividing by $d_{c_l}$ and $d_{a_g}$, which are nonzero since $S_{0\alpha}\ne0$, and $d_X=d_{a_g}d_{c_l}=d_b^2-1$.
Since $X$ has $\tfrac12(N_-{-}1)$ summands $a_g$ and $\tfrac12(N_+{-}1)$ summands $c_l$, with $N_\pm=k\pm2$, this reads $d_b^2-kd_b+1=0$, so $d_b=\lambda^{\pm1}$, $\sum_\alpha d_\alpha^2=\lambda^{\pm1}N_-N_+$, and $s_{a_g}^2=d_{a_g}^2/\sum_\alpha d_\alpha^2=1/N_-$. The same argument gives $s_{c_l}^2=1/N_+$, so the hypothesis $\det(F+D_R)\ne0$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall} is not used. The
proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} then applies.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- observation-9: body_md -->
\label{obs:wcrow}
Let $\operatorname{tr}\varphi$ be odd. At the base vacuum $V_{\varepsilon_0}$ \textup{(}Proposition~\ref{prop:spinq}\textup{)} of every class of
Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords},
\[
W_c=+1\ \text{on the }A_-\text{ sector},\qquad W_c=-1\ \text{on the }A_+\text{ sector},
\]
and at the identity classes $W_c(V^*)=\lambda$ \textup{(}Proposition~\ref{obs:stretch}\textup{)}, and $W_c=\lambda^{-1}$ at the Galois conjugate of the lift $V^*$ (with $z_L=h'(\mathsf m)/h'(\mathsf k)$ as in Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}). That vacuum lies in the class of $\sigma V^*$ but is not $\sigma V^*$ itself.
<!-- end observation-9 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rem:scope}
The hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} that every nonzero kernel vector is non-degenerate holds, among the $102$ cyclic words of odd trace at least $5$
and length at most $11$, for $6$ words, $L^2RLR^2$ among them. For $L^mR^m$ with $m$ prime the $A_-$ classes are degenerate, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:diagonal} replaces Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers} there by Theorem~\ref{thm:aminus}; its other
hypothesis, that the $A_+$ kernel vectors are non-degenerate, holds whenever $m^2+4$ is prime (proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:diagonal}). Among the primes $5\le m\le59$ these are $m=5,7,13,17,37,47$; for the others some $A_+$ kernel vector is degenerate (a computation), and the corollary does not apply. At $m=3$ Theorem~\ref{thm:lines} is not
available, and Observation~\ref{obs:l3r3minus} takes its place. For other words the spins of the degenerate classes, which have a coordinate at
infinity, are not covered by Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers}.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- observation-10: body_md -->
\label{obs:l3r3minus}
At $\varphi=L^3R^3$ the deformed Bethe equations at $\epsilon=10^{-2}$ and $10^{-3}$ have four $A_-$ classes, each continued to $\epsilon=10^{-5}$ with
$\mathcal H_\alpha/2^3\to9$; all four are real. In the notation $z_b=C_b\epsilon^{p_b}(1+o(1))$ of Observation~\ref{obs:strata} their exponent vectors are
$(0,0,2\,|\,0,0,0)$, $(2,0,0\,|\,2,-1,-1)$, $(0,2,0\,|\,-1,2,-1)$ and $(-2,-2,-2\,|\,-1,-1,2)$. Along each continuation $\arg\mathcal F/2\pi$ is
constant modulo $\tfrac14$ to $10^{-8}$, with values $\tfrac1{24},\tfrac18,\tfrac18,\tfrac5{24}$, against $\tfrac18$ at both identity classes.
Relative to the identity classes these are $\tfrac1{6},0,0,\tfrac1{12}\pmod{\tfrac14}$, which lift uniquely to $\tfrac13\mathbb{Z}/\mathbb{Z}$ as
$\tfrac23,0,0,\tfrac13$: the values of the hyperbolic form $x_1x_2/3$ on $(A_-\setminus0)/\!\pm$. The anisotropic form, which takes only the
values $\tfrac13,\tfrac23$ there, is excluded. The same reading on the six $A_+$ classes gives the values $l^2/13$, $l=1,\dots,6$, the form $q_+$ up to isometry, as Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers}
requires. Since the $A_+$ kernel vectors of $L^3R^3$ are non-degenerate, the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} then applies at $m=3$, with these
values on $A_-$ in place of Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers}: the unit is $\sigma V^*$ and $S$ is the grafting of $(\mathbb{Z}_3^2,x_1x_2/3)$ and $(\mathbb{Z}_{13},q_+)$.
These values are numerical: Theorem~\ref{thm:rogers}, which gives the spins modulo $\tfrac14$ at the non-degenerate classes, does not reach the
degenerate ones, and at $m=3$ Theorem~\ref{thm:lines} is not available.
<!-- end observation-10 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:life}
The edge $e$ born at flip $i$ is the Farey slope of flip $i+1$. If $\ell_{i+2}=\ell_{i+1}$ it is the dying slope of flip $i+2$. If
$\ell_{i+2}\ne \ell_{i+1}$ it is the kept slope of flip $i+2$ and of every flip of the run of $\ell_{i+2}$'s starting there, and it is the dying slope
of the first flip after that run.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Eliminate each $R$-run's fan block $F=2M$, $M_{ij}=\min(i,j)$. Since $M^{-1}$ is tridiagonal $(2,-1)$ with last diagonal entry $1$, one has
$M^{-1}(1,\dots,b)^{\mathsf T}=e_b$ and $M^{-1}\mathbf1=e_1$; so the ramp $\mathsf r=2(1,\dots,b)$ and the row $s=-2\cdot\mathbf1$ contribute
$\mathsf r^{\mathsf T}F^{-1}\mathsf r=2b$, $s^{\mathsf T}F^{-1}s=2$ and $\mathsf r^{\mathsf T}F^{-1}s=-2$ to the $L$-Schur complement. The $+2b$ removes the $2b$ on the
diagonal of the first $L$ after the run, and the $-2$ cross term cancels the cyclic $L$--$L$ coupling across the run. What remains decomposes by
$L$-runs, $S=\bigoplus_q2M_{a_q}^{-1}$ --- after the $R$-runs are eliminated the $L$-runs decouple completely --- with $\det=2^{a_q}$ per block,
including $\#L=1$, where the single $L$ is adjacent to itself. Hence $\det K=\prod_q\det(2M_{b_q})\prod_q2^{a_q}=2^{\#R}2^{\#L}=2^r$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
For each of the eight patterns $LLL,\dots,RLR$ listed above, $\sum_tB[e,t]K_{\mathrm{raw}}[t,\cdot]$ is computed from the rows of $K_{\mathrm{raw}}$ listed in Section~\ref{sec:runK} and compared with $A[e,\cdot]$ column by
column. In each case only the columns named in the computation can be nonzero; every other column is zero on both sides.

\emph{$LLL$.} $-2K_{\mathrm{raw}}[i+1,\cdot]$ for a middle $L$ is $-2$ at $i+1$ and $+1$ at its two adjacent $L$'s, $i$ and $i+2$.

\emph{$RRR$.} The second difference along the run of $2\min(j,l)$ in $j$ is $-2\delta_{jl}$; the ramp $j$ at $L^+(\rho)$ is linear in $j$ and
the entry $-1$ at $L^-(\rho)$ is constant, so both difference to zero.

\emph{$RLL$.} $K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_b,\cdot]-2K_{\mathrm{raw}}[L_1,\cdot]$: at $R_l\in\rho$, $2l-2l=0$; at $L_1$, $b-2(1+b/2)=-2$; at $L_2$, $-2\cdot(-\tfrac12)=1$;
at $L^-(\rho)$, $-1-2(-\tfrac12)=0$, the $-\tfrac12$ being the adjacency of $L^-(\rho)$ and $L_1$ across $\rho$. ($L_1$ is not an $L^-$,
since $\ell_{i+2}=L$.)

\emph{$LRR$.} $-2K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_1,\cdot]+K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_2,\cdot]$: at $R_1$, $-4+2=-2$; at $R_l$, $l\ge2$, $-4+4=0$; at $L^+(\rho)$, $-2+2=0$; at
$L^-(\rho)$, $2-1=1$.

\emph{$LLR$.} $-2K_{\mathrm{raw}}[L^-(\rho),\cdot]$: this $L$ is not an $L^+$, its predecessor $i$ being an $L$, so its row is $1$ on the diagonal,
$-\tfrac12$ at $i$ and at $L^+(\rho)$, its two adjacent $L$'s, and $-1$ at every $R$ of $\rho$. Times $-2$: $-2$, $1$, $1$, $2$, as required.

\emph{$RRL$.} $K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_{b-1},\cdot]-2K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_b,\cdot]+2\sum_{s=1}^aK_{\mathrm{raw}}[L_s,\cdot]+K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R'_1,\cdot]$, where $\varsigma=L_1\cdots L_a$,
$L_1=L^+(\rho)$ and $L_a=L^-(\rho')$ for the run $\rho'$ starting at $R'_1$. At $R_l\in\rho$: $2\min(b-1,l)-4l$ from the first two rows
and $2l$ from the ramp of $L_1$, in total $2\min(b-1,l)-2l=-2\delta_{lb}$. At $L^-(\rho)$: $-1-2(-1)+2(-\tfrac12)=0$, from $R_{b-1}$, from $R_b$, and from the adjacency of $L^-(\rho)$ and $L_1$ across $\rho$. At $L_1$: $(b-1)-2b+2(1+b/2)+2(-\tfrac12)=0$, the last term from
$L_2$ if $a\ge2$ and from $K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R'_1,L_1]=-1$ if $a=1$. At a middle $L_s$, $1<s<a$: $2(-\tfrac12+1-\tfrac12)=0$. At $L_a$, $a\ge2$:
$2(-\tfrac12+1)-1=0$, the $-1$ from $R'_1$. At $R'_l\in\rho'$: $2(-1)+2\min(1,l)=0$, the $-1$ from $L_a=L^-(\rho')$. At $L^+(\rho')$:
$2(-\tfrac12)+1=0$, the adjacency of $L_a$ and $L^+(\rho')$ against the ramp of $R'_1$. When runs coincide --- $\rho'=\rho$ for a two-run
word, $L^+(\rho')=L_1$, or $L^-(\rho)\in\varsigma$ --- the extra entries are the ones already listed, landing on the same columns, and the same
sums give the same totals.

\emph{$LRL$.} The same combination without the row $R_{b-1}$ and with $b=1$: $-2K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_1,\cdot]+2\sum_sK_{\mathrm{raw}}[L_s,\cdot]+K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R'_1,\cdot]$.
At $R_1$: $-4+2=-2$. At $L^-(\rho)=i$: $2+2(-\tfrac12)=1$, from $K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_1,L^-(\rho)]=-1$ and the adjacency of $L^-(\rho)$ and $L_1$. At
$L_1$: $-2+2(1+\tfrac12)-1$ or $-2+2(1+\tfrac12)+2(-\tfrac12)$, both $0$. The columns $L_s$, $L_a$, $R'_l$ and $L^+(\rho')$ are as in $RRL$.

\emph{$RLR$.} $K_{\mathrm{raw}}[R_b,\cdot]-2K_{\mathrm{raw}}[L,\cdot]$ with $L=L^+(\rho)=L^-(\rho')$: at $R_l\in\rho$, $2l-2l=0$; at $L$, $b-2(1+b/2)=-2$; at
$L^-(\rho)$, $-1-2(-\tfrac12)=0$; at $R'_l\in\rho'$, $-2(-1)=2$; at $L^+(\rho')$, $-2(-\tfrac12)=1$. For $\#L=1$, $\rho'=\rho$ and
$L^+(\rho')=L$: the entries add to $-1$ at $L$ and $2$ at each $R_l$, which is what the pattern gives when the dying site $L^+(\rho')$ is $L$
itself.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
The identity $A=BK_{\mathrm{raw}}$ gives
$(A\,|\,B)=B\,(K_{\mathrm{raw}}\,|\,I)$, where $(X\,|\,Y)$ denotes the $r\times2r$ matrix whose columns are those of $X$ followed by those of $Y$, with $(K_{\mathrm{raw}}\,|\,I)$ of full row rank, so $\operatorname{rank}B=\operatorname{rank}(A\,|\,B)$. The layered
triangulation of a hyperbolic once-punctured-torus bundle is geometric \cite{Gueritaud06}, so \cite[Proposition~2.3]{NZ85} applies. It states that for an
ideal triangulation of a hyperbolic manifold with $n$ tetrahedra and $h$ cusps, the matrix $R=(R'\,|\,R'')$ of the edge relations
$\prod_\nu z_\nu^{r'_{j\nu}}(1-z_\nu)^{r''_{j\nu}}=\pm1$ has rank $n-h$. Here $n=r$ and $h=1$. Their variables are $(\log z,\log(1-z))$ and
ours are $(Z,Z')=(\log z,\log(1-z)-\log z)$, so $(R'\,|\,R'')=(A-B\,|\,B)$, a column operation on $(A\,|\,B)$; hence
$\operatorname{rank}(A\,|\,B)=\operatorname{rank}R=r-1$, and $\operatorname{rank}B=r-1$.

Put $u=Q^{-1}c$: $u=b/2$ at $L^+(\rho)$ for each run $\rho$ of length $b$, $0$ at every other $L$, and $j$ at the $j$-th $R$ of every run.
Then $Bu=0$ row by row, from the list of patterns: $LLL$, $-2u_{i+1}=0$ at a middle $L$; $RRR$, $(j-1)-2j+(j+1)=0$; $RLL$, $b-2(b/2)=0$;
$LRR$, $-2+2=0$; $LLR$, $-2u_{L^-(\rho)}=0$, this $L$ not being an $L^+$; $RRL$, $(b-1)-2b+2(b/2)+1=0$, the $L$'s of $\varsigma$ other than
$L_1=L^+(\rho)$ contributing $0$; $LRL$, $-2+2\cdot\tfrac12+1=0$; $RLR$, $b-2(b/2)=0$. As $u\ne0$ and $\ker B$ is one-dimensional, $u$ spans
it.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
$(K_{\mathrm{raw}} P)^2=I$ splits into (i) $V^2+CF=I$, (ii) $VC+CV^{\mathsf T}=0$, (iii) $FV+V^{\mathsf T}F=0$, with (i) equivalent to its transpose.

(iii): with $\mathbf1$ the all-ones vector, $Fe_0=2\mathbf1$ and $Fe_{m-1}=2v$, so $FV=2\mathbf1v^{\mathsf T}-2v\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}$ and $V^{\mathsf T}F=2v\mathbf1^{\mathsf
T}-2\mathbf1v^{\mathsf T}$, which sum to zero.

(ii): the interior rows of $C$ are $(-\tfrac12,1,-\tfrac12)$, annihilating both constants and linear ramps; the boundary rows give
$\tfrac{m+2}2-\tfrac12-\tfrac12=\tfrac m2$ and $-\tfrac12(m-1)+m-\tfrac12=\tfrac m2$. The remaining boundary entries vanish: row $0$ of $Cv$ is $\tfrac{m+2}2-1-\tfrac m2=0$, and row $m-1$ of $C\mathbf1$ is
$-\tfrac12+1-\tfrac12=0$. Hence $C\mathbf1=\tfrac m2e_0$ and $Cv=\tfrac m2e_{m-1}$, and
$VC+CV^{\mathsf T}=\tfrac m2(e_0e_{m-1}^{\mathsf T}-e_{m-1}e_0^{\mathsf T}+e_{m-1}e_0^{\mathsf T}-e_0e_{m-1}^{\mathsf T})=0$.

(i), interior rows: for $1\le i\le m-2$, $(CF)_{ij}=2\min(i+1,j+1)-\min(i,j+1)-\min(i+2,j+1)$, the second difference of $k\mapsto\min(k,j+1)$, which
vanishes except at the bend $i=j$ where it equals $1$; and $V^2$ has no support on those rows.

(i), boundary rows: expanding, $V^2=e_0v^{\mathsf T}-m\,e_0\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}-e_{m-1}v^{\mathsf T}+e_{m-1}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}$, so
$(V^2)_{0j}=j+1-m$ and $(V^2)_{m-1,j}=-j$. Row $0$: $(CF)_{0j}=\tfrac{m+2}2F_{0j}-\tfrac12F_{1j}-\tfrac12F_{m-1,j}$ with $F_{0j}=2$, $F_{1j}=2$ for
$j=0$ and $4$ for $j\ge1$, $F_{m-1,j}=2(j+1)$; for $j=0$ this is $(m+2)-1-1=m$, for $j\ge1$ it is $(m+2)-2-(j+1)=m-j-1$. Row $m-1$:
$(CF)_{m-1,j}=-\tfrac12F_{m-2,j}+F_{m-1,j}-\tfrac12F_{0j}$ gives $j$ for $j\le m-2$ and $m$ for $j=m-1$. Adding $(V^2)_{0j}$ and $(V^2)_{m-1,j}$ gives $\delta_{0j}$ in row $0$ and $\delta_{m-1,j}$ in row $m-1$. At $m=2$ the two boundary rows are distinct and the computation above applies, the doubled edge entering as $C_{01}=-1$. At $m=1$,
where they coincide, $V=0$, $C=\tfrac12$ and $F=2$, so $K_{\mathrm{raw}} PK_{\mathrm{raw}}=P$ directly.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:cotsol}
Let $\hat u_i=\sin\psi_i/\sin\vartheta$, $\psi_i=i\vartheta+\phi$, be a frieze row with $1-x_i=\hat u_{i-1}\hat u_{i+1}/\hat u_i^2$. The three-term
recurrence
\[
y_{i-1}+y_{i+1}=\frac{2}{1-x_i}\,y_i
\]
has the fundamental system $\mathfrak f_i=\cot\psi_i$, $\mathfrak g_i=i\cot\psi_i-\cot\vartheta$, with Casoratian $\mathfrak f_i\mathfrak g_{i+1}-\mathfrak f_{i+1}\mathfrak g_i=-1$. It is the recurrence of
the $L$-Schur complement $S_\alpha$ (Schur complement of $K+D$ at the class $\alpha$ whose coordinates give the frieze row) inside an $L$-run \textup{(}where $S_{ii}=4/(1-x_i)$ and the couplings are $-2$\textup{)}, and also, up to the factor $\tfrac12$, that of
$J=F^{-1}+D_R^{-1}$ inside an $R$-run \textup{(}off-diagonal $-\tfrac12$, diagonal $1+1/(\hat u_{i-1}\hat u_{i+1})=1/(1-x_i)$ at the rows $i<b$, and $\tfrac12+1/(\hat u_{b-1}\hat u_{b+1})$ at the last row\textup{)}, where
$F=(2\min(i,k))$ is the fan and $F^{-1}$ the path matrix $\tfrac12\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)$ with last diagonal entry $\tfrac12$. On an $R$-run, $x_i$ in the lemma is the frieze variable and not the Bethe shape $x_{R_i}$; for the latter, $1/(1-x_{R_i})=\hat u_i^2$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
With $u_i=\sin\psi_i$ put $y_i=z_i/u_i$; the recurrence becomes
$u_{i+1}z_{i-1}+u_{i-1}z_{i+1}=2u_iz_i$, and $z_i=\cos\psi_i$ solves it by $\sin(\psi+\vartheta)\cos(\psi-\vartheta)+\sin(\psi-\vartheta)\cos(\psi+\vartheta)=\sin2\psi$,
while $z_i=i\cos\psi_i-\cot\vartheta\sin\psi_i$ solves it because the extra terms are
$\sin(\psi-\vartheta)\cos(\psi+\vartheta)-\sin(\psi+\vartheta)\cos(\psi-\vartheta)=-\sin2\vartheta$ and $-2\cot\vartheta(\sin^2\psi-\sin^2\vartheta)+2\cot\vartheta\sin^2\psi=\sin2\vartheta$.
The Casoratian is $\cot\psi_0\cot\psi_1+\cot\vartheta(\cot\psi_1-\cot\psi_0)=(\cos\psi_0\cos\psi_1-\cos\vartheta)/(\sin\psi_0\sin\psi_1)=-1$. That the recurrence is the one of $S_\alpha$ inside an $L$-run follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}: there $K_{ii}=4$,
$K_{i,i\pm1}=-2$, so $S_{ii}=4+D_i=4+4x_i/(1-x_i)=4/(1-x_i)$ and the row of $S_\alpha$ is $-2y_{i-1}+\tfrac4{1-x_i}y_i-2y_{i+1}=0$. That it is
also the recurrence of $J=F^{-1}+D_R^{-1}$ inside an $R$-run follows from the inverse of the fan matrix, $F^{-1}=\tfrac12\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1)$ with
last diagonal entry $\tfrac12$, together with $D_j^{-1}=(1-x_{R_j})/x_{R_j}=1/(\hat u_j^2-1)=1/(\hat u_{j-1}\hat u_{j+1})$ by the frieze relation.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:floqvec}
Let $\theta:\mathbb{Z}^2\to\mathbb{C}$ be additive, put $f(e)=\sin\theta(e)$, and let $x_t=f(\mathsf k_t)^2/f(\mathsf m_t)^2$ at $L$-flips and
$x_t=1-f(\mathsf k_t)^2/f(\mathsf m_t)^2$ at $R$-flips along the developed word, all finite and different from $0$ and $1$, and suppose $\det(F+D_R)\ne0$ on every $R$-run, so that the corner entries \eqref{eq:corners} are defined; the case
$\theta(e)=\pi\langle v,e\rangle/N$, $v\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, $N\ge1$, is the closed form of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}. Let $h$ be any linear functional on
$\mathbb{Z}^2$, and put
\[
H(e)=h(e)\cot\theta(e),\qquad Y_t=H(\mathsf m_t)-H(\mathsf k_t)\quad(t\text{ an }L\text{-site}).
\]
Index the $L$-sites along the developed word, i.e.\ along the infinite periodic sequence of letters obtained by repeating the word (the \emph{unrolled} recurrence).
The lemma is local: it does not assume the closing-up condition $Y_{t+n}=\Lambda Y_t$, $n=\#L$, which holds only for particular $\theta$ and $h$ and is verified in each application (the proof of (A) below, and Theorem~\ref{thm:Hall}). Then $SY=0$, identically in $\theta$ and $h$, where $S$ here denotes the infinite three-term operator along the developed word whose rows are those of $S$, given locally. This holds for the interior rows $-2Y_{i-1}+\tfrac4{1-x_i}Y_i-2Y_{i+1}$ and for the junction rows, which carry the corner
entries \eqref{eq:corners}.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
\emph{Interior rows.} Along an $L$-run with kept slope $p$, entered from the basis $(p,q)$, the middle slopes are $c_i=q+ip$, so with
$\vartheta=\theta(p)$, $\phi=\theta(q)$ and $\psi_i=i\vartheta+\phi$,
\[
Y_i=\bigl(h(q)+ih(p)\bigr)\cot\psi_i-h(p)\cot\vartheta=h(q)\mathfrak f_i+h(p)\mathfrak g_i
\]
in the fundamental system of Lemma~\ref{lem:cotsol}, whose row is $\hat u_i=f(c_i)/f(p)=\sin\psi_i/\sin\vartheta$ with
$1-x_{L_i}=\hat u_{i-1}\hat u_{i+1}/\hat u_i^2$ (Ptolemy). So the interior rows hold, and the formal extensions $Y_0$, $Y_{a+1}$ of the
run's solution are the same expression at $c_0=q$ and $c_{a+1}=q+(a+1)p$.

\emph{Junction rows.} Let the $R$-run following the run have length $b$, kept slope $q'=c_a$ and middle slopes $w_j=p+jq'$
($w_0=p$, $w_1=c_{a+1}$), so $1-x_{R_j}=\hat v_j^{-2}$ with $\hat v_j=f(w_j)/f(q')=\sin\chi_j/\sin\vartheta'$, $\chi_j=j\vartheta'+\vartheta$,
$\vartheta'=\theta(q')$; the next $L$-run has basis $(w_b,q')$ and kept slope $w_b$. Eliminating $Y_{a-1}$ and $Y'_2$ by the
interior recurrence, the two rows of $S$ at the junction read
\[
E_a=(J^{11}-2)Y_a+2Y_{a+1}-J^{1b}Y'_1,\qquad E'_1=J^{bb}Y'_1+2Y'_0-J^{1b}Y_a ,
\]
with $Y_a=H(q')-H(p)$, $Y_{a+1}=H(w_1)-H(p)$, $Y'_1=H(w_{b+1})-H(w_b)$, $Y'_0=H(q')-H(w_b)$. Here $J^{ik}$ denotes the entries of $J^{-1}$. Put $\eta_k=H(w_k)-H(q')=h(p)\mathfrak f_k+h(q')\mathfrak g_k$, $k=0,\dots,b+1$, with $\mathfrak f_k=\cot\chi_k$ and $\mathfrak g_k=k\cot\chi_k-\cot\vartheta'$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cotsol} the sequence $\eta$ solves the recurrence of the $R$-row. So the interior rows of $J\eta$ vanish, and the first and last rows give
\[
J\eta=\tfrac12\eta_0\,e_1+\tfrac12(\eta_{b+1}-\eta_b)\,e_b .
\]
Here $\eta_0=-Y_a$, $\eta_1=Y_{a+1}-Y_a$, $\eta_b=-Y'_0$ and $\eta_{b+1}-\eta_b=Y'_1$. The first component of $\eta=J^{-1}(J\eta)$ reads $Y_{a+1}-Y_a=-\tfrac12J^{11}Y_a+\tfrac12J^{1b}Y'_1$, which is $E_a=0$. The $b$-th component reads $-Y'_0=-\tfrac12J^{1b}Y_a+\tfrac12J^{bb}Y'_1$, which is $E'_1=0$. A singleton $L$-run carries both corrections at
one site, and its row is $E'_1+E_a$ of the two adjacent junctions, because the interior recurrence at $i=1$ is an identity for the
formal extensions. The identities hold wherever $J^{-1}$ exists.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
At the $L$-site $t$, with kept slope $\mathsf k_t$ and middle slope $\mathsf m_t$, set $Y^-_t=1/(h(\mathsf k_t)h(\mathsf m_t))$, and extend $Y^-$ to the $L$-sites of consecutive periods of the word by $t\mapsto\varphi t$. Then $Y^-$
solves the three-term recurrence of $S$ along the unrolled sequence: for every $L$-site $t$, with the indices running on through consecutive periods,
\[
\beta_{t-1}Y^-_{t-1}+d_tY^-_t+\beta_tY^-_{t+1}=0 ,
\]
including at the junction rows, where one $L$-run ends and the next begins. Since $h(\varphi e)=\lambda h(e)$, one has $Y^-_{t+n}=\lambda^{-2}Y^-_t$ with $n=\#L$: $Y^-$ is a Floquet solution of $S$ with multiplier $\lambda^{-2}$. This is the limit $\epsilon\to0$, taken row by row, of Lemma~\ref{lem:floqvec}, applied with the additive angle
$\theta(e)=\epsilon h(e)$, $\epsilon>0$ small. As $\epsilon\to0$ the coordinates $\sin^2(\epsilon h(\mathsf k_t))/\sin^2(\epsilon h(\mathsf m_t))$ tend to $h(\mathsf k_t)^2/h(\mathsf m_t)^2$,
which is $V^*$ (Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}); and with the contracting height $h'$ in place of the lemma's $h$,
$\epsilon\bigl(H(\mathsf m_t)-H(\mathsf k_t)\bigr)\to h'(\mathsf m_t)/h(\mathsf m_t)-h'(\mathsf k_t)/h(\mathsf k_t)$, a constant multiple of $Y^-_t$, because
$h'(\mathsf m_t)h(\mathsf k_t)-h'(\mathsf k_t)h(\mathsf m_t)$ is a constant multiple of $\det(\mathsf k_t,\mathsf m_t)=\det(\mathsf k_t,\mathsf m_t-\mathsf k_t)=1$.
Since $h(\varphi v)=\lambda h(v)$, $Y^-|_L$ is a Floquet solution with multiplier $\lambda^{-2}$. $S$ is symmetric, so the transfer matrix has
determinant $1$, the other multiplier is $\lambda^2$, and $\operatorname{tr} T=\lambda^2+\lambda^{-2}$. Hill's formula $\det S=(-1)^n\prod\beta_i(\operatorname{tr} T-2)$
then gives (A), since
\[
\lambda^2+\lambda^{-2}-2=(\operatorname{tr}\varphi)^2-4=|A_-||A_+| .
\]
Inside $L$-runs the recurrence has fundamental system $1/v_k$, $v_k^2-1$ (Casoratian $3$), and $Y^-\propto1/v_k$ there.

\emph{Reduction of (B).} The $L$-runs give $\prod_L(1-x)=\prod_qv_0v_{a+1}/(v_1v_a)$, since $1-x_k=v_{k-1}v_{k+1}/v_k^2$. Over one period all
intermediate heights cancel between consecutive $R$- and $L$-run factors, leaving
$\bigl[h(p)h(q)/h(p+q)\bigr]\bigl[h(\varphi p+\varphi q)/(h(\varphi p)h(\varphi q))\bigr]=1/\lambda$; the $(-2)$'s of the $\#L-n_R$ couplings inside
$L$-runs and the $n_R$ factors $-\beta_q/2$, one for each $R$-run, combine with $(-1)^{\#L}$ to $2^{\#L}$. So (B) follows from a single identity for each $R$-run.

\begin{lemma}[The identity for one $R$-run, for any frieze row]
\label{lem:perrun}
Let $(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be any solution of the frieze relation $u_j^2-u_{j-1}u_{j+1}=1$ \textup{(}Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}\textup{)}, and
for $b\ge0$ let $D_R=\operatorname{diag}(u_1^2-1,\dots,u_b^2-1)$, $1-x_j=u_j^{-2}$ $(j=1,\dots,b)$, and $\beta_q=-2-\mathsf r^{\mathsf T}(F_b+D_R)^{-1}s$,
with $\mathsf r=2(1,\dots,b)^{\mathsf T}$ and $s=-2\cdot\mathbf1$ the ramp and the constant row of Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}, the coupling of
the $L$-Schur complement across the run. Then
\begin{equation}
G_b(u):=\det(F_b+D_R)\prod_{j=1}^b(1-x_j)\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac{\beta_q}2\bigr)=\frac{u_0\,u_{b+1}}{u_1\,u_b}.
\label{eq:perrun}
\end{equation}
For the affine row $u_j=u+j$ of the expanding
eigenvector the right side is $u(u+b+1)/\bigl((u+1)(u+b)\bigr)$. The identity \eqref{eq:perrun} is also valid for the trigonometric row
$u_j=\sin(j\vartheta+\phi)/\sin\vartheta$ of a general Bethe class \textup{(}Theorem~\ref{thm:friezeall},
Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}\textup{)}, with the same formula in terms of these $u_j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The argument below uses the chain only through $u_1^2-1=u_0u_2$ --- the frieze relation --- and through the shift of the row by one index, so it is
insensitive to which frieze row $(u_j)$ is. Let $B_b(u)=\begin{psmallmatrix}F_b+D&s\\\mathsf r^{\mathsf T}&-2\end{psmallmatrix}$, so $\det B_b=\det(F_b+D)\,\beta_q$ and
$G_b=-\tfrac12\det B_b\prod_ju_j^{-2}$, with $G_0=1$. Eliminate the first $R$-site: its pivot is $\pi=2+u_1^2-1=u_1^2+1$, assumed nonzero (both sides of the resulting identity are polynomial in the $u_j$, so the case $\pi=0$ follows by continuity), and it couples by $2$ to every
other $R$-site, by $-2$ to the border column and by $2$ to the border row. Writing $2\min(i,j)=2+2\min(i-1,j-1)$ and putting $c:=2-4/\pi$ (a scalar
used only in this proof), the Schur complement is
$\begin{psmallmatrix}F_{b-1}+D'+c\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}&-c\mathbf1\\\mathsf r'^{\mathsf T}+c\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}&-c\end{psmallmatrix}$, with $D'$ the
same diagonal in the shifted variable $u+1$ and $\mathsf r'=2(1,\dots,b-1)$. Adding the border column to every $R$-column removes $c\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf
T}$ and the $c\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}$ in the border row, leaving $B_{b-1}(u+1)$ with its last column scaled by $c/2$. Hence
$\det B_b=\pi\tfrac c2\det B_{b-1}'=(u_1^2-1)\det B_{b-1}'=u_0u_2\det B_{b-1}'$, where $B'$ is the same expression for the row shifted by one index, so
$G_b=\tfrac{u_0u_2}{u_1^2}G_{b-1}'$, which telescopes to $\prod_{j=1}^bu_{j-1}u_{j+1}/u_j^2=u_0u_{b+1}/(u_1u_b)$. The step $\pi c/2=\pi-2=u_1^2-1=u_0u_2$
is the frieze relation and is the only place the chain enters.
\end{proof}
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:perrun}
Let $(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be any solution of the frieze relation $u_j^2-u_{j-1}u_{j+1}=1$ \textup{(}Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}\textup{)}, and
for $b\ge0$ let $D_R=\operatorname{diag}(u_1^2-1,\dots,u_b^2-1)$, $1-x_j=u_j^{-2}$ $(j=1,\dots,b)$, and $\beta_q=-2-\mathsf r^{\mathsf T}(F_b+D_R)^{-1}s$,
with $\mathsf r=2(1,\dots,b)^{\mathsf T}$ and $s=-2\cdot\mathbf1$ the ramp and the constant row of Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}, the coupling of
the $L$-Schur complement across the run. Then
\begin{equation}
G_b(u):=\det(F_b+D_R)\prod_{j=1}^b(1-x_j)\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac{\beta_q}2\bigr)=\frac{u_0\,u_{b+1}}{u_1\,u_b}.
\label{eq:perrun}
\end{equation}
For the affine row $u_j=u+j$ of the expanding
eigenvector the right side is $u(u+b+1)/\bigl((u+1)(u+b)\bigr)$. The identity \eqref{eq:perrun} is also valid for the trigonometric row
$u_j=\sin(j\vartheta+\phi)/\sin\vartheta$ of a general Bethe class \textup{(}Theorem~\ref{thm:friezeall},
Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}\textup{)}, with the same formula in terms of these $u_j$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
The argument below uses the chain only through $u_1^2-1=u_0u_2$ --- the frieze relation --- and through the shift of the row by one index, so it is
insensitive to which frieze row $(u_j)$ is. Let $B_b(u)=\begin{psmallmatrix}F_b+D&s\\\mathsf r^{\mathsf T}&-2\end{psmallmatrix}$, so $\det B_b=\det(F_b+D)\,\beta_q$ and
$G_b=-\tfrac12\det B_b\prod_ju_j^{-2}$, with $G_0=1$. Eliminate the first $R$-site: its pivot is $\pi=2+u_1^2-1=u_1^2+1$, assumed nonzero (both sides of the resulting identity are polynomial in the $u_j$, so the case $\pi=0$ follows by continuity), and it couples by $2$ to every
other $R$-site, by $-2$ to the border column and by $2$ to the border row. Writing $2\min(i,j)=2+2\min(i-1,j-1)$ and putting $c:=2-4/\pi$ (a scalar
used only in this proof), the Schur complement is
$\begin{psmallmatrix}F_{b-1}+D'+c\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}&-c\mathbf1\\\mathsf r'^{\mathsf T}+c\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}&-c\end{psmallmatrix}$, with $D'$ the
same diagonal in the shifted variable $u+1$ and $\mathsf r'=2(1,\dots,b-1)$. Adding the border column to every $R$-column removes $c\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf
T}$ and the $c\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}$ in the border row, leaving $B_{b-1}(u+1)$ with its last column scaled by $c/2$. Hence
$\det B_b=\pi\tfrac c2\det B_{b-1}'=(u_1^2-1)\det B_{b-1}'=u_0u_2\det B_{b-1}'$, where $B'$ is the same expression for the row shifted by one index, so
$G_b=\tfrac{u_0u_2}{u_1^2}G_{b-1}'$, which telescopes to $\prod_{j=1}^bu_{j-1}u_{j+1}/u_j^2=u_0u_{b+1}/(u_1u_b)$. The step $\pi c/2=\pi-2=u_1^2-1=u_0u_2$
is the frieze relation and is the only place the chain enters.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
\emph{Non-degeneracy.} Every kept, dying and newborn slope of the word is the middle slope of another tetrahedron: the newborn slope
of step $t$ is the middle of step $t+1$, and a basis vector at step $t$ is the middle slope of the last flip that replaced that column
(the word contains both letters, so every column is replaced; when that flip lies in the previous period of the developed word, $f\ne0$ there follows from the periodicity (b) in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}). So $f(\mathsf m_t)\ne0$ for all $t$ gives $f\ne0$ on all four slopes of every
tetrahedron, and by Ptolemy $x_t\notin\{0,1,\infty\}$: the class has all coordinates finite and nonzero, the hypothesis of
Lemma~\ref{lem:floqvec}, and $D_R$ is invertible. The second hypothesis is what defines $S$ (it is automatic for $b=1$, where
$J=(2-x_R)/2x_R$ and $x_R<1$, since $1-x_R$ is a ratio of squares of real numbers).

\emph{Periodicity.} Let $h$ be the height functional of Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}, $h(\varphi e)=\lambda h(e)$, and $h'$ the
contracting one. Developing the word once more sends every slope $e$ to $\varphi e$, and
$\langle v,\varphi e\rangle=\langle\varphi^{-1}v,e\rangle\equiv\pm\langle v,e\rangle\pmod N$ for $v\in\mathcal K_\mp$, so, $\cot$ being
$\pi$-periodic, $H(\varphi e)=\pm\lambda H(e)$. Hence the vectors $Y^\pm$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:floqvec} built from $h$ and $h'$ satisfy
$Y^\pm_{t+r}=\pm\lambda^{\pm1}Y^\pm_t$: they are Floquet solutions of $S$ with multipliers $\pm\lambda$ and $\pm\lambda^{-1}$. They are
not both zero: $Y^+\equiv Y^-\equiv0$ would force, $h,h'$ being a basis of the dual, $\cot(\pi\langle v,\mathsf m_t\rangle/N)\,\mathsf m_t=
\cot(\pi\langle v,\mathsf k_t\rangle/N)\,\mathsf k_t$ for every $L$-site, i.e.\ both cotangents zero, i.e.\ $\langle v,\mathsf m_t\rangle\equiv
\langle v,\mathsf k_t\rangle\equiv N/2$, and then $\langle v,\mathsf m_t-\mathsf k_t\rangle\equiv0$ for the dying slope $\mathsf m_t-\mathsf k_t$, which is
excluded. A nonzero Floquet solution with multiplier $\Lambda$ gives $\operatorname{tr} T_\alpha=\Lambda+\Lambda^{-1}$ ($\det T_\alpha=1$), so
\[
\Delta_\alpha=\operatorname{tr} T_\alpha-2=\pm(\lambda+\lambda^{-1})-2=\pm\operatorname{tr}\varphi-2=\pm|\det(\varphi\mp1)|=\pm|A_\mp| .
\]
Hill's formula $\det S=(-1)^{\#L}\prod\beta_i\,\Delta_\alpha$ holds with the couplings of \eqref{eq:corners}, including the folded cases
$\#L=1,2$. For $\#L=1$, $\det S=d+2\beta=-\beta(\operatorname{tr} T-2)$, and for $\#L=2$, $\det S=d_1d_2-(\beta_1+\beta_2)^2=\beta_1\beta_2(\operatorname{tr} T-2)$; the couplings are nonzero, since $G_b\ne0$ and $\det(F+D_R)\ne0$ by hypothesis, so the transfer
matrix $T_\alpha$ is defined.

\emph{$P_\alpha$.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:perrun} on the $R$-row $\hat v_j$ and the $L$-run product $\prod_L(1-x)=\hat u_0\hat u_{a+1}/(\hat
u_1\hat u_a)$, the $(-2)$'s and $\beta_q$'s combining to $2^{\#L}$ exactly as in the reduction of (B),
\[
P_\alpha=2^{\#L}\prod_{L\text{-runs}}\frac{f(q)\,f(c_{a+1})}{f(c_1)\,f(c_a)}\prod_{R\text{-runs}}\frac{f(p)\,f(g_{b+1})}{f(g_1)\,f(g_b)} .
\]
Since $c_{a+1}=g_1$, $c_a=q'$ is the $q$ of the next $L$-run (an $R$-run keeps it), $g_b$ is the $p$ of the next $L$-run and $g_{b+1}$
its $c_1$, the product telescopes around the word to
\[
\frac{f(p_0)}{f(\varphi p_0)}\cdot\frac{f(q_0)}{f(\varphi q_0)}\cdot\frac{f(\varphi c_1)}{f(c_1)},\qquad c_1=p_0+q_0 ,
\]
for the basis $(p_0,q_0)$ at the start of the first $L$-run. By periodicity (b) of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords},
$f(\varphi e)=\pm(-1)^{\langle w,e\rangle}f(e)$, and $\langle w,p_0\rangle+\langle w,q_0\rangle+\langle w,p_0+q_0\rangle$ is even, so
the product is $\pm1$: $P_\alpha=\pm2^{\#L}$ with the sector sign.

\emph{$W_c^2$.} By \eqref{eq:wcmono} at $\epsilon=0$ and $1-x_{L_i}=\hat u_{i-1}\hat u_{i+1}/\hat u_i^2$, the $L$-run product
$\prod_{i=1}^a(1-x_{L_i})^{-2i}$ telescopes to $\hat u_a^{2(a+1)}/(\hat u_0^2\hat u_{a+1}^{2a})=f(c_a)^{2a+2}/\bigl(f(q)^2f(c_{a+1})^{2a}\bigr)$,
and the following $R$-run contributes $(1-x_{R_1})^{-a}=f(g_1)^{2a}/f(q')^{2a}$ with $g_1=c_{a+1}$, $q'=c_a$; the pair leaves
$f(c_a)^2/f(q)^2=f(q')^2/f(q)^2$, the ratio of the squares of the second basis vector at the end and at the start of the $L$-run. Around
the word this telescopes to $f(\varphi q_0)^2/f(q_0)^2=1$.

\emph{$\mathcal H_\alpha$.} $\mathcal H_\alpha=W_c^2\,\Delta_\alpha P_\alpha=1\cdot(\pm|A_\mp|)(\pm2^{\#L})=2^{\#L}|A_\mp|$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
\emph{Rows.} Fix an $L$-run of length $a\ge2$, entered from the basis $(p,q)$, with middle slopes $c_i=q+ip$, and put
$u_i=\pm x_{L_i}^{-1/2}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:friezeall} and Remark~\ref{rem:friezesign} the signs can be chosen so that
$u_i^2-u_{i-1}u_{i+1}=1$ at every interior site (a flip of $u_c$ changes the sign of the relation at $c\pm1$ and at no other site: go through the interior sites $i=2,3,\dots$ in turn and, if the relation at $i$ has the wrong
sign, flip $u_{i+1}$, which corrects the relation at $i$ and affects only the relation at $i+2$, still to come). The row then satisfies $u_{i+1}=\tau u_i-u_{i-1}$ with $\tau$ constant, extended to $u_0$ and
$u_{a+1}$ by the recurrence. To see that $\tau$ is constant, let $i$ and $i+1$ be two consecutive interior sites. Subtracting the relations
$u_i^2-u_{i-1}u_{i+1}=1$ and $u_{i+1}^2-u_iu_{i+2}=1$ gives
\[
u_i^2+u_iu_{i+2}=u_{i+1}^2+u_{i-1}u_{i+1},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad u_i(u_i+u_{i+2})=u_{i+1}(u_{i+1}+u_{i-1}),
\]
and dividing by $u_iu_{i+1}\ne0$ (non-degeneracy) gives $(u_i+u_{i+2})/u_{i+1}=(u_{i-1}+u_{i+1})/u_i$. So the quantity $\tau=(u_{i-1}+u_{i+1})/u_i$ takes the same value at
every interior site. For $a=3$ there is a single interior site and $\tau$ is its value; for $a=2$, where there is no interior site, $\tau$ is defined by $\tau u_1u_2=u_1^2+u_2^2-1$ so that
the extended row satisfies the relation. If $\tau\ne\pm2$, the solutions $c\mu^{\pm i}$ of the recurrence, $\mu+\mu^{-1}=\tau$, have $u_i^2-u_{i-1}u_{i+1}=0$ and are excluded by the frieze relation, and Remark~\ref{rem:friezedef}(ii) gives $\vartheta,\phi\in\mathbb{C}$, $\sin\vartheta\ne0$, and a constant $A$ (the \emph{amplitude}, the overall multiplier of the sine row) with
$u_i=A\sin(i\vartheta+\phi)/\sin\vartheta$ for $i=0,\dots,a+1$. Substituting in $u_i^2-u_{i-1}u_{i+1}=1$ and using
$\sin^2\psi-\sin(\psi-\vartheta)\sin(\psi+\vartheta)=\sin^2\vartheta$ gives $A^2=1$, and replacing $\phi$ by $\phi+\pi$ if necessary, $A=1$. We set $F(p)=\sin\vartheta$, $F(c_i)=\sin(i\vartheta+\phi)$: a function on
the run's slopes with $x_{L_i}=F(p)^2/F(c_i)^2$. If $\tau=\pm2$ the row is affine, $u_i=\pm(u_0+i)$ at $\tau=2$ and $u_i=\pm(-1)^i(u_0+i)$ at $\tau=-2$; only $u_i^2$ enters below, so the second case reduces to the first, and we set $F(p)=1$,
$F(c_i)=u_0+i$ instead, a linear function. The same with $q'=c_a$ and $g_j=p+jq'$ for the following $R$-run, $\hat v_j=\pm(1-x_{R_j})^{-1/2}$,
$F(q')=\sin\vartheta'$, $F(g_j)=\sin(j\vartheta'+\phi')$. Non-degeneracy gives $F\ne0$ on every slope of every run, including the
extensions $c_0,c_{a+1}$ and $g_0,g_{b+1}$, since $1-x_{L_1}=u_0u_2/u_1^2$, $1-x_{L_a}=u_{a-1}u_{a+1}/u_a^2$ and
$x_{R_1},x_{R_b}$ likewise. Each run's $F$ is defined up to a scalar, which is immaterial below.

\emph{The equations at the run ends.} With the rows in place, the interior $L$-site equations are identities (Proposition~\ref{prop:runreduce}); the $R$-site equations are the $(R_k)$ below, and
summation by parts along the $R$-row gives $\prod_ix_{R_i}^{2\min(i,k)}=(\hat v_0/\hat v_k)^2(\hat v_{b+1}/\hat v_b)^{2k}$,
$\prod_jx_{R_j}^{2j}=(\hat v_{b+1}/\hat v_b)^{2b}(\hat v_0/\hat v_b)^2$ and $\prod_jx_{R_j}=\hat v_0\hat v_{b+1}/\hat v_1\hat v_b$.
Reading the exponents off Theorem~\ref{thm:Kformula}, the equations at the sites $R_1,\dots,R_b$ of the run, at the last $L$ before
it and at the first $L$ after it (whose run has basis $(g_b,q')$ and row $u'_i$) are
\begin{align*}
(R_k)\quad&1=u_a^2\hat v_0^2\bigl[u'^{-2}_1(\hat v_{b+1}/\hat v_b)^2\bigr]^k,\qquad k=1,\dots,b,\\
(L_a)\quad&(u_{a-1}u_{a+1})^2=u_{a-1}^2\,u'^2_1\,(\hat v_1\hat v_b/\hat v_0\hat v_{b+1})^2,\\
(L'_1)\quad&(u'_0u'_2)^2=u'^{-2b}_1u'^2_2\,u_a^2\,(\hat v_{b+1}/\hat v_b)^{2b}(\hat v_0/\hat v_b)^2 .
\end{align*}
Since $b\ge2$, $(R_1)$ and $(R_2)$ give $u_a^2\hat v_0^2=1$ and $u'^2_1=(\hat v_{b+1}/\hat v_b)^2$, and then
$(L_a)$ and $(L'_1)$ reduce to $u_{a+1}^2=u'^2_1(\hat v_1\hat v_b/\hat v_0\hat v_{b+1})^2$ and $u'^2_0=u_a^2\hat v_0^2/\hat v_b^2$.
Now the two runs share the three slopes $p=g_0$, $q'=c_a$ and $c_{a+1}=g_1$, and the next $L$-run shares $q'$, $g_b$ and
$g_{b+1}$ with the $R$-run; writing $\rho_e=F_L(e)/F_R(e)$ and $\varsigma_e=F_R(e)/F_{L'}(e)$ for the ratios on the shared slopes,
$u_a\hat v_0=\rho_{q'}/\rho_p$, $u_{a+1}=(\rho_{c_{a+1}}/\rho_p)\hat v_1/\hat v_0$, $u'_1=(\varsigma_{g_b}/\varsigma_{g_{b+1}})\hat v_{b+1}/\hat v_b$
and $u'_0=(\varsigma_{g_b}/\varsigma_{q'})/\hat v_b$, so the four equations say exactly
\[
\rho_p^2=\rho_{q'}^2=\rho_{c_{a+1}}^2,\qquad \varsigma_{q'}^2=\varsigma_{g_b}^2=\varsigma_{g_{b+1}}^2 :
\]
\emph{the rows of adjacent runs agree, up to a common factor and up to the sign of each entry, on the three slopes they share.}
Conversely these conditions imply $(R_k)$ for all $k$, $(L_a)$ and $(L'_1)$. So, for a word with no singleton run, the Bethe equations
\eqref{eq:bethex} are equivalent to the junction conditions at every junction.

\emph{Gluing.} The three shared slopes form a Farey triangle $(e_1,e_2,e_1+e_2)$ --- $(p,q',p+q')$ at an $L\to R$ junction, $(g_b,q',g_b+q')$ at an $R\to L$ junction --- and on it a sine row has values
$(\sin A,\sin B,\sin(A+B))$ with $(A,B)$ the angles of $(e_1,e_2)$: $(\vartheta,a\vartheta+\phi)$ for the $L$-run, $(\phi',\vartheta')$ for the
$R$-run. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sine}, the junction condition forces $(\phi',\vartheta')\equiv\pm(\vartheta,a\vartheta+\phi)\pmod\pi$ with a common sign, which is
absorbed into the $R$-run's parametrisation. Inductively there is a single additive $\Theta:\mathbb{Z}^2\to\mathbb{C}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$ with
$F(e)^2=\sin^2\Theta(e)$ on every slope of the developed word, hence $x_t=\sin^2\Theta(\mathsf k_t)/\sin^2\Theta(\mathsf m_t)$ at $L$-steps and
$1-$that at $R$-steps. Lemma~\ref{lem:sine} also excludes a sine row adjacent to an affine one, so either all runs are affine or none is. In the
affine case $F$ is a linear function $h$ on every run, consistency on the shared basis makes it one linear function on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ (the signs of the three shared entries agree because $F\ne0$ on them), and
the wrap-around junction gives $h\circ\varphi=ch$ for a scalar $c$; so $h$ is an eigenfunctional of $\varphi$, and $x$ is $V^*$ or
$\sigma V^*$ (Theorem~\ref{prop:propagated}).

\emph{Closure.} In the sine case the wrap-around junction compares the last run's row on the slopes $\varphi p_0,\varphi q_0$ with the
first run's row on $p_0,q_0$: Lemma~\ref{lem:sine}, applied to the first run's Farey triangle and to its image under $\varphi$, on which $x$ takes the same values by periodicity, gives $\Theta\circ\varphi\equiv\pm\Theta\pmod\pi$ on a basis, hence on $\mathbb{Z}^2$. Lift $\Theta$ to an
additive $\tilde\Theta:\mathbb{Z}^2\to\mathbb{C}$: choose lifts of $\Theta(e_1)$ and $\Theta(e_2)$ to $\mathbb{C}$ and extend linearly, which agrees with
$\Theta$ modulo $\pi$ because both are additive on the free group $\mathbb{Z}^2$. Then $\tilde\Theta\circ(\varphi\mp1)$ takes values in $\pi\mathbb{Z}$, so $\tilde\Theta\circ(\varphi\mp1)=\pi m$
for some $m\in\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{Z})$ and $\tilde\Theta=\pi\,m\circ(\varphi\mp1)^{-1}=\pi\langle v,\cdot\rangle/N$ with
$v\in\mathbb{Z}^2$, $N=|\det(\varphi\mp1)|=|A_\mp|$: the angles are rational multiples of $\pi$, with denominator $N$. Periodicity now reads
$\langle v,(\varphi\mp1)e\rangle\equiv0\pmod N$ for all $e$, i.e.\ $v\in\mathcal K_\mp$ (proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords}), and
$v\not\equiv0$ since $F\ne0$. So $x$ is the class of Theorem~\ref{thm:allwords} at $v$. Finally $x$ determines each run's $(\vartheta_\rho,\phi_\rho)$
modulo $\pi$ up to a common sign (a row of length $\ge2$ determines $\cos\vartheta$ up to sign, the sign being the alternating flip $(\vartheta,\phi)\mapsto(-\vartheta,-\phi)$ modulo $\pi$; and the sign choices compatible with the frieze
relation are the shifts by $\pi$), the junctions correlate the signs, so $\Theta$ is determined up to sign and $v$ up to sign modulo $N$. No $x$ arises from both sectors, since $\Theta\circ\varphi\equiv\Theta$ and $\Theta\circ\varphi\equiv-\Theta$ together give $2\Theta\equiv0$, and then $f$ vanishes somewhere. No kernel-vector class is $V^*$ or $\sigma V^*$, since a sine row is never affine (Lemma~\ref{lem:sine}).

\emph{Where the hypothesis is used.} That no run is a singleton enters at three points. In \emph{Rows}, a run of length $\ge2$ carries at
least two coordinates, which fix $\tau$ and the amplitude; a singleton run carries one coordinate for a row with two parameters. At
\emph{the run ends}, $b\ge2$ is needed to use both $(R_1)$ and $(R_2)$. On an $L$-run of length $\ge2$ the site $L_a$ serves only the
junction after the run and $L'_1$ only the junction before the next one; at a singleton $L$-run one site would serve both. In
\emph{Closure}, a row of length $\ge2$ determines $\cos\vartheta_\rho$ up to the sign just described. Remark~\ref{rem:singleton}
describes what changes at a singleton run.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:steps}
The two identities \eqref{eq:steps} hold for all real $\alpha,\beta$ at which their arguments are defined.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
(Algebraically, the first is Abel's five-term identity \cite{Zagier07} at $(x,y)=(z,\bar z)$: $z\bar z=s$ and
$z(1-\bar z)/(1-z\bar z)=z(\alpha,\alpha+\beta)$; the second is the same identity applied to $1-z$.) Write $\psi=\alpha+\beta$,
$\Theta_x=\log|\sin x|$, $\omega(X,Y)=X\,dY-Y\,dX$ (a $1$-form on the $(\alpha,\beta)$-plane, with $dX$, $dY$ the differentials of the functions $X$, $Y$), and
\[
\eta(\alpha,\beta)=\omega(\Theta_\alpha,\Theta_\beta)+\omega(\Theta_\beta,\Theta_\psi)+\omega(\Theta_\psi,\Theta_\alpha).
\]
Consider the first identity on a connected component $C$ of the complement of the lines $\alpha,\beta,\psi,2\alpha+\beta\in\pi\mathbb{Z}$, on which all
terms are real-analytic. For real $s\notin\{0,1\}$, $d\operatorname{Re}R(s)=-\tfrac12\omega(\log|1-s|,\log|s|)$; with $\log|s|=2(\Theta_\alpha-\Theta_\psi)$ and
$\log|1-s|=\Theta_\beta+\Theta_{2\alpha+\beta}-2\Theta_\psi$ (Ptolemy) this expands to $\eta(\alpha,\beta)-\eta(\alpha,\psi)$. On $C$, $z$ and $1-z$ are not
real, so $\arg z=-\beta+\pi k_0$ and $\arg(1-z)=\alpha+\pi k_1$ with $k_0,k_1\in\mathbb{Z}$ constant, and
$d\operatorname{Re}R(z)=\tfrac12\omega(\log|z|,\log|1-z|)-\tfrac12\omega(\arg z,\arg(1-z))$; since $\log|z|=\Theta_\alpha-\Theta_\psi$ and $\log|1-z|=\Theta_\beta-\Theta_\psi$,
this gives $d\mathcal G=\eta(\alpha,\beta)-\omega(\alpha,\beta)$. As $\omega(\alpha,\psi)=\omega(\alpha,\beta)$, the left side of the first identity has
zero differential on $C$, so it is constant there. Each component is a bounded polygon with edges in at least three of the four directions,
so it has an edge on a line $\alpha=m\pi$ or $\beta=m\pi$. On approaching an interior point of an edge $\alpha=m\pi$, $s\to0$, $z\to0$,
$z(\alpha,\psi)\to0$, $\arg(1-z)\to0$, and the constant becomes $-m\pi\bigl(\arg z-\arg z(\alpha,\psi)\bigr)=-m\pi^2(k_0+m-k_0')\in\pi^2\mathbb{Z}$.
On approaching an edge $\beta=m\pi$, $s\to1$, $z\to1$, and $z':=z(\alpha,\alpha+m\pi)=e^{-i\alpha}/2\cos\alpha$ satisfies $1-z'=\overline{z'}$, so
$2\operatorname{Re}R(z')=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(R(z')+R(1-z')\bigr)=\pi^2/6$ and $\mathcal G(\alpha,\alpha+m\pi)=\pi^2/6-m\pi\arg z'$; the constant becomes
$\pi^2/6-\pi^2/3-m\pi(\alpha+\pi k_1)+\pi^2/6+m\pi(\alpha-\pi\epsilon)\in\pi^2\mathbb{Z}$, where $\arg z'=-\alpha+\pi\epsilon$ at the edge point. The second identity is proved
in the same way on the complement of $\alpha,\beta,\psi,\alpha+2\beta\in\pi\mathbb{Z}$: at $\alpha=m\pi$ one has $s\to1$, $z\to0$ and
$z(\psi,\beta)\to e^{-i\beta}/2\cos\beta$, and at $\beta=m\pi$ one has $s\to0$ and $z,z(\psi,\beta)\to1$. Writing $\arg z=-\beta+\pi k_0$ and $\arg(1-z)=\alpha+\pi k_1$ on the component,
$\arg\bigl(e^{-i\beta}/2\cos\beta\bigr)=-\beta+\pi\epsilon'$ at the edge point and $\arg\bigl(1-z(\psi,\beta)\bigr)=\psi+\pi k_1''$ on the component, the
constant is $m\pi^2(\epsilon'-k_0)$ at an edge $\alpha=m\pi$ and $m\pi^2(m+k_1''-k_1)$ at an edge $\beta=m\pi$; both lie in $\pi^2\mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:telescope}
Let $\gcd(k,m)=1$, $\vartheta=k\pi/m$, $g=j\vartheta$, and $\varsigma_i=\sin(\psi+ig)$ for an arbitrary $\psi\in\mathbb{C}$. Then, for every $\psi$,
\[
\textup{(T1)}\ \varsigma_{i+m}=(-1)^{jk}\varsigma_i,\qquad
\textup{(T5)}\ 1-\frac1{w_l}=\frac{\sin^2g}{\varsigma_l^2},\qquad w_i:=\frac{\varsigma_i^2}{\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_{i+1}},
\]
and
\[
\textup{(T2)}\ \prod_{i=1}^mw_i=1,\qquad
\textup{(T3)}\ \prod_{i=1}^mw_i^{2i}=\Bigl(\frac{\varsigma_0}{\varsigma_1}\Bigr)^{2m},\qquad
\textup{(T4)}\ \prod_{i=1}^mw_i^{2\min(i,l)}=\frac{\varsigma_l^2}{\varsigma_0^2}\Bigl(\frac{\varsigma_0}{\varsigma_1}\Bigr)^{2l}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
(T1) is $mg=jk\pi$; (T5) is $\sin^2x-\sin(x-g)\sin(x+g)=\sin^2g$ at $x=\psi+lg$. For the products take logarithms: with $L_i=\log\varsigma_i$ and a weight
$f$, $\sum_{i=1}^mf_i(2L_i-L_{i-1}-L_{i+1})$ has all interior coefficients equal to the second difference $2f_l-f_{l+1}-f_{l-1}$, leaving
\[
-f_1L_0+(2f_1-f_2)L_1+(2f_m-f_{m-1})L_m-f_mL_{m+1}+\sum_{l=2}^{m-1}(2f_l-f_{l+1}-f_{l-1})L_l .
\]
For $f\equiv1$ this is $-L_0+L_1+L_m-L_{m+1}$, and (T1) gives $L_m-L_0=L_{m+1}-L_1$, whence (T2). For $f_i=2i$ the second differences vanish and the
boundary terms are $-2L_0+(2m+2)L_m-2mL_{m+1}$, which by (T1) is $2m(L_0-L_1)$ plus an even multiple of $\log(-1)$; that is (T3). For $f_i=2\min(i,l)$ the
second difference is $2\delta_{il}$ and the boundary terms give $2L_l-2L_0+2l(L_0-L_1)$, which is (T4).
<!-- end proof-55 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
\label{prop:reduction}
Let $\gcd(k,m)=1$, and with the chains $\rho_i=\sin((i-j)\vartheta+\alpha)$, $\varsigma_i=\sin((ij-1)\vartheta+\beta)$,
$C_i=\rho_i^2/\sin^2\vartheta$ and $w_i=\varsigma_i^2/(\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_{i+1})$ of Section~\ref{sec:leading}, with arbitrary phases $\alpha,\beta$, set
\[
\Lambda=C_1\Bigl(\frac{\varsigma_0}{\varsigma_1}\Bigr)^2,\qquad \Xi=\frac{\sin^2(j\vartheta)}{\varsigma_0^2\,C_m}.
\]
Then, for all $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{C}^2$ at which all the coordinates $C_i$ and $w_i$ of the chains are finite and nonzero, the interior $L$-equations and $(B_2)$ hold, $(B_1)=\Lambda^m$,
and $(R_l)=\Xi\Lambda^l$ for $1\le l\le m$, where each equation is written as its left side. So the shifted chains solve the deformed Bethe system
\emph{exactly} if and only if
\[
\textup{(III)}\ \ \Lambda=1+\epsilon,\qquad\qquad \textup{(IV)}\ \ \Xi=1 .
\]
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-56: body_md -->
The $L$-chain satisfies $C_i-1=\rho_{i-1}\rho_{i+1}/\sin^2\vartheta$, hence $(C_i-1)^2=C_{i-1}C_{i+1}$, and $\rho_{i+m}=(-1)^k\rho_i$ gives $C_0=C_m$,
$C_{m+1}=C_1$. In $(B_2)$, (T2) kills the $w$-product and $(C_m-1)^2=C_{m-1}C_{m+1}$ leaves $C_{m+1}/C_1=1$. In $(B_1)$, $(C_1-1)^2=C_0C_2$ cancels
$C_2$ and (T3) supplies $(\varsigma_0/\varsigma_1)^{2m}$, leaving $(C_0/C_m)[C_1(\varsigma_0/\varsigma_1)^2]^m=\Lambda^m$. In $(R_l)$, (T5) and (T4) give
$\frac{\sin^2(j\vartheta)}{\varsigma_l^2}\cdot\frac{\varsigma_l^2}{\varsigma_0^2}(\frac{\varsigma_0}{\varsigma_1})^{2l}C_1^l/C_m=\Xi\Lambda^l$. Comparing $(R_l)$ and
$(R_{l+1})$ gives $\Lambda=1+\epsilon$, then $(R_1)$ gives $\Xi=1$, and $(B_1)$ follows. Every identity used holds for arbitrary complex phases, so nothing here is an approximation.
<!-- end proof-56 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
\label{prop:jac4}
In logarithmic form the Jacobian of \textup{(III)}, \textup{(IV)} in $(\alpha,\beta)$ at the base point is
\[
\frac{\partial(\log\Lambda,\log\Xi)}{\partial(\alpha,\beta)}=\begin{pmatrix}-2c&-2c-2A\\ 2B&2A\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det=-4,
\]
with $c=\cot((j-1)\vartheta)$, \emph{independently of $m$, $k$ and $j$}. Hence, within the family of shifted chains of Section~\ref{sec:leading}, the two flat directions of the leading order, the chain shifts $(\alpha,\beta)$ left free by Proposition~\ref{prop:shifts}, are fixed uniquely at next
order at every placement where the logarithms are defined, which is every one except $j\equiv1$ \textup{(}$C_1=0$\textup{)} and $j\equiv0$
\textup{(}$\sin(j\vartheta)=0$\textup{)}.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-57: body_md -->
Differentiating $\log\Lambda=2\log\rho_1+2\log\varsigma_0-2\log\varsigma_1-2\log\sin\vartheta$ and $\log\Xi=2\log\sin(j\vartheta)-2\log\varsigma_0-\log C_m$ at
$\alpha=\beta=0$ gives the matrix, using $\rho_1=\sin((1-j)\vartheta)$, $\varsigma_0=\sin(-\vartheta)$, $\varsigma_1=\sin((j-1)\vartheta)$ and
$\rho_m=\pm\sin(j\vartheta)$. Then $\det=4[c(B-A)+AB]$, and $c(B-A)=-(AB+1)$, so $\det=-4$.
<!-- end proof-57 -->
<!-- proof-58: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction} it suffices to solve (III) and (IV). The only values of the chains $\rho_i$, $\varsigma_i$ that can vanish are $\rho_{j}=\sin\alpha$ and
$\varsigma_p=\pm\sin\beta$, so the coordinates are finite and nonzero once $\alpha,\beta\ne0$.

\textup{(i)} At $\alpha=\beta=\epsilon=0$ both conditions hold, $\log\Lambda$ and $\log\Xi$ are analytic in $(\alpha,\beta)$, and their Jacobian is
$-4$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:jac4}). The implicit function theorem gives unique analytic $\alpha(\epsilon),\beta(\epsilon)$ vanishing at $0$, with the
first-order terms \eqref{eq:shifts}; these are nonzero, since $\vartheta,j\vartheta\notin\tfrac\pi2\mathbb{Z}$ for odd $m$. The functions $\log\Lambda$ and $\log\Xi$ have real Taylor coefficients in $(\alpha,\beta,\epsilon)$, so $\overline{\alpha(\bar\epsilon)},\overline{\beta(\bar\epsilon)}$ solve the same equations; by uniqueness they are $\alpha(\epsilon),\beta(\epsilon)$, which are therefore real for real $\epsilon$. Take $\epsilon_0$ below the radius given by the implicit function theorem and so small that $\alpha,\beta\ne0$ for $0<|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0$.

\textup{(ii)} At $j=1$ the chains are $\rho_i=\sin((i-1)\vartheta+\alpha)$ and $\varsigma_i=\sin((i-1)\vartheta+\beta)$, and since $m\vartheta\in\pi\mathbb{Z}$,
\[
\Lambda=\frac{\sin^2\alpha\,\sin^2(\beta-\vartheta)}{\sin^2\vartheta\,\sin^2\beta},\qquad
\Xi=\frac{\sin^4\vartheta}{\sin^2(\alpha-\vartheta)\,\sin^2(\beta-\vartheta)} .
\]
Put $\beta=t\alpha$. Then $\Lambda$ is analytic near $(\alpha,t)=(0,-1)$ with $\Lambda(0,t)=t^{-2}$, and, as $\Xi(0,t)=1$, so is
$G:=(\Xi-1)/\alpha$, with $G(0,t)=2(1+t)\cot\vartheta$. At $(0,-1)$, $\Lambda=1$, $G=0$, and
\[
\frac{\partial(\Lambda,G)}{\partial(\alpha,t)}=\begin{pmatrix}2\cot\vartheta&2\\ 2/\sin^2\vartheta&2\cot\vartheta\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det=4\bigl(\cot^2\vartheta-\sin^{-2}\vartheta\bigr)=-4 .
\]
The implicit function theorem gives analytic $\alpha(\epsilon)$, $t(\epsilon)$ with $\Lambda=1+\epsilon$, $G=0$, $\alpha(0)=0$, $t(0)=-1$; they are real for real $\epsilon$ by the same conjugation argument as in (i). Linearising,
$\alpha=-\tfrac\epsilon2\cot\vartheta+O(\epsilon^2)$ and $t=-1+\epsilon/(2\sin^2\vartheta)+O(\epsilon^2)$, so $\alpha+\beta=\alpha(1+t)$ is as stated. For
small $\epsilon\ne0$, $\alpha\ne0$, so $G=0$ is $\Xi=1$, and $\beta=t\alpha\ne0$. No other solution with $\alpha,\beta\to0$ exists on the family. Along a sequence of such solutions with $\epsilon\to0$, every limit point $t_0$ of $t=\beta/\alpha$ in $\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ is $-1$: it cannot be $0$ or $\infty$, nor $t_0\ne\pm1$, since $\Lambda(0,t)=t^{-2}$ while $\Lambda\to1$; and
it cannot be $+1$, since $G(0,1)=4\cot\vartheta\ne0$. So $t\to-1$, and the uniqueness in the implicit function theorem identifies the solution.
<!-- end proof-58 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:arc}
Fix odd $m\ge5$ and $j,k\in(\mathbb{Z}/m)^\times$, represented by integers (the identities hold for every choice of representatives); put $\vartheta=k\pi/m$, $t=j\vartheta$, $s=\sin t$, and $\varsigma_i=\sin(it-\vartheta)$ for $i\in\mathbb{Z}$.  Let $p\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ satisfy $pj\equiv1\pmod m$, so $\varsigma_p=0$ (the triple of the
placement is centred at $R_p$), and let the \emph{arc} be the $n=m-3$ consecutive sites $i=p+2,\dots,p+m-2$, the $R$-sites with finite nonzero limits.
Two tridiagonal $n\times n$ matrices on the arc are considered: with $d_i=\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_{i+1}/s^2$, the \emph{$d$-form} $\mathrm{arc}_d$, with
diagonal entries $-(2+2d_i)$ and off-diagonal entries $d_{i\mp1}$, which at $j=1$ (that is, $p=1$) arises from the $R$-block of $\hat J_0$ in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:corank} at $j=1$, and is used only there; and the \emph{$\varsigma$-form}
$\mathrm{arc}_\varsigma$, with diagonal $-2\varsigma_i$ and off-diagonals $\varsigma_{i\mp2}$, obtained from it by rescaling the rows. Then
\[
\det(\mathrm{arc}_d)=\frac{m^3}{2^{2m}\sin^{2m}(j\vartheta)},\qquad
\det(\mathrm{arc}_\varsigma)=\varepsilon\,2^{m-3}\prod_{i\in\mathrm{arc}}\varsigma_i^2,\quad \varepsilon=(-1)^{(1+jk)(m+1)/2}.
\]
In particular neither continuant vanishes, for any $m$ and any class.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-59: body_md -->
Let $L[\psi]_i=\varsigma_{i-2}\psi_{i-1}-2\varsigma_i\psi_i+\varsigma_{i+2}\psi_{i+1}$, and write $\gamma_i=\cos(it-\vartheta)$,
$\Pi_i=\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_i\varsigma_{i+1}$. Here the index $i$ is an integer, not a residue modulo $m$: $\varsigma_i$ is defined for every $i\in\mathbb{Z}$, and shifting $i$ by $m$ changes it by the sign $\varsigma_{i+m}=(-1)^{jk}\varsigma_i$, which has to be tracked in the proof. Three product-to-sum identities hold:
\[
L\Bigl[\frac{\gamma_i}{\Pi_i}\Bigr]=0,\qquad L\Bigl[\frac{i\gamma_i}{\Pi_i}\Bigr]=-\frac{\sin2t}{\Pi_i},\qquad
L\Bigl[\frac{\varsigma_i}{\Pi_i}\Bigr]=-\frac{2s^2}{\Pi_i}.
\]
For the first, $\varsigma_{i-2}\varsigma_{i+1}-\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_i=\varsigma_{i+2}\varsigma_{i-1}-\varsigma_i\varsigma_{i+1}=\tfrac12(\cos3t-\cos t)$, so
$1/(\varsigma_i\varsigma_{i+1})$ and $1/(\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_i)$ have the same residual $-s\sin2t/\Pi_i$ and their difference
$(\varsigma_{i-1}-\varsigma_{i+1})/\Pi_i=-2s\gamma_i/\Pi_i$ is annihilated. Hence
\[
u_i=\frac{\gamma_i}{\Pi_i},\qquad \chi_i=\frac{i\gamma_i-\cot t\,\varsigma_i}{\Pi_i}
\]
span the two-dimensional solution space of $L[\psi]=0$.

Both have poles exactly where $\Pi_i=0$, i.e.\ at $i\equiv p,p\pm1\pmod m$: on $[p+1,p+m-1]$ that means the two sites flanking the arc and no site of
the arc itself. The arc matrix is the full recursion with exactly the two out-of-range terms deleted, and both their coefficients vanish
($\varsigma_p=\varsigma_{p+m}=0$) while the products are finite and nonzero:
\[
A\,\psi|_{\mathrm{arc}}=-B_1[\psi]e_1-B_2[\psi]e_n,\qquad B_1[\psi]=\varsigma_p\psi_{p+1},\quad B_2[\psi]=\varsigma_{p+m}\psi_{p+m-1}.
\]
Each boundary term is of the form $0\cdot\infty$: for instance $B_1[u]=\varsigma_pu_{p+1}$ is the product of the vanishing coefficient $\varsigma_p$ and of $u_{p+1}$, which has a pole because $\Pi_{p+1}=\varsigma_p\varsigma_{p+1}\varsigma_{p+2}$ contains $\varsigma_p$. Its value is defined by continuity in a phase: with $\varsigma_i=\sin(it-\vartheta+\phi)$ the recursion and $u,\chi$ are regular for small $\phi\ne0$, and $B_1[u]=\gamma_{p+1}/(\varsigma_{p+1}\varsigma_{p+2})$ is continuous at $\phi=0$. The value is finite and nonzero, and it is these boundary terms that carry the determinant: they are why $u$ solves the recursion at every site of the arc and yet is not in the kernel of
the arc matrix $A$.

Since $pj\equiv1\pmod m$, $pt-\vartheta=(pj-1)k\pi/m$ is an integer multiple of $\pi$; write $pt-\vartheta=\nu_0\pi$ with $\nu_0\in\mathbb{Z}$, and put
$\nu=(-1)^{\nu_0}$, $\eta=(-1)^{jk}$ and $q=p+m$; then $\varsigma_{p+l}=\nu\sin lt$, $\gamma_{p+l}=\nu\cos lt$ and
$\varsigma_{q+l}=\nu\eta\sin lt$, $\gamma_{q+l}=\nu\eta\cos lt$. Evaluating the four boundary quantities,
\[
B_1[u]=\frac{\nu\cos t}{s\sin2t},\qquad B_1[\chi]=p\,B_1[u],\qquad B_2[u]=\eta B_1[u],\qquad B_2[\chi]=\eta\,q\,B_1[u].
\]
The combination $\zeta=B_1[\chi]u-B_1[u]\chi$, that is $\zeta_i=B_1[u][(p-i)\gamma_i+\cot t\,\varsigma_i]/\Pi_i$, kills the first boundary term, so
$A\zeta=-We_n$ with $W=B_1[\chi]B_2[u]-B_1[u]B_2[\chi]=\eta B_1[u]^2(p-q)=-m\eta B_1[u]^2$. The adjugate on the last column --- whose cofactor is the product
of the superdiagonal entries, $M=\prod_{i=p+4}^{p+m-1}\varsigma_i$ --- gives $\det A\cdot\zeta_1=(-1)^nWM$ without assuming $A$ invertible, and $\zeta_1\ne0$, so $\det A=(-1)^nWM/\zeta_1$, and at $i=p+2$ the bracket is
$\nu(-2\cos2t+2\cos^2t)=2\nu s^2$ while $\Pi_{p+2}=\nu s\sin2t\sin3t$, so $\zeta_1=2B_1[u]s/(\sin2t\sin3t)$. Writing $P=\prod_{i\in\mathrm{arc}}\varsigma_i$ and $M=-\eta\nu Ps/(\sin2t\sin3t)$, every
trigonometric factor cancels and $\det(\mathrm{arc}_\varsigma)=(-1)^nmP/(4s^2)=mP/(4s^2)$, because $n=m-3$ is even.

Finally, $\prod_{a=1}^{m-1}2\sin(a\pi/m)=m$ together with $\sin((m-l)t)=(-1)^{jk+1}\sin(lt)$ gives
\[
P=(-1)^{(1+jk)(m+1)/2}\,\frac m{2^{m-1}s^2},
\]
which is the $\varepsilon$-form. Row $i$ of $\mathrm{arc}_d$ is $(\varsigma_i/s^2)$ times row $i$ of $\mathrm{arc}_\varsigma$, since $d_{i\pm1}=\varsigma_i\varsigma_{i\pm2}/s^2$
and $2+2d_i=2\varsigma_i^2/s^2$; hence
\[
\det(\mathrm{arc}_d)=(P/s^{2n})\det(\mathrm{arc}_\varsigma)=\frac{mP^2}{4s^{2n+2}}=\frac{m^3}{2^{2m}s^{2m}},
\]
which involves only $P^2$ and is therefore free of every sign.
<!-- end proof-59 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:lblock}
Let $j=1$, $\vartheta=k\pi/m$ and $\rho_\nu=\sin\nu\vartheta$. The \emph{finite-$L$ block} is the block of $\hat J_0$ on the $L$-sites whose coordinates
have finite nonzero limits, here $L_3,\dots,L_{m-1}$. With its rows halved it is tridiagonal, with off-diagonals $-1$ and diagonal entry $2\rho_\nu^2/(\rho_{\nu-1}\rho_{\nu+1})$
at $L_{\nu+1}$, $\nu=2,\dots,m-2$, and the determinant of this half is $m\cot^2\vartheta$. Hence
\[
\det(\mathrm{block}_L)=2^{m-3}\,m\cot^2\vartheta\ne0 .
\]
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-60: body_md -->
Since $\rho_\nu^2-\rho_{\nu-1}\rho_{\nu+1}=\sin^2\vartheta$, the recurrence $y_{\nu-1}+y_{\nu+1}=2\rho_\nu^2/(\rho_{\nu-1}\rho_{\nu+1})\,y_\nu$ is that of
Lemma~\ref{lem:cotsol} with $\phi=0$, with solution $g_\nu=\nu\cot\nu\vartheta-\cot\vartheta$; $g_1=0$, $g_2=-\tan\vartheta$. The continuant on
$\nu=2,\dots,n$ is the solution with $y_1=0$, $y_2=1$ evaluated at $n+1$, i.e.\ $g_{n+1}/g_2$. At $n=m-2$, $\cot((m-1)\vartheta)=-\cot\vartheta$ gives
$g_{m-1}=-m\cot\vartheta$, so the determinant of the half block is $m\cot^2\vartheta$, nonzero since $m$ is odd. The block itself has $m-3$ rows, each twice that of the half block.
<!-- end proof-60 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:modp}
Let $m\ge5$ be prime and $\mathfrak p$ the ramified prime of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_m)$ above $m$, with residue field $\mathbb{F}_m$. Every entry of the
finite block of $\hat J_0$ is $\mathfrak p$-integral, and its reduction is \emph{independent of the class label $k$}. To describe the reduction, index the
$L$-sites by $\nu=n-j\in\{2,\dots,m-2\}$ and the $R$-sites by $x=i-p$. The $L$-sites form a single chain in $\nu$, because $L_m$ and $L_1$, at $\nu=-j$ and $1-j$, are adjacent. Then the $L$-column $\nu$ has diagonal $2\nu^2/(\nu^2-1)$ and off-diagonals $-1$.
The $R$-column $i$ has $2\min(i,l)$ on row $R_l$ and diagonal entry $2i+(i-p)^2-1$, the fan's $2i$ plus $(i-p)^2-1$. The exceptional entry $m$ on the $L_1$ diagonal reduces to $0$. In this description the rows of the $L$-sites are halved relative to $\hat J_0$, and the $L$--$R$ entries are those of the proof of the \hyperref[thm:modp]{finite-block lemma}. The determinant of the finite block of $\hat J_0$ is congruent modulo $\mathfrak p$ to $2^{m-3}$ times that of the reduced block, and $2$ is a unit.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-61: body_md -->
$v_{\mathfrak p}(\sin(a\pi/m))=1$ for $a\not\equiv0$ and $\cos(a\pi/m)$ is a unit, so each diagonal --- a ratio of two products of two sines,
$2\rho_n^2/(\rho_{n-1}\rho_{n+1})$ and $\varsigma_{i-1}\varsigma_{i+1}/s^2$ --- has valuation $0$; the off-diagonals of the finite block (the entries $-1$ and $2\min(i,l)$ of the description above, not $0$) are rational integers; and
$v_{\mathfrak p}(m)=m-1>0$. For the reductions, $\sin(ak\pi/m)/\sin(k\pi/m)\equiv(-1)^{k(a-1)}a$ and $\cos(a\pi/m)\equiv(-1)^a\pmod{\mathfrak p}$. In each
diagonal the total index shift is even, so the signs cancel and the $k$-dependence disappears:
$2\rho_n^2/(\rho_{n-1}\rho_{n+1})\equiv2\nu^2/(\nu^2-1)$, and
\[
d_i\equiv\frac{((i-1)j-1)((i+1)j-1)}{j^2}=\Bigl(i-\frac1{j}\Bigr)^2-1=(i-p)^2-1 .
\]
Equivalently $\varsigma_i/\sin(k\pi/m)\equiv(-1)^{kij}j(i-p)$: the whole $\varsigma$-chain linearises modulo $\mathfrak p$, up to sign.
<!-- end proof-61 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:modp}
For every prime $m\ge5$ and every placement $j\ne1$ with $\mathsf P(p)\not\equiv0\pmod m$, where $p=j^{-1}$ and $\mathsf P$ is the polynomial \eqref{eq:Ppoly}, the reduced block of the \hyperref[prop:modp]{reduction lemma} has
\[
\det\equiv-\tfrac12\,j^4\pmod m,
\]
a unit. Hence the determinant of the finite block is a $\mathfrak p$-adic unit, in particular nonzero.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-62: body_md -->
Write $B$ for the reduced finite block of the \hyperref[prop:modp]{reduction lemma}, $T$ for its $L$-block (on the finite $L$-sites), $M$ for its $R$-block (on the
finite $R$-sites, $M_{il}=2\min(i,l)+\delta_{il}((i-p)^2-1)$), and $X$, $Y$ for the two off-diagonal blocks, so that
$B=\begin{psmallmatrix}T&Y\\X&M\end{psmallmatrix}$.

\emph{The $L$-side.} The block $T$ is tridiagonal on $\nu=2,\dots,m-2$ with diagonal $2\nu^2/(\nu^2-1)$ and off-diagonals $-1$, independently
of $j$. The recursion
\begin{equation}
y_{\nu-1}+y_{\nu+1}=\frac{2\nu^2}{\nu^2-1}\,y_\nu
\label{eq:kerrec}
\end{equation}
that defines the kernel of $T$ (the \emph{kernel recursion}) has the two solutions $\psi_\nu=1/\nu$ and $\chi_\nu=\nu^2-1$, as one checks by substitution; their bracket (Casoratian) is
\[
[\psi,\chi]_{c,d}=\frac{(d-c)(d^2+cd+c^2-1)}{cd},\qquad\text{so}\qquad[\psi,\chi]_{a-1,a}=3
\]
for every $a$; hence a run of sites $[a,b]$ has continuant $[\psi,\chi]_{a-1,b+1}/3$, and in particular
\[
\det(\mathrm{run}[2,b])=\tfrac13b(b+2),\qquad \det(\mathrm{run}[a,m-2])\equiv\tfrac13a(a-2)\pmod m.
\]
Three consequences: the full run gives
$\det T\equiv0$; the vector $t_\nu=\nu^2-1$ solves the recursion and vanishes
at both boundary sites $\nu=\pm1$, so it spans $\ker T$; and the $(\nu,\nu')$ cofactor is $t_\nu t_{\nu'}/9$, so $\operatorname{adj}T=\tfrac19tt^{\mathsf T}$. The two
coupling sites $L_1$ and $L_m$ sit at $\nu=1-j$ and $\nu=-j$, \emph{adjacent}, so deleting both splits the run and
\[
D_2:=\det\bigl(T\smallsetminus\{L_1,L_m\}\bigr)=\frac{j(j-2)(j^2-1)}9=\frac{t_{1-j}t_{-j}}9 .
\]

\emph{The assembly.} With $\gamma_l=l$ and $\delta_l=-1$ on the finite $R$-sites, the off-diagonal blocks are
$Y=e_{L_1}\gamma^{\mathsf T}+e_{L_m}\delta^{\mathsf T}$ (an $L\times R$ block) and $X=2Y^{\mathsf T}$, so $YM^{-1}Y^{\mathsf T}$ is supported in the $2\times2$ corner
$(L_1,L_m)$. The Schur complement gives $\det B=\det M\cdot\det(T-2YM^{-1}Y^{\mathsf T})$, a perturbation of the singular $T$ in a $2\times2$ corner. Expanding it multilinearly with $\det T=0$ and $\operatorname{adj}T=\tfrac19tt^{\mathsf T}$ gives
\[
\det B=\det M\Bigl[-\tfrac29\bigl(t_1^2a+2t_1t_2b+t_2^2c\bigr)+\tfrac49t_1t_2(ac-b^2)\Bigr],\qquad t_1=j(j-2),\ t_2=j^2-1,
\]
in the three scalars $a=\gamma^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}\gamma$, $b=\gamma^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}\delta$, $c=\delta^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}\delta$.

\emph{The $R$-side.} The scalars $a,b,c$ require $M^{-1}\gamma$ and $M^{-1}\delta$, i.e.\ the solutions $z$ of $Mz=f$ for $f=\gamma,\delta$. Take the
second difference in $i$ of the equation $(Mz)_i=f_i$: since $2\min(i,l)$ has second difference $-2\delta_{il}$ in $i$, and $f_i=i$ or $-1$ has
second difference $0$, the non-local equation becomes the local three-term recursion $((x-1)^2-1)z_{i-1}-2x^2z_i+((x+1)^2-1)z_{i+1}=0$ in $x=i-p$,
the same recursion as for the kernel of the $d$-form reduced modulo $\mathfrak p$. Its solutions are $z_i=\alpha_r+\beta_r/\bigl((x-1)x(x+1)\bigr)$ on each of the runs $[1,p-2]$ and $[p+2,m]$, four parameters fixed by the four
undifferenced boundary equations at $l=1,p-2,p+2,m$ --- in each of which the $\min$-sum collapses, since
$\sum_i\min(i,l)z_i=\sum_{i\le l}iz_i+l\sum_{i>l}z_i$ telescopes against the run structure. For $p=2,3,m-2,m-1$ a run is empty or a single site, and some of the four equations coincide. Solving on the actual run structure with $m$ symbolic and then reducing gives the same rational functions of $p$. Every sum telescopes,
\[
\sum_{x=u}^v\frac1{(x-1)x(x+1)}=\tfrac12\Bigl[\tfrac1{(u-1)u}-\tfrac1{v(v+1)}\Bigr],\qquad
\sum_{x=u}^v\frac1{x^2-1}=\tfrac12\Bigl[\tfrac1{u-1}+\tfrac1u-\tfrac1v-\tfrac1{v+1}\Bigr],
\]
so $a,b,c$ are rational in $p$ with coefficients independent of $m$.

\emph{The determinant of $M$.} Write $M=F+D$ with $F=2\min(i,l)$ on the finite $R$-sites $y_1<\dots<y_n$ and $D=\operatorname{diag}((i-p)^2-1)$. The kernel $\min(y_k,y_l)$ has determinant $\prod_k(y_k-y_{k-1})$, with $y_0=0$. This is $4$, from the one gap of $4$ across the triple, except at $p=m-1$, where the triple
$R_{m-2},R_{m-1},R_m$ is at the end and the determinant is $1$. Its inverse is tridiagonal, with off-diagonal $-1/(y_{k+1}-y_k)$ and diagonal $1/(y_k-y_{k-1})+1/(y_{k+1}-y_k)$, the last diagonal entry being $1/(y_n-y_{n-1})$. So $\det M=\det F_1\det D\,\det G$ with $G=F_1^{-1}+2D^{-1}$, where $F_1=\min(y_k,y_l)$. By Wilson's theorem,
\[
\det D=\prod_{x=-(p-1)}^{-2}(x^2-1)\prod_{x=2}^{m-p}(x^2-1)\equiv\frac{(p-2)!\,p!}2\cdot\frac{p(p-1)}{2(p!)^2}=\frac14\pmod m .
\]
On each run $G$ is tridiagonal with off-diagonals $-1$ and diagonal $2x^2/(x^2-1)$, $x=i-p$, which is the kernel recursion \eqref{eq:kerrec}, with the solutions $1/x$ and $x^2-1$. So the determinant of a run $[u,v]$ is $C[u,v]=[\psi,\chi]_{u-1,v+1}/3$. The two runs $x\in[1-p,-2]$ and $x\in[2,m-p]$ are coupled by the entry $-\tfrac14$ across the gap. The diagonal is changed by $-\tfrac34$ at the two sites next to the gap and by $-1$ at the last site. Expanding in these changes and in the coupling, and reducing $m\equiv0$, gives a rational function of $p$. It is $\det M\equiv-\mathsf P/(24p^2(p-1))$, an identity of rational functions of $p$ obtained by computer algebra with the run lengths kept symbolic (Appendix~\ref{sec:repro}); as a check it was also evaluated directly at every placement for primes $m\le43$. At the edge placements the expansion is short. At
$p=2$ the left run is empty and $G$ is the run $x\in[2,m-2]$ with the changes $-\tfrac34$ at its first site and $-1$ at its last. By
multilinearity, $\det G=C[2,m-2]-\tfrac34C[3,m-2]-C[2,m-3]+\tfrac34C[3,m-3]\equiv0-\tfrac34-1+\tfrac34=-1$. So
$\det M\equiv4\cdot\tfrac14\cdot(-1)=-1=-\mathsf P(2)/96$. At $p=m-1$ there is no gap, $G$ is the run $x\in[2,m-2]$ with the change $-1$
at its last site, and $\det G=C[2,m-2]-C[2,m-3]\equiv-1$. So $\det M\equiv1\cdot\tfrac14\cdot(-1)=-\tfrac14=\mathsf P(-1)/48$. Both agree with
the general formula.

Reducing $m\equiv0$ and solving gives, with $\mathsf P(p)$ as above
(irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$),
\[
\det M=\frac{-\mathsf P}{24p^2(p-1)},\quad a=\frac{(p-1)(p^2-3)(p^4+p^2+4)}{2\mathsf P},\quad b=-\frac12-\frac{3p^2(p-1)}{\mathsf P},
\]
\[
c=\frac{4p^6-12p^5+13p^4-6p^3+p^2-12}{2(p-1)\mathsf P}.
\]
Substituting these into the assembly with $j=1/p$, the whole expression collapses identically as a rational function of $p$ to
$\det B=-1/(2p^4)=-j^4/2$.

At $j=2$ the site $L_1$ is a neighbour of the small $L$, and at $j=m-1$ so is $L_m$; the corresponding coupling site is then not in $T$. The formula still holds, because $t_1=j(j-2)=0$ at $j=2$ and $t_2=j^2-1\equiv0$ at $j=m-1$, which removes exactly the terms of the missing site. (At $j=2$ one has $p=(m+1)/2$.)
